title: HKFP Lens: A year of grief and inquiry, after Tai Po blaze
zh_title: HKFP 镜头：大埔大火后悲痛与质询的一年
summary: 宏福苑是一个建于 20 世纪 80 年代靠近吐露港的八座住宅屋村，拥有近 2,000 户家庭。消防处于 2026 年 11 月 26 日对宏福苑致命火灾作出反应。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。大埔综合楼的家庭辛辛苦苦买了一套舒适的公寓并养育了他们的孩子——其中一些人后来成为了公寓的业主，在同一片土地上养育了第三代。 2025 年 11 月 27 日，大埔致命火灾发生一天后，一名男子站在被毁坏的宏福苑屋苑前。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。
content:
宏福苑是一个建于 20 世纪 80 年代靠近吐露港的八座住宅屋村，拥有近 2,000 户家庭。消防处于 2026 年 11 月 26 日对宏福苑致命火灾作出反应。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。大埔综合楼的家庭辛辛苦苦买了一套舒适的公寓并养育了他们的孩子——其中一些人后来成为了公寓的业主，在同一片土地上养育了第三代。 2025 年 11 月 27 日，大埔致命火灾发生一天后，一名男子站在被毁坏的宏福苑屋苑前。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。它曾是香港梦的缩影，直到去年11月26日下午，社区发生致命火灾。由于当时正在进行大规模翻修工程，火势迅速蔓延到八栋用泡沫板和脚手架网覆盖的建筑物中的七栋。 2025 年 11 月 27 日，家人在辨认大埔大火受害者亲人的尸体后哭泣。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。在平常的工作日下午，老年人、儿童、全职妈妈、夜班后休息的爸爸以及家政工人都被困在火灾中。 2025年11月28日，在致命的大埔火灾中失去家园的人们暂时住在广福村的大厅，这是一个公共屋村，靠近遭受火灾的宏福苑。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。
这场大火最终夺去了 168 人的生命，导致数千人无家可归，标志着充满无尽悲伤、愤怒和疑问的一年的开始。香港摄影记者回顾了过去一年的照片，我们的摄影记者跟踪了香港数十年来最严重火灾后的重大事件和事态发展。火灾发生后，数以千计的香港人动员线上线下支持受害者。照片显示，2025 年 11 月 27 日，志愿者在宏福法院附近集会，设立摊位，提供免费食物、衣服和生活用品。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。 2025 年 12 月 1 日，人们在大埔地铁里阅读对火灾受害者的支持信息。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。 2025年12月5日，数千人献花和玩偶，哀悼宏福苑火灾中的遇难者。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。 2025 年 12 月 1 日，一名学生在哀悼死者时流下了眼泪。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。 2025 年 12 月 1 日，道士为死者举行仪式。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。火灾发生后，宏福苑部分建筑物发现非阻燃脚手架网。后来被证实是导致火势迅速蔓延的原因之一。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。火灾发生后不久，立法会于 2025 年 12 月 7 日举行选举。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。 11月底，香港警务处命令义工拆除广福村平台的临时补给站。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。
2025 年 12 月 19 日，消防员聚集在一起哀悼在大埔火灾中因公殉职的消防员何伟豪。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。悲剧发生后，2026年1月16日，宏福苑居民江志强（左一）、李家强（中）和叶家驹（右一）回忆起居民如何徒劳地试图报告火灾风险。他们敦促政府调查火灾原因。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。 2026年2月5日，独立委员会召开了上市前第一次公开会议。

【原文 English Original】
Wang Fuk Court, an eight-block residential estate built in the 1980s near Tolo Harbour, was home to nearly 2,000 households. The Fire Services Department responds to the fatal blaze at Wang Fuk Court on November 26, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. The families at the Tai Po complex had worked hard to purchase a comfortable flat and raise their children – some of whom later became flat owners, bringing up a third generation on the same estate. On November 27, 2025, one day after the fatal Tai Po fire started, a man stands in front of the ravaged Wang Fuk Court housing estate. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. It was the epitome of the Hong Kong dream, until a fatal fire struck the community on the afternoon of November 26 last year. The blaze quickly spread through seven of the eight buildings which were covered with foam board and scaffolding nets, as a large-scale renovation project was underway at the time. On November 27, 2025, family members cry after identifying the bodies of loved ones who fell victim to the fatal Tai Po fire. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Seniors, children, full-time moms, dads who were taking a break after night shifts, and domestic workers were among those trapped in the fire during the otherwise ordinary weekday afternoon. On November 28, 2025, people who lost their homes in the deadly Tai Po fire stay temporarily in the hall of Kwong Fuk Estate, a public housing estate near the fire-ravaged Wang Fuk Court. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. The fire eventually claimed 168 lives, left thousands homeless, and marked the start of a year of relentless grief, anger and questions. HKFP looks back at images from the past year, as our photojournalist followed the major events and developments surrounding the aftermath of Hong Kong’s worst fire in decades. Following the fire, thousands of Hongkongers mobilised online and offline to support victims. The photo shows volunteers rallying to set up booths to provide free food, clothes and daily necessities near Wang Fuk court on November 27, 2025. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. People read supportive messages for the fire victims in a subway in Tai Po on December 1, 2025. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. On December 5, 2025, thousands of people presented flowers and dolls to mourn those killed in the Wang Fuk Court fire. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. A student sheds tears while mourning the deceased on December 1, 2025. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Taoist priests hold rituals for the deceased on December 1, 2025. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Following the fire, non-flame retardant scaffolding nets were identified on some buildings of Wang Fuk Court. They were later confirmed as one of the causes leading to the rapid spread of the blaze. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Soon after the fire, the Legislative Council held elections on December 7, 2025. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. In late November, the Hong Kong Police Force orders volunteers to remove the makeshift supply stations at a podium of Kwong Fuk Estate. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. On December 19, 2025, firefighters gathered and mourned Ho Wai Ho, a firefighter who died in the line of duty during the Tai Po fire. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Following the tragedy, on January 16, 2026, Wang Fuk Court residents Jason Kong (first from left), Garrick Lee (middle) and Yip Ka-kui (first from right) recalled how residents made futile attempts to flag fire risks. They urged the government to investigate the causes of the fire. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. On February 5, 2026, an independent committee held the first public meeting before starting hearings to probe the Tai Po fire. Judge David Lok (3rd left), chair of the committee, is seen walking out of the hearing. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Tony Tsui (centre right), the former chair of Wang Fuk Court owners’ corporation management committee, leaves after attending a public hearing to probe the Tai Po deadly fire on March 20, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. A Wang Fuk Court resident talks with the press after attending a public hearing on March 26, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. On April 20, 2026, nearly half a year after the fire, Wang Fuk Court residents are allowed to return to their fire-ravaged homes to retrieve belongings. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Wang Fuk Court residents return home to retrieve belongings on May 4, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. A resident of Wang Fuk Court is seen in his fire-ravaged flat as he looks to retrieve personal belongings on April 23, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. A Wang Fuk Court resident finds his wedding rings in his flat at Wang Fuk Court on April 20, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. On July 19, 2026, the administrator of the Wang Fuk Court housing estate hosted a special owners’ meeting at four different venues, after a months-long wait. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Jason Kong, a flat owner of Wang Fuk Court and a former member of the owners’ board, was arrested over alleged fraud in May 2026 and charged in August after he organised a petition for a homeowners’ meeting. The photo shows Kong leaving the Shatin Law Courts Buildings on September 1, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Nearly one year after the tragedy, Hong Kong leader John Lee led top officials to bow in apology as he introduced reforms related to the Tai Po fire. The press conference was held on October 29, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Roman Catholic bishop Joseph Ha offers blessings to Wang Fuk Court residents during a mass at the Immaculate Heart of Mary Church on November 15, 2026. The church revised the theme of the mass from one dedicated to the fire victims to one for “remembering all who had passed away over the past year.” The change came after they reportedly faced police enquiries. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. A fire-ravaged Wang Fuk Court flat is seen with banners stating “I love Wang Fuk” and “I want to move back” on the window. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. A community art exhibition by NGO Forget Thee Not in Central called “Life Goes On” on November 25, 2026. Several Wang Fuk Court residents participated in the show, expressing their feelings and experiences through text and photos. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Wang Fuk Court on November 19, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP.

title: Police officer fined HK$8,000 for dangerous driving as doctors unable to link woman’s death to crash
zh_title: 医生无法将女子死亡与车祸联系起来，警员因危险驾驶被罚款港币8,000元
summary: 一名香港警察因去年圣诞节发生车祸而危险驾驶，被罚款8000港元，并吊销驾驶执照15个月。然而，法庭周三获悉，医生无法确定碰撞是否导致一名妇女死亡。东部裁判法院。照片：何凯莉/HKFP。据报道，31岁的叶家豪周三在东区裁判法院承认一项危险驾驶罪名，该起事故于去年12月25日发生在跑马地摩理臣山道东行线和南行线交界处。
content:
一名香港警察因去年圣诞节发生车祸而危险驾驶，被罚款8000港元，并吊销驾驶执照15个月。然而，法庭周三获悉，医生无法确定碰撞是否导致一名妇女死亡。东部裁判法院。照片：何凯莉/HKFP。据当地媒体报道，31岁的叶家豪周三在东区裁判法院承认一项危险驾驶罪名，该起事故于去年12月25日发生在跑马地摩利臣山道东行线和南行线交界处。法庭获悉，事件发生时，这名警官正在下班，他没有在“停车”标志前停车，结果撞上了一名 71 岁女性驾驶的另一辆车。尽管现场没有被送往医院，但该女子在感觉不适后寻求医疗救治，并于一周后死亡。叶先生最初被指控“危险驾驶致人死亡”，最高可判处10年监禁和5万港元罚款，但检察官在8月将罪名降级为“危险驾驶”，最高可判处25,000港元罚款和三年监禁。周三，裁判官朱加里询问为何检方在叶氏案件中没有提及该女子的死亡。双方均向法庭表示，医生无法确定她是否因碰撞而死亡。
辩方称，叶先生在警队服务了11年，是一名“受人尊敬的警察”，并敦促法院宽大处理，处以罚款和吊销驾驶执照六个月。裁判官指出，叶先生在2021年因超速定罪，当时他的驾驶执照被暂停九个月，并表示需要更重的罚款作为威慑。他对被告罚款8,000港元，吊销其驾照15个月，并责令其自费完成驾驶改进课程。

【原文 English Original】
A Hong Kong police officer has been fined HK$8,000 and had his driving licence suspended for 15 months for dangerous driving over a car crash last Christmas. However, a court heard on Wednesday that doctors could not determine whether the collision had caused a woman’s death. Eastern Magistrates’ Courts. Photo: Kelly Ho/HKFP. Yip Ka-ho, 31, pleaded guilty on Wednesday at the Eastern Magistrates’ Courts to one count of dangerous driving over the incident, which occurred on December 25 last year at the junction of the eastbound and southbound lanes of Morrison Hill Road in Happy Valley, according to local media. The officer, who was off duty at the time of the incident, failed to stop at a “stop” sign and crashed into another vehicle driven by a 71-year-old woman, the court heard. Although she was not taken to hospital at the scene, the woman subsequently sought medical care after feeling unwell and died a week later. Yip was initially charged with “causing death by dangerous driving,” which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years’ imprisonment and a HK$50,000 fine, but prosecutors downgraded the charge to “dangerous driving” in August – an offence punishable by a fine of up to HK$25,000 and three years in jail. Magistrate Gary Chu on Wednesday asked why prosecutors did not mention the woman’s death in the case against Yip. Both parties told the court that doctors could not determine whether she died because of the collision. The defence submitted that Yip was a “well-regarded police officer” after 11 years of service in the force and urged the court to show leniency by imposing a fine and a six-month driving licence suspension. The magistrate noted that Yip had a speeding conviction in 2021, when his licence was suspended for nine months, and said a heavier fine was needed as a deterrent. He fined the defendant HK$8,000, suspended his licence for 15 months, and ordered him to complete a driving improvement course at his own expense.

title: Hong Kong rules out government-run matchmaking services amid low birth rate, delayed marriages
zh_title: 由于出生率低、晚婚，香港排除政府经营的婚介服务

content:
一名政府官员表示，香港当局不会效仿新加坡等国家推出婚介服务来解决晚婚和低出生率问题。一对情侣在西九龙的港口接吻。资料照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。民政及青年事务局局长麦家丽周三在书面答复立法会议员朱汉基有关家庭政策的问题时表示，政府知道其他司法管辖区已推出“官方或准官方的婚介活动”。 “鉴于各地社会背景、人口结构、制度体系等差异，相关经验不一定适用于香港。”麦说。她补充说，从约会到结婚的转变涉及“许多不同的因素和个人考虑”。香港中环斑马线上的人们。照片：香港政府一站通。 “是否组建家庭的最终决定并不一定取决于是否组织相亲活动，”她说。与许多发达城市一样，香港近几十年来也出现了推迟结婚的趋势。 2006年，25岁至29岁之间的未婚男性比例为81%。到2021年，这一比例已增至87%。对于同一年龄段的女性，这一数字从 68% 上升至 76%。从未结婚的人数也有所增加，而登记结婚的人数却有所下降。情人节相亲？
9月，新加坡政府为政府工作人员试行了一项婚介服务。该平台名为FirstDate，承诺结束“刷卡疲劳”并提供“不同的约会方式”。它向年龄在 21 岁至 45 岁之间为政府工作的人开放。根据 FirstDate 的网站，用户必须使用政府颁发的身份证明进行注册，并填写一份调查问卷，询问他们的“兴趣、习惯、价值观和偏好”。朱询问香港是否也会举办“相亲节活动，并允许参加者向政府报销部分相亲费用”。新加坡。照片：Virginia Chien，来自 Pexels。他还建议政府可以将此类举措与情人节结合起来，并补贴非营利组织和地区团体提供约会活动。楚说，社区中“私人约会服务”的质量参差不齐，并补充说，这削弱了“单身人士使用这些服务的信心”。香港生育率下降一直是政府近年来的政策重点。 2023年，推出“婴儿奖金”计划，为每个新生儿的家庭发放2万港元。 9月，政府将奖励金额提高至3万港元，并增加了家长的税收优惠。香港民意研究所2024年的一项调查发现，香港的教育制度和政治是香港人不想要孩子的主要原因。

【原文 English Original】
Hong Kong authorities will not follow countries like Singapore in launching matchmaking services to address delayed marriages and low birth rates, a government official has said. A couple kiss by the harbour in West Kowloon. File photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak said in a written reply on Wednesday to lawmaker Roy Chu’s questions about family policies that the government was aware that other jurisdictions had launched “official or quasi-official matchmaking activities.” “Given the differences in social backgrounds, demographic structures, and institutional systems across different places, the relevant experience may not be necessarily applicable to Hong Kong,” Mak said. She added that the move from dating to marriage involves “many different factors and personal considerations.” People at a zebra crossing in Central, Hong Kong. Photo: GovHK. “The ultimate decision on whether to start a family does not necessarily hinge on whether matchmaking activities are organised,” she said. Like many developed cities, Hong Kong has seen a trend of marriage postponement in recent decades. The percentage of unmarried men aged between 25 and 29 was 81 per cent in 2006. By 2021, it had increased to 87 per cent. For women of the same age group, the figure rose from 68 per cent to 76 per cent. The number of people who have never been married has also increased, while the number of registered marriages has fallen. Valentine’s Day matchmaking? In September, the Singapore government piloted a matchmaking service for government workers. Named FirstDate, the platform promised an end to “swipe fatigue” and a “different approach” to dating. It was open to people aged between 21 and 45 who work for the government. According to FirstDate’s website, users must sign up with their government-issued identification and fill in a questionnaire that asks about their “interests, habits, values and preferences.” Chu asked if Hong Kong would also organise “matchmaking festival activities and allow participants to claim reimbursement from the Government for part of their dating expenses.” Singapore. Photo: Virginia Chien, via Pexels. He also suggested the government could combine such initiatives with Valentine’s Day, as well as subsidise non-profit-making and district groups to offer dating activities. The quality of “private dating services” in the community varies, Chu said, adding that this undermines the “confidence of single persons in using them.” Hong Kong’s falling fertility rates have been a policy focus for the government in recent years. In 2023, it introduced a “baby bonus” scheme, giving HK$20,000 to families for every newborn. In September, the government raised the incentive to HK$30,000, and also increased tax concessions for parents. A 2024 survey by the Hong Kong Public Opinion Research Institute found that the city’s education system and politics were the main reasons why Hongkongers did not want children.

title: Local Elections to set Stage for Taiwan’s Next President
zh_title: 地方选举为台湾下任总统奠定基础
summary: 摘要：台湾 11 月 28 日的地方选举重点关注民生问题，包括交通、住房负担能力、基础设施和社会福利。他们还将塑造 2028 年总统选举之前的政治格局。结果将反映选民对赖清德总统领导下的现任民进党政府的满意度。强劲的表现将表明该党能够在台湾南部的传统据点之外维持支持。国民党目前拥有 22 名最高前任中的 16 名
content:
摘要：台湾 11 月 28 日的地方选举重点关注民生问题，包括交通、住房负担能力、基础设施和社会福利。他们还将塑造 2028 年总统选举之前的政治格局。结果将反映选民对赖清德总统领导下的现任民进党政府的满意度。强劲的表现将表明该党能够在台湾南部的传统据点之外维持支持。国民党目前占据 22 个最高行政职位中的 16 个。台北、新北和台中的关键选举结果将影响2028年的候选人名单，其中包括现任台中市长卢秀妍和台北市长蒋万安。台湾人民党 (TPP) 正在合作推翻民进党候选人，不过结果将决定这种合作是否持续到 2028 年。北京的干预并不是这次选举的主要话题，但它提供了竞选资金，创建了机器人账户来影响媒体叙事，并对与民进党结盟的个人进行跨国镇压。台湾将于11月28日举行四年来首次地方选举。
近2000万符合资格的成年人（20岁或以上）将投票选出从市长、县长到当地村长的九个职位的代表，因此俗称“九合一选举”。地方选举通常关注基础设施发展和电价等民生问题。今年也不例外，候选人强调解决生活成本和生活质量问题的政策。台湾的党派政治不太关注意识形态，而是关注实际问题和政治人物，因此候选人的日常媒体露面和政策辩论在选民心目中的影响力更大。房间里的大象是迫在眉睫的总统选举，定于 2028 年初举行，九合一选举将有助于奠定基础。这是因为，无论哪个政党在 11 月份脱颖而出，都将为在地方一级获得多数席位的政党提供动力，而且地方政治也为通往国家办公室提供了共同的垫脚石。该国的集权化，加上其规模较小，为市长——特别是直辖市的市长——提供了一条相当直接的通往国家级权力的道路。其强大的媒体环境，对地方政客的频繁报道，也支持了他们的崛起。
民生问题候选人竞选进入本周期，国民党占据了22个地方高级行政职位中的16个。这使其有些脆弱，因为它有更多席位可以失去，包括新北、台中和彰化等摇摆城市和县。而民进党则拥有五个辖区，均位于传统据点南方。尽管民进党可能会获得更多好处，但其最近在地方选举中的记录值得警惕。该党在2018年惨败，2022年再次表现不佳，导致台湾前总统蔡英文辞去党主席职务（台湾电视台[台视]，2022年11月26日）。金门县是唯一的另一个县，由曾短暂加入台湾人民党（TPP）的无党派人士控制。对于第三

【原文 English Original】
Executive Summary: Taiwan’s local elections on November 28 are focused on bread-and-butter issues, including transportation, housing affordability, infrastructure, and social welfare. They will also shape the political landscape leading up to the 2028 presidential elections. Results will reflect voter satisfaction with the incumbent Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) administration under President Lai Ching-te. A strong showing will be a sign that the party is able to maintain support beyond its traditional stronghold in Southern Taiwan. The Kuomintang (KMT) currently holds 16 of the 22 top executive posts. Outcomes of key races in Taipei, New Taipei, and Taichung will affect its pool of candidates for 2028, including current Taichung mayor Lu Shiow-yen and Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an. The Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) is cooperating to unseat DPP candidates, though results will determine whether that cooperation continues through to 2028. Beijing’s interference is not a major talking point in this election, but it has provided campaign funds, created bot accounts to influence media narratives, and engaged in transnational repression against individuals aligned with the DPP. Taiwan is set to hold local elections for the first time in four years on November 28. Nearly 20 million eligible adults (those aged 20 or older) will vote for representatives in nine positions ranging from city mayors and county magistrates down to local village chiefs—hence the colloquial name the “nine-in-one elections” (九合一選舉). Local elections typically focus on bread-and-butter issues such as infrastructure development and electricity prices. This year is no different, with candidates emphasizing policies to tackle cost-of-living and quality-of-life concerns. Partisan politics in Taiwan is less focused on ideology than on practical issues and political personalities, and so candidates’ day-to-day media appearances and policy debates carry more weight in the minds of voters. The elephant in the room is the looming presidential election, scheduled for early 2028, for which the nine-in-one elections will help set the stage. This is because candidates who come out on top in November will provide momentum for whichever party manages to secure a majority at the local level, and because local politics also provides a common stepping stone to national office. The country’s centralization, coupled with its small size, provides mayors—specifically those of special municipalities (直轄市)—a fairly direct path to national-level prominence. Its robust media environment, which provides frequent coverage of local-level politicians, also supports their ascendance. Candidates Campaign on Bread-and-Butter Issues Going into this cycle, the Kuomintang (KMT) holds 16 of 22 top local executive posts. This makes it somewhat vulnerable, as it has more seats to lose, including swing cities and counties such as New Taipei, Taichung, and Changhua. The Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), meanwhile, holds five jurisdictions, all of which are located in the South, a traditional stronghold. Although the DPP might have more to gain, its recent record in local elections is a cautionary one. The party suffered a heavy defeat in 2018 and another poor showing in 2022 led to former Taiwan president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) resigning as party chair ( Taiwan Television [TTV] , November 26, 2022). Kinmen, the only other county, is held by an independent that briefly joined the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP). For these elections, the TPP has decided to cooperate with the KMT in a “blue-white coalition” (藍白合), and is contesting only the Chiayi County magistrate election. Local campaigns tend to focus on the day-to-day issues that fall within the purview of local governments, such as urban renewal and transportation development. Housing affordability is a major issue in Taiwan, especially in the north, and some candidates have unveiled plans to construct more public housing, with priority given to young people who do not own property ( United Daily News [UDN] , November 20). Others are promising new transportation infrastructure. In New Taipei, for instance, KMT candidate Lee Shu-chuan (李四川) has proposed a metro line crossing the Dahan River and light-rail connections linking Linkou, Bali, and Tamsui with the nearby Taoyuan Metro network ( Mirror Media , July 31). In Taichung, KMT candidate Johnny Chiang (江啟臣), who is currently deputy speaker of the Legislative Yuan, is proposing a “20-minute city” (20分鐘生活圈) in which residents can access essential services close to home. His opponent, DPP legislator Ho Hsin-chun (何欣純), is running on a platform to reduce traffic congestion and make improvements to the city’s transportation system ( UDN , September 15; Ho Hsin-chun Campaign Office , accessed November 12). Demographic challenges are also prominent. Taiwan has had declining birth rates and an aging population since the 2010s, but people are only now starting to feel the economic impact of these changes. As municipal governments are responsible for much of the service delivery for social welfare, candidates are responding to a growing demand for childcare, maternal health services, hospice care, and migrant caregiver policies. These issues are particularly relevant to younger voters, who face rising housing costs and the financial burden of supporting older family members ( Now News , November 23). Alongside the nine-in-one elections, voters are asked to decide on specific national issues at the polls. Unusually, the franchise is expanded for these referenda to those aged 18 and 19. This year, the issue on the ballot is whether to use nuclear power to revitalize the economy, overturning the Tsai Ing-wen government’s “nuclear-free homeland” (非核家園) policy. Nuclear energy has been a topic of perennial political contestation in Taiwan. The latest referendum—the fourth on the issue since 2018—comes on the heels of Taiwan becoming “nuclear-free” in 2025, when its last reactor reached the end of its 40-year lifespan ( China Brief , August 23, 2024; Taiwan Central News Agency [CNA] , November 12). President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) has previously indicated openness to restarting nuclear energy production, saying that he “does not wish to exclude any particular energy source due to ideology” (不要因為意識形態，而排除任何一種能源) ( UDN , October 16). Elections to set Stage for 2028 The upcoming election will likely have a significant impact on how parties approach 2028. This is particularly true for the KMT, who will use the vote to assess candidates’ viability for the country’s highest office. Lai will likely attempt to seek a second term for the DPP, while the TPP will have choices to make depending on both its own performance and that of the KMT. The six special municipalities (直轄市)—Taipei, New Taipei, Taoyuan, Taichung, Tainan, and Kaohsiung—are politically the most consequential. These cities account for the majority of the population and of economic activity on the island, and their mayors have greater national visibility than other local officials. Among these, the Taipei mayor is the most prominent. Three of five previous presidents had previously served in this role, while others have gone on to chair their respective political parties ( GTI , October 30). Some see the KMT incumbent, Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安), as a torchbearer for a younger KMT, and pundits—including former 2024 vice presidential candidate Jaw Shaw-kong (趙少康)—have speculated about a 2028 presidential run ( TTV News , October 20). But even though Taipei is traditionally a stronghold for the KMT, Chiang has seen his polling numbers slip to an innovative campaign by DPP challenger Shen Pao-yang (沈伯洋; a.k.a. Puma Shen). Shen, whose campaign is colloquially called “ocean current” (洋流), punning on a homophone of his name, has overcome a more than 20-point deficit over the last six months, making the race too close to call ( SET News , May 7; TVBS , May 27; Initium Media , November 17).  [1] His popularity has even led other DPP candidates to vie for joint appearances, in the hope of boosting their own chances ( Liberty Times [LTN] , November 23). Taichung will be a key bellwether for the KMT, where incumbent mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) has reached the end of her second term. The party hopes to retain the mayoralty and preserve Lu’s political legacy, as she is widely considered a presidential contender ( Storm Media , September 15). If Johnny Chiang successfully defends the seat, his win would preserve the KMT’s political patronage network in central Taiwan and allow Lu to claim credit for managing the succession and for good governance. Conversely, a DPP victory would weaken her position and damage her chances for a 2028 bid, while potentially strengthening the standing of other figures, such as KMT chairperson Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文). New Taipei City, the country’s most populous administrative division, is home to four million people, making it a key battleground. The DPP last governed the city in 2005, under Su Tseng-chang (蘇貞昌), who later served as premier in both the Chen Shui-bian (陳水扁) and Tsai Ing-wen administrations. His daughter, Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧), is running as the DPP candidate against KMT candidate Lee Shu-chuan. Su Chiao-hui has touted her experience as a sitting legislator and announced family-oriented neonatal and hospice care policies, while Lee, drawing on his technocratic background as a civil engineer and his long stints as deputy mayor of Taipei, New Taipei, and Kaohsiung, has focused on urban renewal projects ( CNA , August 19; Su Chiao-hui New Taipei City Mayoral Campaign Office , accessed November 10). Polling numbers indicate both candidates are within a few percentage points of each other and the race has been described as a toss-up ( Legislator Lin Chu-yin , November 13; TTV , November 16). A DPP win would likely shock the KMT, and improve the party’s assessments of its chances for 2028. In Kaohsiung, a southern port metropolis of 2.5 million people, both candidates are sitting legislators. In the campaign, the DPP’s Lai Jui-lung (賴瑞隆) has attacked the KMT’s Ko Chi-en (柯志恩) and her party’s legislative caucus for passing amendments to the revenue allocation law, which controls how much funding municipalities receive from the central government. Kaohsiung was one of the losers after the reallocation, leading to accusations from the pan-Green camp that the amendments are the latest manifestation of the sentiment that resources and capital often “prioritize the North at the expense of the South” (重北輕南) in Taiwan ( FTV News , August 29).  [2] The Kaohsiung City Government has argued that the city needs more funds because it is in the midst of industrial upgrading and that it has borne the brunt of environmental pollution arising from its massive industrial economy ( Kaohsiung City Government , December 21, 2024). Current polling indicates a DPP win is likely in Kaohsiung ( Radio Taiwan International , November 16). Outside of the special municipalities, Changhua stands out as the most crucial race. The largest county by population, it is home to 1.25 million people. The primary process for selecting candidates was marred by controversy, mainly arising from factional politics. The KMT candidate, Wei Cheng-ping (魏政平), does not come from the factions system and is seen as a compromise, which has led to local resentment against Cheng Li-wun’s electoral strategy (Cheng is personally acting as the head of Wei’s campaign) ( UDN , October 13). The DPP candidate, Chen Su-yueh (陳素月), has the backing of some local factions, but faces a split pan-Green ticket. DPP Changhua County Party Chapter chair Chiu Chien-fu (邱建富) is also running, but as an independent. Polls have Chen in the lead, but 40 percent of Changhua voters are still undecided ( CNA ; UDN , October 19). (Source: Author research) At the national level, the DPP’s primary concern is whether it can maintain its electoral coalition after holding the presidency for three consecutive terms. Lai’s 2024 victory, with 40 percent of the popular vote, fell short of a majority. The ensuing lack of control over the legislature has rendered him unable to effectively enact his agenda. Partisan fights over the central budget, defense, and legislative power have resulted in legislative gridlock throughout much of 2025 and 2026. When coupled with the failure of a set of recall campaigns to remove KMT legislators in mid-2025, the party’s legitimacy may have suffered in the eyes of voters ( China Brief , July 7, 2025). A strong DPP showing in northern and central Taiwan would show that the party can maintain support beyond its traditional southern strongholds. Optimistic projections for the DPP describe the party as “sitting on three, looking at four, and gazing at five” (坐三望四看五) of the six special municipalities. This refers to the party having a good chance of taking Tainan, Kaohsiung, and New Taipei, an even chance of taking Taipei, and an outside chance in Taichung ( LTN , November 12). Conversely, a poor performance could reinforce perceptions of public dissatisfaction with the administration and may spell trouble for Lai’s reelection bid. The elections may help clarify the TPP’s future, too. In 2024, presidential candidate Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) received roughly 26 percent of the vote, while his party secured just over 22 percent of the party-list vote. The TPP has struggled with an identity crisis since then, however, and under the leadership of chairperson Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌) has closely aligned itself with KMT legislative priorities and pursued a confrontational approach with the DPP. Its decision to cooperate with the KMT in the 2026 local elections may be a marriage of convenience where both opposition parties coordinate to improve their chances of defeating DPP candidates. A strong KMT performance could encourage the two opposition parties to pursue another joint presidential ticket in 2028, though the coalition is already fraying in some places, raising the chances that they will fail to coordinate effectively, just as happened in 2024 ( CNA , September 9). Two alternative options involve the TPP either concluding that its independent electoral base remains sufficiently large to justify fielding its own candidate, or deciding to enter a quid-pro-quo arrangement where it runs a joint ticket with the KMT in exchange for political or legislative concessions. Persistent PRC Pressure Through Interference and Transnational Repression Cross-Strait relations are not a priority issue for this election, but attempts by the People’s Republic of China (PRC) to interfere, including through ongoing acts of transnational repression, loom large over the election. Candidates have had different reasons for avoiding the issue. DPP candidates may be downplaying the issue to shake the label that the party simply campaigns on the platform of “protecting Taiwan through opposing the PRC” (抗中保台). KMT and TPP candidates, conversely, may avoid the subject because PRC electoral interference efforts often benefit their candidates. For instance, a TPP candidate for Taoyuan City councilor, Chou Hsiao-yun (周曉芸), was recently indicted for allegedly taking campaign funds from Chinese Communist Party (CCP) officials and collecting photos of Taiwanese citizens for PRC bot farms to deploy to influence electoral narratives ( SET News ; KNews , November 20; Taipei Times , November 24). PRC disinformation campaigns appear to have stepped up this year. Taiwan’s National Security Bureau recorded more than 2.5 million instances of misleading online content between January and September, compared to 1.7 million during the same period in 2025. These campaigns have targeted issues such as energy policy, food safety, defense, candidate platforms, and local infrastructure development ( TaiSounds , October 21). The PRC also seems to have escalated its transnational repression to include physical intimidation. Recent cases include an assault on comedian Huang Yi-hao (黃逸豪) that is alleged to have been directed by PRC-based instigators, a smear campaign against entertainment personality Tsai Kang-yong (蔡康永) for attending a Puma Shen rally, and an outstanding arrest warrant and cash bounty against Shen himself. These incidents remind voters that the PRC remains a factor, even in an election mainly fought over domestic priorities ( UDN , October 7; China Brief , November 5).  [3] Conclusion The results of the nine-in-one elections will predominantly reflect voter sentiment on quality-of-life issues and political personalities. They will also provide a temperature check on the Lai administration, and signal whether voters are satisfied after a decade of DPP rule. Shifting political alliances and factional politics will likely dominate the political landscape for the next two years, as parties assess the viability of their potential candidates. The results will also have significant implications for cross-Strait relations. A strong KMT performance could strengthen the party’s argument that Taiwanese voters favor a less confrontational approach to Beijing and improve the political standing of candidates advocating renewed cross-Strait dialogue. A strong DPP performance would instead lend credence to the party’s belief that Taiwanese voters are skeptical of the KMT’s more dovish approach to Beijing. [2] Political parties in Taiwan and their allies are referred to in different colors. The DPP is the Green camp (綠營) or pan-Green camp (泛綠), the KMT is the Blue camp (藍營) or pan-Blue camp (泛藍), and the TPP’s colors are white. [3] The impact of Beijing’s traditional united front activities appears more limited in scope. Twenty-five “Chinese spouses” (中配)—that is, immigrants from the PRC who have acquired Taiwanese citizenship through marriage—registered as candidates in the local elections, with some candidates failing to provide evidence that they have abandoned their PRC citizenship ( LTN , September 8; TaiSounds , October 1). 摘要：在党的二十大上，以前组织部部长陈曦为中心的清华系是习近平周围的权力极之一。随着中央政治局委员陈吉宁被立案调查，清华13名正部级以上官员中，有7人被立案调查、下台或撤职。派系的崩溃是从陈汐的失宠开始的。 6月，习近平破格保留的中央党校校长职务在陈曦任期结束前由蔡奇接任。一个失宠的派系没有人为其担保，并担任其他人觊觎的职位，从而加速其崩溃。该集团的核心成员陈吉宁被空降到上海，在那里的四年里几乎没有什么表现。对人工智能的大量投资并没有取得重大突破。这使得习近平很容易将他视为五中全会全面从严治党运动的反面典型。 11月24日，新华社发布消息称，中共中央政治局委员、上海市委书记陈吉宁涉嫌严重违纪违法，目前正接受中央纪律检查委员会组织调查（新华社11月24日电）。上海市委当晚表示支持这一决定（上海市人民政府，11月24日）。
陈是继2006年陈良宇之后第四位落马的第20届政治局委员，也是第二位被落马的上海市委书记（中国网，2006年9月25日）。他曾被广泛视为2027年下半年党的第二十一次代表大会政治局常委的竞争者（华尔街日报，11月24日）。同日，原西安市委书记方红卫与陈清华一样，均是清华大学毕业生，被起诉（财新网，2021年11月7日；新华社，11月24日）。陈吉宁的事业与习近平总书记的清华同学陈希密不可分。陈曦留在了大学，并通过共青团和学生事务晋升为校党委书记。 2013年起，主持中组部日常工作，后出任中组部部长（人民网，2017年10月25日；路透社，2022年10月10日）。他以清华为基地，建立了一个高层网络，被称为“清华帮”。 [1] 2023年，本应完全退休的他却破格留任中央党校校长，从而保留了影响力（人民网，2017年10月25日；联合早报，6月5日）。但从那时起，由于一些成员受到控制或调查，该集团逐渐衰落。 6月，陈曦在任期届满前突然交出国家主席职务（《联合早报》6月5日）。
同月，据信与陈曦关系密切的北京政协主席魏小东受到调查（新华社，6 月 6 日；中国主义，6 月 8 日）。陈吉宁的倒台可能标志着清华系的终结。清华派大半出局，陈吉宁的每次升迁，都追随着陈曦的位置。陈吉宁在2006年和2007年担任清华大学副校长和常务副校长时，陈希担任清华大学党委书记。当他直接从清华大学校长那里走出来的时候

【原文 English Original】
Executive Summary: At the 20th Party Congress, the Tsinghua Clique—centered on former Organization Department head Chen Xi—was one of the poles of power around Xi Jinping. With Politburo member Chen Jining now under investigation, seven of the 13 Tsinghua-affiliated officials at full ministerial rank or above have been placed under investigation, stepped down, or been moved out of their posts. The clique’s collapse began with Chen Xi’s fall from favor. In June, the Central Party School presidency, which Xi had kept for him as an exception, went to Cai Qi before Chen Xi’s term was up. A faction that has lost favor has no one to vouch for it and holds posts others covet, accelerating its collapse. Chen Jining, a core member of the clique, was parachuted into Shanghai and had little to show for his four years there. Heavy investment in artificial intelligence produced no major breakthroughs. This made it easy for Xi to discard him as a negative example for the Fifth Plenum’s campaign of full and rigorous Party self-governance. On November 24, Xinhua announced that Politburo member and Shanghai Party Secretary Chen Jining (陈吉宁) is under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) for suspected serious violations of discipline and law ( Xinhua , November 24). Shanghai’s Party committee pledged its support for the decision that evening ( Shanghai Municipal Government , November 24). Chen is the fourth member of the 20th Politburo to fall, and the second Shanghai Party secretary brought down in office, after Chen Liangyu (陈良宇) in 2006 ( China.org.cn , September 25, 2006). He had been widely seen as a contender for the Politburo Standing Committee at the 21st Party Congress in the second half of 2027 ( Wall Street Journal , November 24). The same day, Fang Hongwei (方红卫), a former Party secretary of Xi’an who, like Chen, is a Tsinghua graduate, was indicted ( Caixin , November 7, 2021; Xinhua , November 24). Chen Jining’s career is inseparable from that of Chen Xi (陈希), General Secretary Xi Jinping’s classmate at Tsinghua. Chen Xi stayed on at the university and rose through the Communist Youth League and student affairs to become its Party secretary. From 2013, he ran the Central Organization Department’s day-to-day work, later becoming its head ( People’s Daily Online , October 25, 2017; Reuters , October 10, 2022). With Tsinghua as his base, he built a high-level network known as the “Tsinghua Clique” (清华帮).  [1] In 2023, when he should have fully retired, he was granted an exception to stay on as president of the Central Party School, allowing him to retain his influence ( People’s Daily Online , October 25, 2017; Lianhe Zaobao , June 5). Yet from then on the clique declined, as some of its members were reined in or investigated. In June, Chen Xi abruptly handed over the presidency before his term was up ( Lianhe Zaobao , June 5). That same month, Wei Xiaodong (魏小东), chairman of the Beijing Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) who is believed to have close ties to Chen Xi, was placed under investigation ( Xinhua , June 6; Sinocism , June 8). Chen Jining’s fall likely marks the end of the Tsinghua Clique. Most of the Tsinghua Clique Is Out Each of Chen Jining’s promotions tracked Chen Xi’s position. When Chen Jining became vice president and then executive vice president of Tsinghua in 2006 and 2007, Chen Xi was the university’s Party secretary. When he went straight from Tsinghua president to minister of environmental protection in 2015, and when he became acting mayor of Beijing in 2017, Chen Xi was running the day-to-day work of the Organization Department. In October 2022, Chen Xi personally announced Chen Jining’s appointment as Shanghai Party secretary ( People’s Daily Online , February 27, 2015; Xinhua , October 28, 2022). Around the 20th Party Congress, Tsinghua cadres with ties to Chen Xi held posts in the Organization Department, the Central Party School, and other central bodies, as well as in Shanghai, Beijing, and several other provinces and cities. Counting only those who studied full-time or worked at Tsinghua, 13 officials held full ministerial rank or above after the 20th Party Congress.  [2] Of these, seven are now out (see Table 1). Hu Heping (胡和平) stepped down as minister of culture and tourism at the end of 2023, retaining only his deputy post at the Propaganda Department (Xinhua, December 29, 2023 , October 30 ). Former Organization Department head Li Ganjie (李干杰), a core figure in Chen Xi’s control over personnel, was transferred in April 2025 to the less influential United Front Work Department ( Central News Agency , April 2, 2025). Hubei Party Secretary Wang Menghui (王蒙徽) and Henan Party Secretary Liu Ning (刘宁) were moved to sinecures at the National People’s Congress (NPC) as they neared retirement age, and Hebei Party Secretary Ni Yuefeng (倪岳峰) followed suit well before reaching it (Xinhua, February 25, 2025 , August 28 , November 6 ). In little more than a year, Fang Hongwei, Qin Weizhong (覃伟中), Xia Linmao (夏林茂), and Chen Jining have all been placed under investigation (Xinhua, November 7, 2025 , September 21 , October 22 ). Everyone Kicks a Faction When It Is Down The two most important posts Chen Xi’s network lost have gone to others. Shi Taifeng (石泰峰), head of the Organization Department since April 2025, was one of Xi’s deputies when Xi was president of the Central Party School, and later served as governor of Jiangsu under Party Secretary—and now second-ranking Politburo Standing Committee member—Li Qiang (李强) ( Xinhua , June 11, 2017; People’s Daily Online , October 25, 2017). In June, the Central Party School presidency went to Cai Qi (蔡奇), Xi’s chief of staff ( Lianhe Zaobao , June 5; Xinhua , June 18). Once a faction’s patron loses favor, its collapse feeds on itself, for three reasons. First, no one will vouch for its members. Under a 2016 Party directive, when officials with a record of poor conduct are promoted (带病提拔), every stage of their selection is reviewed, and the organization departments and leading officials involved are held accountable ( People’s Daily Online , August 29, 2016). To speak up for a member of a fallen faction is to stake one’s own future on him. Second, faction members are now in the way. Every post they hold can go to someone else’s protégés, and those who take over have every incentive to consolidate their positions and none to defend their predecessors. Third, the investigations necessarily target the work that the fallen patron had overseen. In the case of Chen Xi, Cao Xingxin (曹兴信), Chen’s former subordinate at the Organization Department, was investigated in 2024 and punished for having “sought benefits for others in the selection and appointment of officials” (在干部选拔任用工作中为他人谋取利益) (Xinhua, September 28, 2024 , February 24, 2025 ; The Paper , September 28, 2024). As the Organization Department was Chen’s portfolio for a decade, pulling on this thread has led mostly to officials he promoted. And as each cadre has fallen, the remaining members have become more isolated and at the mercy of rivals. later placed under investigation September 2026 Xia Linmao 夏林茂 Beijing Party Standing Committee member; vice mayor (vice-ministerial) Under investigation October 2026 Wang Weizhong 王伟中 Guangdong Governor (full ministerial) Promoted to Inner Mongolia Party Secretary September 2025 Yin Yong 殷勇 Beijing Mayor (full ministerial) In office — Chen Xu 陈旭 Deputy head of the United Front Work Department; Chairman of the All-China Federation of Industry and Commerce (vice-national) In office — Wang Guangqian 王光谦 Executive Vice Chairman of the China Democratic League; CPPCC Vice Chairman from March 2023 (vice-national) In office — (Source: Author’s compilation from official appointment announcements by Xinhua, People’s Daily Online, the NPC, and others. Besides the 13 officials at full ministerial rank or above, the table lists four vice-ministerial officials: Wang Xiqin, Fang Hongwei, Qin Weizhong, and Xia Linmao.) Chen Jining Had No Record to Shield Himself Chen Jining’s achievements lay in sectoral work. His signature accomplishment came as minister of environmental protection. By 2016, his second year in the post, PM2.5 concentrations in the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei region had fallen 33 percent from 2013 levels ( People’s Daily Online , January 5, 2017). Yet after becoming Shanghai’s “number one” (一把手), he had little to show for four years at the helm. Instead, the most notable event on his watch was the protest on Urumqi Middle Road less than a month after he took office ( BBC , November 27, 2022; China Brief , December 8, 2022). Though he had little to do with it, it became the first mark on his record. Xi directed Shanghai to make building its “five centers” (五个中心) the main thrust of its work and to “take the lead” (走在前列) in artificial intelligence (AI) (Xinhua, December 3, 2023 , April 29, 2025 ). To this end, Shanghai set up a string of government- and university-branded AI research institutes, established a renminbi (RMB) 22.5 billion ($3.4 billion) AI fund of funds, and in 2025 issued RMB 1 billion ($149 million) in vouchers for computing power, models, and training data in a single round ( SSCI Leading Fund , accessed November 24; Shanghai Municipal Government , July 28, 2025). The spending has not produced convincing results. MiniMax (稀宇科技), Shanghai’s best-known large-model company, fell below its offering price less than a year after listing and is down more than 88 percent from its peak ( Caixin , October 22). Shanghai’s own auditors found that subsidies for three “high-quality incubators” sat idle, that only 33 of the 279 companies backed by an incubator-linked investment fund actually came from incubators, and that RMB 18.5 billion ($2.8 billion) in technology loans had been diverted to urban renewal ( Shanghai Municipal Government , September 20). Shanghai—a higher-ranking municipality directly under the central government—threw the whole city’s resources at AI and still did no better than Hangzhou, which relied on private companies.  [3] This likely disappointed Xi, falling short of both his ambitions and his expectations. Conclusion Chen Jining is the first Politburo member to fall since the Fifth Plenum in late October. The plenum’s Resolution states that the Party has “removed serious dangers hidden within the Party, the state, and the military” (消除了党、国家、军队内部存在的严重隐患), and traces most remaining problems to the officials at all levels who carry out policy ( China Brief , November 18). Less than a month later, accountability for implementation has come down on a Politburo member with an iron fist. Xi had singled out Shanghai to lead in AI. Chen Jining could not deliver, and no one would vouch for him over his other problems. The Resolution also calls for improving “the mechanisms for holding to account those responsible for promoting officials with a record of poor conduct” (干部“带病提拔”责任追究机制) and “firmly eliminating self-serving cliques” (坚决破除“小圈子”) ( Xinhua , November 1). The Tsinghua Clique fits that description—and has consequently lost favor. The rest of Chen Xi’s network can be expected to exit one by one around the 21st Party Congress, and accountability may yet reach Chen Xi himself. Any group that loses Xi’s trust will meet the same fate, as rivals pile on and allies scatter. Notes [1] Here, the Tsinghua Clique refers to officials centered on Chen Xi who studied full-time or worked at Tsinghua, plus his former subordinates at the Organization Department, rather than Tsinghua alumni in general. Xi himself and 20th Politburo members Li Xi (李希) (EMBA), Huang Kunming (黄坤明), and Zhang Guoqing (张国清) (both in-service doctorates) are excluded. On the system for cultivating and transferring cadres that Chen Xi built while running Tsinghua, see Wen-Hsuan Tsai and Xingmiu Liao, “The Impending Rise of the ‘Tsinghua Clique’: Cultivation, Transfer, and Relationships in Chinese Elite Politics,” Journal of Contemporary China 28, no. 120 (2019): 948–64, https://doi.org/10.1080/10670564.2019.1594106 . [2] The 13 are Chen Xi, Chen Jining, Li Ganjie, Hu Heping, Chen Xu, Wang Menghui, Ni Yuefeng, Liu Ning, Wang Weizhong, Yin Yong, Liu Xiaokai, Gao Yunlong, and Wang Guangqian. The count covers the period from the 20th Party Congress to the March 2023 leadership transition and is based on official biographies. In-service graduate degrees and EMBAs are not counted. [3] Hangzhou’s momentum in AI is clearly stronger than Shanghai’s. DeepSeek, Unitree, and the rest of the “six little dragons of Hangzhou” (杭州六小龙) all come from the city ( South China Morning Post , February 10, 2025; China Brief , March 19, 2025). According to a report by the China Academy of Urban Planning and Design, Hangzhou accounted for 16 percent of the notable AI models released worldwide over the past year and a half, the highest share of any Chinese city ( Yicai Global , November 24). The Chinese model most downloaded and most widely adapted in the global open-source community is Alibaba’s Qwen (通义千问), developed in Hangzhou ( Hugging Face , August 14). title: Hong Kong’s Police Training Advances Beijing’s Global Reach
zh_title: 香港警察培训提升北京的全球影响力
summary: 内容提要 香港新成立的警察学院为北京提供了一种通过国际公认的机构输出中国安全实践的途径。随着北京的警察机构与中华人民共和国的警察机构趋同，这座城市剩余的独特性可能对北京变得更有用。英国的学术声望可以促进香港警务转型。剑桥大学培训的导师可以为当地学位提供可信度，重现中国机构的优先事项，从而使代际变革能够在不立即与英国决裂的情况下继续进行。
content:
内容提要 香港新成立的警察学院为北京提供了一种通过国际公认的机构输出中国安全实践的途径。随着北京的警察机构与中华人民共和国的警察机构趋同，这座城市剩余的独特性可能对北京变得更有用。英国的学术声望可以促进香港警务转型。剑桥大学培训的导师可以为复制中国机构优先事项的本地学位提供可信度，从而允许代际变革在不立即打​​破英国教育传统的情况下进行。海外培训可以塑造对中国装备的需求，并培养外国安全机构内部的联系。将指导与采购和专业标准联系起来还可以将北京的影响力从个别官员扩展到受援机构的运作方式。 11月11日，香港国际警务学院揭牌，并与柬埔寨和沙特阿拉伯的警察学院签署培训协议（香港警务处，11月11日）。除了这个国际平台之外，学院还将提供专门从事安全和刑事调查的应用学位课程（香港电台 [RTHK]，10 月 9 日）。这些举措将在国内培养政治上可靠的官员与输出香港的专业声誉联系起来。
北京将获得一个培训体系，其国际身份仍明显保留香港的特色，但其机构内容越来越多地反映中国公共安全的优先事项。 学院扩展香港的警察外交 学院的目标是通过 20 多个项目和论坛，每年培训约 1,000 名警官，其中包括约 200 名海外人员（香港政府，11 月 11 日）。课程涵盖刑事调查和反恐、战术指挥和情报等更敏感的职能。只有五名官员将协调现有的培训资源（文汇报，10 月 9 日）。因此，香港可以通过汇集其警察机构内现有的专业知识来扩大其外交作用。香港警方最近与柬埔寨警察学院、澳大利亚警察管理学院、埃及警察学院和哈萨克斯坦阿拉木图学院合作（另类，2025年12月17日；香港警务处，11月13日访问）。这些关系的范围从交流到培训外国教练。香港于2026年3月培训柬埔寨战术教官，并与荷兰、泰国、新加坡和越南进行交流（另类，2025年6月11日；4月15日；大公报，5月23日）。将这些联系纳入一个共同机构可以使香港成为海外官员专业发展的经常参考点。
领导人论坛将针对东南亚、中东和其他“一带一路”合作伙伴（香港警务处，11月11日）。香港即将主办国际刑事警察组织（国际刑警组织）大会，香港海关担任世界海关组织亚太区副主席，为推动“一国两制”提供平台（文汇报，10月9日；香港海关，10月） 15）。这一框架利用香港的国际地位来支持这样的说法，即香港保留着独特的、与全球相连的地位。

【原文 English Original】
Executive Summary Hong Kong’s new police academy offers Beijing a way to export Chinese security practices through an internationally recognizable institution. The city’s remaining distinctiveness may become more useful to Beijing as its police institutions converge with those of the People’s Republic of China’s (PRC). British academic prestige can facilitate Hong Kong’s policing transition. Cambridge University-trained supervisors can lend credibility to a local degree that reproduces Chinese institutional priorities, allowing generational change to proceed without an immediate break with British educational traditions. Overseas training can shape demand for Chinese equipment and cultivate contacts inside foreign security institutions. Linking instruction to procurement and professional standards also could extend Beijing’s influence beyond individual officers into how recipient agencies operate. On November 11, Hong Kong inaugurated its International Academy of Policing and signed training agreements with police academies in Cambodia and Saudi Arabia ( Hong Kong Police Force , November 11). Alongside this international platform, the academy will offer an applied degree program specializing in security and criminal investigations ( Radio Television Hong Kong [RTHK] , October 9). These initiatives link the cultivation of politically reliable officers at home with the export of Hong Kong’s professional reputation. Beijing stands to gain a training system whose international identity remains recognizably Hong Kong’s but whose institutional content increasingly reflects Chinese public security priorities. The Academy Extends Hong Kong’s Police Diplomacy The academy aims to train approximately 1,000 officers annually, including around 200 overseas personnel, through more than 20 programs and forums ( Hong Kong Government , November 11). Courses span criminal investigation and more sensitive functions such as counterterrorism, tactical command, and intelligence. Just five officers will coordinate existing training resources ( Wen Wei Po , October 9). Hong Kong can therefore expand its diplomatic role by pooling expertise already available within its police institutions. Hong Kong’s police have recently worked with Cambodia’s Police Academy, the Australian Institute of Police Management, Egypt’s Police Academy, and Kazakhstan’s Almaty Academy ( Offbeat , December 17, 2025; Hong Kong Police Force , accessed November 13). These relationships range from exchanges to training foreign instructors. Hong Kong trained Cambodian tactical instructors in March 2026, and held exchanges with the Netherlands, Thailand, Singapore, and Vietnam (Offbeat, June 11, 2025 ; April 15 ; Ta Kung Pao , May 23). Bringing these contacts into a common institution can make Hong Kong a recurring reference point in overseas officers’ professional development. Leadership forums will target Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, and other One Belt One Road (OBOR) partners ( Hong Kong Police Force , November 11). Hong Kong’s forthcoming hosting of the International Criminal Police Organization (INTERPOL) General Assembly and its Customs service’s Asia-Pacific vice-chairmanship of the World Customs Organization offer platforms for promoting “one country, two systems” (一國兩制) ( Wen Wei Po , October 9; Hong Kong Customs and Excise Department , October 15). This framing uses Hong Kong’s international standing to support the claim that the city retains a distinct and globally connected role under Chinese sovereignty. Participation in the Association of Police Training Institutions in Asia and Dubai’s international policing best-practice conference provides established channels (Offbeat, April 22, 2015 , December 23, 2020 ). These forums could give Hong Kong a wider role in defining the terms of international police cooperation. Training Can Export an Integrated Policing System Hong Kong offers Beijing an intermediary whose international credibility partly rests on relationships predating its convergence with the People’s Republic of China’s (PRC) public security system. Foreign agencies may find cooperation with Hong Kong easier to justify than direct engagement with Chinese public security authorities. Expertise acquired through international partnerships can be adapted to Chinese priorities and circulated under a familiar institutional identity. Hong Kong’s distinctiveness can thus lower the political barriers to accepting Chinese policing practices. This advantage depends on partners continuing to treat Hong Kong’s police as institutionally distinct. The potential export is an integrated system of operations, equipment, organization, and training. Teaching officers how to identify threats and organize a response also shapes which capabilities they consider necessary. If these methods become routine, Chinese influence can persist beyond the course itself, embedded in everyday institutional decisions. A regular role in multilateral training, potentially through INTERPOL-related cooperation, could also confer authority over professional standards. Selecting which threats deserve attention and which responses count as best practice can give Chinese security assumptions the status of technical expertise. Recipient agencies could absorb those assumptions through professional learning without making an explicit political commitment to Beijing. Training also offers access to foreign officers’ institutional priorities, procedures, and vulnerabilities, creating opportunities for intelligence collection and cultivation. Alumni networks could serve united-front objectives by sustaining contacts inside overseas security establishments. These remain potential uses of the relationships, not demonstrated activities of the academy. Where security-sector reform connects policing with border management, intelligence, disaster response, or military organizations, shared personnel and practices could carry that influence into the wider security apparatus. Police Education Cultivates Political Reliability At home, the degree conferred by the training program opens a door for integration within Hong Kong’s political elite. Full police funding gives serving officers without a first degree an incentive to participate ( RTHK , October 9). This builds on a model pioneered by Tsinghua University, which launched its Executive Master of Public Administration program for Hong Kong governance professionals in 2018. Alumni reported in May 2025 included constitutional affairs official Clement Woo (胡健民), the chief executive’s special assistant Jenny Wong (黃芷淵), and legislators Carmen Kan (簡慧敏), Shang Hailong (尚海龍), Edward Leung (梁熙), and Gary Zhang (張欣宇) ( Ta Kung Pao , May 17, 2025). It also builds on a separate Police College partnership, formalized in 2021, which was renewed in 2023 for three further cohorts ( Offbeat , May 24, 2023). The new degree program emerges during a period in which Hong Kong’s police force is already undergoing practical and symbolic convergence with the PRC. Chinese-style foot drills became standard in 2022 ( Deutsche Welle , January 14, 2022). Earlier revisions to its published history removed or softened references to the 1989 pro-democracy movement and the 1967 riots ( Radio France Internationale , July 19, 2016). A phased replacement program introduced Chinese-made CF98-A and CS/LP5 pistols from 2024. By May 2026, police had also confirmed adoption of CS/LS7 submachine guns by the Counter Terrorism Response Unit and Airport Security Unit ( Xinhua , November 18, 2024; China News Service , May 7). Academic credentials follow these means of institutionalizing the transition. Political education and technological familiarization already form part of professional training. The People’s Public Security University of China has hosted Hong Kong police study programs since 2001 ( People’s Public Security University of China , May 18, 2011). Partnerships also include Shanghai Police College and Guangdong Police College. A January 2024 agreement with the PRC Ministry of Public Security expanded the “6+2” training framework to “6+2+N,” which included six study programs at police institutions, two exchange programs for police tactical instructors, and multiple programs on the PRC’s national affairs. A 2023 university study program combined police developments with teaching on the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) 20th National Congress and a visit to Huawei’s Beijing research institute (Offbeat, August 16, 2023 ; January 8, 2025 ). A Hong Kong police alumni association for the People’s Public Security University of China was established in 2006, and the university’s then-president, Wang Yanji (王彦吉), attended its inauguration ( Offbeat , November 22, 2006). In November 2024, two superintendents and three Police College staff joined national affairs training organized by Renmin University and Beijing’s Liaison Office in Hong Kong ( Offbeat , January 22, 2025). The inclusion of teaching staff extends the reach of exchanges, because their experience can shape the curriculum for subsequent cohorts. Hong Kong’s very firstfive-year plan (2026–2030), unveiled in September 2026, explicitly connects regular training cooperation with institutions in the PRC to strengthening civil servants’ patriotic commitment ( Hong Kong Government , September 16). The new degree can give that objective a continuing institutional form. British Credentials Can Ease Institutional Change What sets Hong Kong’s police degree apart from other programs is its supervisory arrangement. Final projects are to be supervised by officers of superintendent rank or above with qualifications from Tsinghua or Cambridge University in the United Kingdom, building authority through academic pedigree ( RTHK , October 9). Hong Kong’s collaboration with Cambridge on the Master of Studies in Applied Criminology and Police Management began in 2017. Senior officers completed the course, and Cambridge academics traveled to Hong Kong for dissertation presentations and alumni exchanges ( Offbeat , December 18, 2019). These relationships supplied expertise and an internationally recognizable mark of professional status that remains available to officers trained under the earlier arrangement. Cambridge still advertises its police executive master’s program, despite the United Kingdom suspending military training for Hong Kong police in 2020 ( The Observer , August 15, 2020; University of Cambridge , accessed November 13). Hong Kong police sponsorship arrangements remain unclear, as a supervisor’s Cambridge qualification does not imply Cambridge oversight of the new degree. This gives British academic prestige a new political use: British-trained officers can validate a locally controlled degree whose graduates enter an institution increasingly shaped by Chinese priorities. As British institutional influence gradually recedes, Hong Kong is trying to establish its own prestigious academic institutions. Creating local degrees that offer sufficient recognition and career opportunities would weaken demand for overseas study, reducing the political cost of changing the force’s educational orientation. Under “patriots administering Hong Kong” (愛國者治港), familiarity with the PRC’s governance and Hong Kong’s circumstances (知國情、懂港情) may increasingly function as an informal credential for political office ( Wen Wei Po , January 24, 2021). The degree could give that political expectation a routine place in police career development. Training Connects Officers to Chinese Suppliers The 2026 Global Public Security Cooperation Forum in Lianyungang combined an equipment exhibition with initiatives on public security standardization and international police education ( Xinhua , September 9). Local authorities promoted exports of Chinese security technologies, equipment, and integrated systems through the city’s security-industry platform ( Lianyungang Fabu , September 9). Bringing training and suppliers into the same cooperation agenda can help Chinese products become familiar answers to the operational problems foreign officers are taught to address. Hong Kong’s police academy already provides a concrete connection. On November 4, Offbeat , the force’s official journal, reported that its Advanced Tactics Application Course would include visits to firearms and ammunition factories in the PRC ( Offbeat , November 4). Such visits make suppliers part of professional instruction. If agencies adopt the associated equipment and routines, maintenance, software, and retraining costs can make switching systems harder, locking the force in to dependence on PRC supply chains. Where suppliers and technologies serve both policing and defense, these relationships could also support military–civil fusion. Communications, surveillance, and border management provide plausible points of overlap. Procurement choices originating in police training could spread through shared personnel, equipment, and operating practices, connecting a wider range of security institutions to Chinese supply chains. Conclusion Under Hong Kong’s diminishing autonomy, its police force seeks to retain a British-derived professional identity while Chinese institutions increasingly shape how officers are trained and equipped. This combination uses credibility accumulated under an earlier political order to advance Chinese security priorities. Abroad, it offers a way to embed Chinese practices in institutions that might resist an overt partnership with PRC institutions. Its new International Academy of Policing could turn the distinction promised by “one country, two systems” into a means of extending one system’s influence overseas. 【原文 English Original】
This is part of a series examining the central importance of critical minerals and the race to ensure Western supply. Multiple US government agencies released a series of funding vehicles and new policies in August as part of efforts to build a reliable, non-Chinese, critical minerals supply chain for defense production. The announcements received relatively little fanfare outside the trade and business media, yet their ambitious goal is to reshape global supply chains. China has spent decades developing an industrial ecosystem “from soup to nuts” controlled by the Communist Party. It built an integrated natural resource supply chain, financing system, production industry, trained labor force, and large domestic market as it pursued modernization and national security. The US and Europe now see China’s dominance in critical minerals as a Western national security vulnerability . Without the minerals and rare earths China supplies, modern defense technology cannot be made at scale in the near term. To address this immediate threat, US President Donald Trump announced $3bn for mining and processing projects in August, while his administration also moved to secure supply from allied producers abroad. In March, the Pentagon had already signed a binding letter of intent to buy about $96m of light and heavy rare earth oxides from Australia’s Lynas Rare Earths over four years, redirecting funds originally earmarked for a processing facility in Texas. That month, Lynas produced the first samarium oxide at its Malaysian plant, which it says is the only commercial producer of separated samarium, terbium and dysprosium outside China. In parallel, the Pentagon is investing in domestic processing capacity, including through a 2025 loan of $150m to expand heavy rare earth separation at MP Materials’ Mountain Pass facility in California. The US cannot replicate China’s integrated critical-minerals industrial ecosystem within the timeframe required by its defense industry, and deals like these are key to protecting critical supply chains from Chinese economic coercion. Samarium is a good example. It is primarily used in samarium-cobalt (SmCo) permanent magnets, which can withstand very high temperatures and are essential in advanced technologies , such as Patriot missiles and F-35 fighter jets. Patriots are vital for missile interception, while 14 NATO allies rely on F-35 jets as a cornerstone of their modern combat air fleets. It is critical that the US and Europe work together to secure the basic supply chain that powers these integrated defense systems. In 2025, the overwhelming majority of samarium used in US production was imported from China. That year, China imposed export licensing schemes on samarium, other processed critical minerals, rare earths, and specialized processing technology, giving Beijing discretion over supply. Mines take 5-10 years to become fully productive, while processing facilities can take up to 15 years to make reliable defense-grade products. The accumulated workforce expertise required to master this complex, precise processing can take even longer to develop. Rare earth concentrate from mines like Mt. Weld in Western Australia, the source of Lynas’ samarium, is several processing stages away from magnet-grade material. Two leading American processing projects, MP Materials in California and Energy Fuels in Utah, are not expected to reach their planned expanded heavy rare earth production until 2028 or later. If China cuts off samarium, US defense output, along with allied production, would be at risk once stockpiles ran down. triggerPostRender(); } } );} ); While it is impractical for the US to build a critical minerals system comparable to China’s, working with Europe and other key allies, there is a good chance of building resilience in the face of potential market manipulation. USA Rare Earth, another recipient of US government investment, has acquired a samarium production chain which relies on a British factory and a French stockpile with enough supply for between one and three years of US defense industry consumption. These types of industrial partnerships with Europe can fill American critical gaps. What Europe lacks in scale and investment, it makes up for in specialized expertise which is difficult, expensive, and time-consuming to replicate. Solvay, USA Rare Earth’s partner, has both a stockpile and rare-earth know-how. Its plant at La Rochelle, France, has been processing rare earths since 1948. Less Common Metals, a British metal and alloy producer, is now owned by USA Rare Earth and has a proprietary SmCo magnet production process that rivals China’s. Other German, Finnish, Swedish, and Estonian firms also have current or planned capacities across the rare earth permanent magnet supply chain—ranging from upstream mining and separation to SmCo magnet production. The European Union’s vast market offers a strong demand base for the expanding Western critical minerals production. Since adopting the Critical Raw Materials Act in 2024, the bloc has built a regulatory and policy framework for both internal investment and multilateral cooperation. The European Commission plans to establish a European Critical Raw Materials Center, designed to coordinate demand aggregation and project financing for minerals by drawing on some of the continent’s comparative strengths: market intelligence and cross-country coordination. The Center could provide a critical channel for information sharing and stakeholder mapping for US firms. This year, Washington and Brussels agreed to discuss border-adjusted price floors and offtake agreements. In addition, there are national initiatives; German companies, including BMW and Rheinmetall, said on November 23 that they planned a trading house to secure critical minerals. Europe is also widening its supplier base, and two partnerships stand out. The EU and Canada are pursuing multiple streams for critical mineral industry partnership, including closer cooperation on stockpiling and batteries, while in the longer run, the bloc’s relationship with Ukraine offers downstream demand. In July, the EU launched a defense industrial partnership with Kyiv covering drones, missile defense, artillery and other key components. Ukraine, which already mines titanium ore, has a critical minerals strategy and action plan and is actively seeking partners. No individual country has the scale or financing capability to build a fully self-reliant minerals supply chain to offset potential Chinese market manipulation. And time is short: China already dominates and has shown it is willing to restrict supplies, as it did to Japan in 2010 and to the US in 2025 , and has undercut competitors on price. Twelve NATO allies took an important step at this year’s NATO Ankara summit by formally launching a joint defense-critical raw materials initiative. The US, which is not a participant, should embrace this initiative and work with its allies to complement strategic reserves with long-term purchasing commitments and coordinated industrial investment. The immediate challenge is not to eliminate every dependency on China, but to ensure Beijing cannot interrupt essential Western defense production. The US should embrace Europe’s existing critical minerals capabilities as strategic assets, not simply temporary substitutes until American production comes online. Partnership on critical mineral supply chains both increases transatlantic security and serves as a nexus of transatlantic market growth and expertise-sharing that could move from catch-up to innovation and true resiliency. The goal should be to build a competitive allied industrial ecosystem that China cannot easily disrupt. Sharon Hudson-Dean is a Senior Fellow at the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA) and an Associate Fellow at Chatham House in London. She is a veteran diplomat and senior foreign policy leader who has managed complex strategic, defense, and political policies throughout her career. Most recently, she served as US Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Northern Europe, NATO, and Arctic Security (2024-25). Anping Zhu is a Yale University student majoring in global affairs, economics, and mathematics. He is a research assistant to CEPA Fellow Sharon Hudson-Dean for her expert comment series on critical minerals and the race to secure Western supply. He is a member of the Yale Foreign Policy Initiative and has worked as a policy research intern and adviser to the governments of Lesotho and Rwanda. title: USTR Makes Determinations and Proposes Actions in 14 Section 301 Investigations Relating to Structural Excess Capacity and Production in Manufacturing Sectors

content:
美国贸易代表办公室就与制造业结构性产能过剩和生产相关的 14 项 301 条款调查做出决定并建议采取行动 2026 年 11 月 25 日星期三 - 06:19 华盛顿 — 今天，美国贸易代表杰米森·格里尔 (Jamieson Greer) 根据 1974 年《贸易法》第 301 条确定 14 个经济体与结构性过剩产能和生产相关的行为、政策和做法制造业的过剩产能和生产是不合理的，会给美国商业带来负担或限制，因此可以根据《贸易法》第 301(b) 条提起诉讼。美国贸易代表办公室（USTR）也发布了支持这些决定的具体经济报告。今天的决定涵盖的 14 个经济体是中国、欧盟、新加坡、瑞士、印度尼西亚、马来西亚、柬埔寨、泰国、韩国、越南、台湾、孟加拉国、日本和印度。贸易代表目前尚未就墨西哥或挪威做出决定。格里尔大使表示：“几十年来，我们的许多贸易伙伴采取了针对制造业、工资和劳动力抑制、金融和其他支持、非市场经济投入以及其他市场扭曲做法的产业战略，这些做法使贸易平衡向有利于他们的方向倾斜，同时侵蚀了美国的制造业基础。”
“认识到这一点，自2016年以来，从唐纳德·特朗普、乔·拜登、习近平到埃马纽埃尔·马克龙等领导人都认识到结构性产能和生产过剩对全球经济构成的威胁。但是，在七国集团、二十国集团、世贸组织和其他论坛上的连续声明没有带来变化的情况下，特朗普总统提议采取行动，消除这些不公平的行为、政策和做法。通过这样做，我们可以为美国工人创造公平的竞争环境，并制定一个新的、更世界经济的可持续发展之路。”  对于以下 14 个经济体，美国贸易代表已确定某些造成、维持或导致结构性产能和生产过剩的行为、政策和做法是不合理的，会给美国商业带来负担或限制。孟加拉国：孟加拉国的不合理行为、政策和做法包括（1）维持和扩大其制造业，特别是关键部门的工业计划； (2) 生产激励措施，促进生产和出口； （三）劳动保护不完善的； （4）金融抑制政策； (5) 未能解决全球产能和生产过剩问题，包括通过来自非市场经济体的进口和外国直接投资。这些法案、政策和做法通过以下方式给美国商业带来负担或限制：(1) 减少美国生产商和出口商在孟加拉国和第三国市场的商业机会； （二）损害美国利益
导致美国制造业的生产、出口、就业和投资损失； (3) 增加美国经济安全风险，包括对 NME 投入的依赖。在成衣和服装领域尤其如此。请在此处阅读美国贸易代表办公室的报告。柬埔寨：柬埔寨的不合理行为、政策和做法包括（1）产业政策规定了明确的出口和制造目标，而不是基于市场原则； (2) 吸收或扩大外国制造能力，特别是非市场经济国家制造能力的投资激励措施； （三）全球产能过剩问题未能解决
