USTR Makes Determinations and Proposes Actions in 14 Section 301 Investigations Relating to Structural Excess Capacity and Production in Manufacturing Sectors myarbrough Wed, 11/25/2026 - 06:19 WASHINGTON – Today, United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer determined under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 that the acts, policies, and practices of 14 economies relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce, and are thus actionable under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act. The Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) has also published economy-specific reports that support the determinations. The 14 economies covered by today’s determinations are China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India. The Trade Representative has not made determinations with respect to Mexico or Norway at this time.  “For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America’s manufacturing base,” said Ambassador Greer . “In recognition of this, since 2016, leaders ranging from Donald Trump, to Joe Biden, to Xi Jinping, to Emmanuel Macron have recognized the threat that structural excess capacity and production poses for the global economy. But where successive statements at the G7, G20, WTO and other fora have not resulted in change, President Trump is proposing to take action to bring about the elimination of these unfair acts, policies, and practices. In doing so, we can level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.”  For the following 14 economies, the U.S. Trade Representative has determined that certain acts, policies, and practices which create, sustain, or contribute to structural excess capacity and production are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce. Bangladesh: Bangladesh’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans to maintain and expand its manufacturing sector, particularly in key sectors; (2) production incentives to promote production and exports; (3) inadequate labor protections; (4) financial repression policies; and (5) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Bangladesh and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in the ready-made garment and apparel sector. Read USTR’s Report here . Cambodia: Cambodia’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial policies providing explicit export and manufacturing targets not based on market principles; (2) investment incentives to absorb or expand foreign manufacturing capacity, particularly from non-market economy countries; (3) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies; and (4) inadequate labor protections. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Cambodia and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like apparel, solar, and tires. Read USTR’s Report here . China: China’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) long-standing industrial plans and targeting; (2) extensive financial and other support to manufacturers; (3) support to state-owned enterprises on non-commercial terms; (4) extensive forced technology transfer; (5) wide-spread intellectual property theft; (6) inadequate labor protections, including the use of forced labor; (7) lax environmental enforcement; (8) financial repression and currency practices; and (9) encouraging the expansion of capacity and production in third countries. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in China and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in U.S. manufacturing, and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks. This is especially true in the aluminum, automotive, battery, chemical, consumer electronics, glass, machine tool, medical devices, non-ferrous metals, paper, plastics, power equipment, rail, robotics, semiconductors, ship, solar, steel, telecommunications, textiles, tires, and wind sectors. Read USTR’s Report here . European Union: The European Union’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans to expand manufacturing; (2) policies to promote production and exports with high volumes of export credit; (3) sustained market access barriers; (4) preferential lending through centralized investment banks that target specific manufacturing sectors; and (5) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters to compete in the European Union and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like automotive, chemicals, and pharmaceuticals.   Read USTR’s Report here . India: India’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans to expand manufacturing; (2) inadequate labor protections; (3) financial repression policies; (4) sustained market access barriers; and (5) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in India and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like health (pharmaceuticals and medical devices), steel, solar, and information and communications technology (ICT).  Read USTR’s Report here . Indonesia: Indonesia’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) government industrial policies to promote production and export; (2) inadequate labor laws, conditions, and enforcement; (3) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies; (4) financial repression; and (5) sector-specific acts, policies, and practices, such as “downstreaming”. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Indonesia and third country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like textiles and apparel, mining and metals production, and renewable energy. Read USTR’s Report here . Japan: Japan’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans and strategies; (2) financial repression; (3) household investment promotion; (4) support for unprofitable firms; (5) inadequate labor protections; (6) financial support for the auto, steel, semiconductor, and optical fiber industries; and (7) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Japan and third-country markets, (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector, and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like automotive, steel, semiconductors, and optical fiber. Read USTR’s Report here . Republic of Korea: Korea’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial and sectoral plans to maintain and expand manufacturing; (2) preferential lending through state-owned banks; and (3) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Korea and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like automotive, semiconductor, and petrochemicals.  Read USTR’s Report here . Malaysia: Malaysia’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial and sectoral plans to promote production and exports; (2) preferential capital through national funding vehicles that target manufacturing; (3) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies; and (4) inadequate labor protections. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Malaysia and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like information and communication technology and automotive. Read USTR’s Report here . Singapore: Singapore’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans; (2) financial repression; (3) savings promotion policies that suppress domestic consumption; (4) inadequate labor protections; (5) financial support for key sectors; and (6) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Singapore and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like electronics and semiconductors, health, and petrochemicals. Read USTR’s Report here . Switzerland: Switzerland’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) suppressing the appreciation of its currency below the level that would otherwise prevail under market conditions; (2) supporting its pharmaceutical sector via extensive public investment and fiscal incentives; (3) reducing a major production cost—electricity—for its steel producers; and (4) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Switzerland and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in U.S. manufacturing; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in the pharmaceutical, steel, and chemicals sectors. Read USTR’s Report here . Taiwan: Taiwan’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) the recurring use of industrial and economic plans to support the manufacturing sector, particularly high-technology manufacturing; (2) legislation that incentivizes and provides support for the architecture of its industrial ecosystem; (3) state-directed and supported research and development; (4) state-directed and industrial clustering to support industry; (5) various financing mechanisms to support industry; (6) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports from non-market economies; (7) practices that equate to financial repression; (8) past purchases of U.S.-sanctioned Russian feedstock; and (9) inadequate protection of labor rights. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Taiwan and third country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like the electronics, semiconductor, and telecommunications sectors. Read USTR’s Report here . Thailand: Thailand’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial and economic plans that target manufacturing and export; (2) sustained market access barriers; (3) preferential lending and other government support to industry; (4) inadequate labor protections; and (5) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Thailand and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in the electronics, automobile, machinery, and electrical equipment sectors. Read USTR’s Report here . Vietnam: Vietnam’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) government industrial plans and its state planning system; (2) its land planning system; (3) inadequate labor laws, conditions, and enforcement; (4) financial repression; (5) allocation of financial capital to priority sectors; (6) price regulation; (7) encouragement of or failure to address foreign direct investment from other non-market economies; (8) encouragement of or failure to address imports from other non-market economies; (9) encouragement of or failure to address transshipment from other non-market economies; and (10) sector-specific acts, policies, and practices.  These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Vietnam and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on other NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like textiles, apparel, and footwear; shipbuilding; cement; and information and communications technology. Read USTR’s Report here . As a result of these determinations, the U.S. Trade Representative has proposed responsive action in each investigation for public comment. Specifically, the U.S. Trade Representative has proposed additional tariffs on the following investigated economies except for certain products identified in the annexes of the respective Federal Register notices. Bangladesh: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Bangladesh of up to 18 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Bangladesh on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Agreement between the United States of American and the People’s Republic of Bangladesh on Reciprocal Trade. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Cambodia: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Cambodia of up to 18 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Cambodia on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Agreement between the United States and Cambodia on Reciprocal Trade. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . China: The Trade Representative proposes appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs of up to 20 percent, net of the rate of duty applied to the good under the Section 301 investigation related to the prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor, on goods of China not identified in the annexes to the relevant Federal Register notice and up to 10 percent tariffs on goods identified in Annex A to the Federal Register notice with exemptions for certain goods identified in Annex B to the Federal Register notice. The products in Annex B are products on the U.S. Imports List of the U.S.-China Board of Trade “30-For-30” Lists of Products Recommended for Reduced Tariff Treatment. This proposal accounts for the commitments and 20 percent tariff rate announced as part of the Kuala Lumpur Joint Arrangement reached by President Trump and President Xi on October 30, 2025. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . European Union: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying on all goods of the EU a tariff rate of 15 percent, net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with the EU on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the United States-European Union Framework Agreement on Reciprocal, Fair, and Balanced Trade. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . India: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices would include applying tariffs of up to 25 percent on all goods of India, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. The Trade Representative further proposes to consider whether the additional duties applied should be adjusted to account for, among others, duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions, or were India to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States that is responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies, and practices of India, a tariff rate of 17 percent.  Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . The Trade Representative further proposes to consider adjusting the tariff rate applied to each good to 10 percent to account for any commitments in the event that Singapore were to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States, or conclude other negotiations that are responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies, and practices of Singapore. The Trade Representative further proposes to consider whether the additional duties applied should be adjusted to account for, among others, duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; or the commitments and a tariff rate of 20 percent, were Vietnam to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States that is responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies, and practices of Vietnam. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . To be assured of consideration, interested persons should submit requests to appear at the hearings, along with a summary of testimony by January 5, 2027 . Written comments are due by January 5, 2027 . USTR will hold hearings about the proposed actions in these investigations on January 25, 2027 , continuing as appropriate. Background: Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (Trade Act), is designed to address unfair foreign practices affecting U.S. commerce. Section 301 may be used to respond to unjustifiable, unreasonable, or discriminatory foreign government practices that burden or restrict U.S. commerce. Under Section 302(b) of the Trade Act, the United States Trade Representative may self-initiate an investigation under Section 301. On March 11, 2026, the United States Trade Representative initiated investigations into the acts, policies, and practices of various economies relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors. The 16 economies subject to these investigations are: China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Norway, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Mexico, Japan, and India. Pursuant to Section 304(b)(1)(A) of the Trade Act, USTR provided the public and interested persons with opportunities to present their views through a public comment process and through a public hearing. USTR received testimony of nearly 140 witnesses and 1,070 comments in response to the initiation notice and pertaining to all 16 investigated economies. Today, the U.S. Trade Representative determined, in each of 14 investigations, that the acts, policies, and practices of China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce, and are thus actionable under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act. ###

打印文章 分享文章内容 展开菜单 关闭 COP31 发生了什么？对总统职位的反应是什么？石油资源丰富的国家的角色是如何描述的？发达国家的角色是如何描绘的？发展中国家的作用是如何描述的？中国的角色是如何描绘的？这对于共识进程和改革意味着什么？ COP31能否发出“积极信号”？上周末，COP31 戏剧性地结束，多个国家联盟拒绝了拟议的“安塔利亚协议”，理由是该协议未提及化石燃料。紧张的最后时刻和缺乏备受期待的“协议”引发了世界各地媒体的广泛报道。许多评论家纷纷将 COP31 的结果称为“失败”，质疑这对联合国气候进程的未来和“分裂的世界”意味着什么。各方相互指责，一些媒体将 COP31 的“失败”归咎​​于“石油资源丰富的国家”，而另一些媒体则指责欧洲“不愿”提供更多气候融资。虽然说 COP31 上“没有达成一致”并不准确，但媒体的反应表明安塔利亚会议上所表现出的不同观点的复杂性。在本文中，Carbon Brief 汇集了世界各地媒体的反应，展示了对 COP31 成果的不同反应。 COP31 发生了什么？对总统职位的反应是什么？石油资源丰富的国家的角色是如何描述的？
发达国家的作用如何？发展中国家的作用如何？中国的角色是如何描绘的？这对于共识进程和改革意味着什么？ COP31能否发出“积极信号”？ COP31 发生了什么？第三十一届缔约方会议未能就土耳其和澳大利亚轮值主席国推动的拟议“安塔利亚协定”达成一致。最终文本被包括欧盟、英国和一些气候脆弱国家在内的至少 32 个国家否决，谈判拖延了两天，场面一片混乱。 《爱尔兰时报》的一篇社论称，这一结果是“在没有达成任何协议或前进路线图的情况下，缔约方会议以前所未有的方式结束”。这种观点虽然在媒体上经常表达，但却是不正确的。正如资深“COP 观察员”在 CB Connect 上的一篇文章中所解释的那样，尽管总统的“掩护决定”失败了，但峰会就许多决定达成了一致。在谈到拒绝封面决定时，墨尔本大学气候研究人员杰奎琳·皮尔教授和凯瑟琳·鲍文教授在对话中写道，“这些文本一直是正式谈判过程的附加内容”。

What does this mean for the consensus process and reform? Could COP31 send a ‘positive signal’? COP31 came to a dramatic close last weekend when a coalition of nations rejected the proposed “Antalya pact”, citing its failure to mention fossil fuels. The tense final moments and lack of a much-anticipated “pact” have sparked extensive media coverage around the world. Many commentators have rushed to label the COP31 outcome a “ failure ”, questioning what it means for the future of the UN climate process and a “ divided world ”. There has been much finger-pointing, with some outlets attributing COP31’s “collapse” to “ oil-rich nations ”, while others blame Europe’s “ reluctance ” to provide more climate finance. While it is not accurate to say there was “ no agreement ” at COP31, the media response demonstrates the complexity of the divergent views on display at the Antalya conference. In this article, Carbon Brief draws together media reactions from around the world to show the diversity of responses to the COP31 outcome. What happened at COP31? What has the reaction to the presidency been? How has the role of oil-rich nations been portrayed? How has the role of developed nations been portrayed? How has the role of developing nations been portrayed? How has the role of China been portrayed? What does this mean for the consensus process and reform? Could COP31 send a ‘positive signal’? What happened at COP31?  COP31 ended without agreement on a proposed “Antalya pact”, which had been pushed by the Turkey-Australia presidency. The final text was rejected by at least 32 countries, including the EU, the UK and some climate-vulnerable countries, in chaotic scenes as the talks overran by two days. An Irish Times editorial said the outcome was an “unprecedented ending of a COP without any agreement or roadmap forward”.  This view, while commonly expressed in the media, is incorrect.  As veteran “COP-watchers” explained for an article on CB Connect , the summit reached agreement on many decisions, even though the presidency’s “cover decision” failed.  Referring to the rejection of the cover decision, Melbourne University climate researchers Prof Jacqueline Peel and Prof Kathryn Bowen wrote in the Conversation that “these texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process”. .cb-membership-banner.alignfull { box-sizing: border-box; Similarly, climate-sceptic journalist Graham Lloyd wrote in the Australian that “globally, Bowen has embarrassed himself and diminished Australia’s reputation”.  For Australian news outlet Crikey , journalist Royce Kurmelovs said that Bowen “tried to run the world’s climate talks the way Labor [Australia’s ruling party] runs climate policy at home: quiet, pragmatic and without mentioning fossil fuels”, adding that “in Turkey, it didn’t work”. A commentary by journalist Xu Luyi in Chinese financial news outlet Caixin said that future COP presidencies should “distinguish achievable implementation measures from ambitions that lack a coalition capable of delivering them”. Separately, an editorial in the National – a UAE state-owned English-language daily newspaper – said “the next UN secretary general needs to restore the art of diplomacy”.  How has the role of oil-rich nations been portrayed?  In media coverage, much of the blame for the perceived failure of COP31 has been placed on oil-producing nations – particularly with the final cover decision draft containing no mention of fossil fuels.  Even before the summit had finished, Panama’s minister of environment Juan Carlos Navarro warned that the COP process was being “held hostage by the petroleum mafia”. After the talks had closed without a deal on the Antalya pact, a Guardian editorial said that responsibility lay with “petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels”, along with a lack of climate finance . The “fossil-fuel backsliding” was being led by a “Saudi-Russian coalition”, it said. A Bloomberg editorial also noted that the omission of fossil fuels from the decision text came “amid pressure from Russia, Saudi Arabia and other fossil fuel producers”. A Times editorial described oil-rich nations, “led by Saudi Arabia”, as the “culprits” for the lack of an agreement, because they “insisted on dropping a reference to phasing out hydrocarbons”. In the i newspaper , David Shukman, a former BBC News science editor, described a “deception” at the “heart” of the COP process: “This pattern of lobbying by oil-rich nations has become increasingly blatant and aggressive over more than three decades.” Despite signing up to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, the participation of the “oil-rich minority” has been “in name only”, wrote Shukman: “At more than a dozen of the UN’s giant conferences, I’ve seen for myself the tactics of trench warfare and how well they’ve worked. It’s why fossil fuels remain so dominant and why the climate is turning so hostile.” Writing for the Guardian , University College London’s Prof Bill McGuire warned that the COP process had been “deeply compromised” by the “major fossil-fuel producers”. For Al Jazeera , York University’s Prof Ilan Kapoor added that “fossil-fuel power operates well beyond the conference hall”. ( Reuters reported that, according to negotiators from Europe, small-island states, Latin America, Asia and Africa, Saudi officials had “regular access” to the summit’s presidents, “allowing them disproportionate influence”.) In Australian outlet Inside Story , the University of Sheffield’s Prof Michael Jacobs wrote that since “transitioning away from fossil fuels” language was included in COP28 , fossil-fuel producers “have been determined to ensure the phrase would never be used again”.  Nick O’Malley, national environment and climate editor for the Sydney Morning Herald , noted: “The tension between the action the world knows it must take on climate change and that which a handful of oil-rich nations will allow it to take has been growing for years.” At the summit itself, shortly after rejecting the cover decision on behalf of the EU, Irish environment minister Darragh O’Brien told Agence France-Presse that the talks had been “hijacked by some oil states”.  The Backchannel substack collated reactions from negotiators and observers. Among them, Dr Mary Robinson – former president of Ireland – warned of the “disturbing politicised attacks on [climate] science from those still clinging to fossil fuels and looking to sabotage climate action”. In contrast, an editorial in the National loosely described a failure of the talks to “bridge divisions over fossil-fuel language, carbon capture and adaptation finance in the final draft”. It added: “Unfortunately, the gap between countries – major emitters, energy producers and the more vulnerable nations demanding accessible funding – proved too wide to close.” How has the role of developed nations been portrayed?  Much of the commentary about developed countries’ role at COP31 focused on the EU and the UK blocking the final “Antalya pact”, due to its lack of language about fossil fuels. A cover-decision text without such language was “vehemently opposed by dozens of countries, including the EU delegation strongly led by [Irish] minister for climate Darragh O’Brien”, according to the Irish Times .  Similarly, an editorial in the UK’s Times concluded that “several countries, including the UK, rejected a draft omitting the not insignificant matter of winding down fossil-fuel use”. Peter Prengaman, climate news director for the Associated Press , wrote that the EU and its allies “were no longer willing” to leave out fossil-fuel language. (He noted that “top polluter” the US was not present at the summit.) Other media outlets took a more balanced approach to the role of developed nations at COP31. A Guardian editorial concluded:  “European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action.” Reflecting on the need for “funding to help the poorest countries adapt to global warming”, an editorial in Le Monde noted that “the most developed nations have been reluctant to increase their contributions, despite their historic responsibility for CO2 emissions”. An editorial in the Hindu stressed:  “It stands to reason that developed countries, which have committed to providing climate finance in recognition of their historical emissions, make good on past promises to shoulder the cost of the carbon emissions that are responsible for warming.” Writing in US outlet Drilled , reporter Rishika Pardikar noted that “wealthy countries like Japan, the UK and Canada…largely aligned with the EU in opposing support mechanisms for developing countries like long-term finance, adaptation finance and just transition”. Climate campaigner John Gibbons wrote in the Irish Examiner that the EU was “right to reject” carbon capture and storage in the COP31 outcome, but accused O’Brien of “cosplay[ing] at being a progressive climate leader”, despite Ireland’s poor climate record. Many developed countries were not particularly vocal at COP31, and an editorial in Japan’s Yomiuri Shimbun lamented a general “low level of interest in and low priority given to global warming”. The editorial concluded: “It is hoped that Japan will continue to fulfill the practical roles expected of it and contribute to the international community in ways unique to Japan.” How has the role of developing nations been portrayed?  Equity, historical responsibility for climate change and a need for finance have all been portrayed at the centre of developing countries’ positions at COP31. A comment in the Hindu said that “India’s insistence on historical responsibility, climate finance and adaptation belongs at the centre of any credible plan to cut emissions”. It added that India had played a “constructive role” to “provide bridging language” in texts on adaptation and the just transition work programme. Down to Earth noted that “India has referred to historical responsibility in submissions at previous climate summits, but rarely with the emphasis evident” at COP31. Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative , told Radio France Internationale that those who criticise India’s opposition to fossil-fuel phaseout “need to acknowledge that there has been a lot of mistrust between India and developed countries”. Other developing countries also held firm, particularly on the issue of finance. Kenya’s the Star said the country had “drawn a firm line” at COP31 and would not “back down until an acceptable deal is secured on climate finance”. The outlet added that the country had “ruled out walking away from the negotiations”. Inter Press Service , a global south-focused news agency, noted that the “deadlock” at the talks leaves COP32 host Ethiopia “to pick up the pieces”. An editorial in the Mexican newspaper La Jornada called the failure to reach consensus “suicidal”, adding: “The conflict is far more complex than a mere opposition between the global north and south, or between hydrocarbon producers and consumers.” Indeed, some developing countries sided with developed countries in blocking the final passage of the Antalya pact.  The Fiji Times reported that Fiji “held the line in the final negotiating rooms”, joining the EU, the UK and several other Pacific countries in “refus[ing] to endorse a weakened compromise that avoided to mention fossil fuels [sic]”. It added: “Yet standing on principle carries heavy practical consequences…COP31’s breakdown is a sobering reminder that, while Fiji must keep fighting in global arenas, its sharpest shield remains regional solidarity and rapid, resilient action at home.” How has the role of China been portrayed? Major Chinese news outlets largely portrayed China as a constructive participant in the COP31 negotiations, a defender of multilateralism and an active advocate for international climate cooperation. State news agency Xinhua reported that “China acted responsibly and advanced the conference process, earning widespread recognition from all parties”. State broadcaster CCTV similarly said that the “international community recognised the positive role China played in addressing climate change”. People’s Daily , the official newspaper of the Communist Party of China, reported that China played a “constructive role” in building consensus and promoting cooperation. It quoted COP31 president Murat Kurum as saying that China was a “key participant” in the multilateral climate process and that its support was “crucial to the summit”. State news agency China News Service said that China demonstrated “ability to act” amid divisions at COP31, highlighting China’s participation in negotiations and initiatives on international cooperation in carbon credits and its climate actions in the global south.  Financial newspaper 21st Century Business Herald said that the Chinese delegation “actively participated in negotiations across all agenda items” and highlighted China’s efforts to advance practical cooperation on climate change.   Three of China’s main state media outlets, Xinhua , CCTV and People’s Daily , covered the COP31 outcome.  Xinhua said that climate multilateralism “moves forward under pressure” as COP31 concluded without a deal. Citing Chinese experts, Shanghai-based outlet the Paper reported that China, the African group and south-east Asian countries were among the parties “willing to accept a compromise [deal] to uphold multilateralism, despite being dissatisfied with the draft text”. CCTV reported that, although COP31 ended without adopting an “outcome document”, this did not mean international climate action had “come to a halt” or that previously agreed climate agreements and international promises would “automatically become invalid”.   State-run newspapers China Daily and the Global Times both published editorials on COP31.  China Daily argued that the COP31 “impasse” underscored the “need to strengthen multilateral cooperation”. It continued that China was “committed to addressing the climate crisis through real action.” The Global Times editorial, meanwhile, responded to criticism that China was “unwilling to take the lead”. It said: “With its own climate governance arrears unpaid, how can western media expect China to ‘pick up the tab’?” Regarding China’s role at COP31, several western news outlets’ coverage focused on its approach to climate diplomacy, trade and the proposed final agreement.  Ahead of the summit’s conclusion, Reuters cited diplomats and observers in reporting that China’s envoys to COP31 stuck to the country’s “accustomed low-key playbook”.  The Financial Times reported that China used the climate talks to “complain about tariffs on EVs and green energy products”.  On the final day of the summit, the Guardian said that China was among the parties that “did not object to the deal”.  Bloomberg also reported that while Chinese diplomats maintained a “relatively low profile”, its “world-leading” companies featured in China pavilion events.  Bloomberg continued: “at a United Nations climate conference that was low on delivery and high on dysfunction, China’s clean-technology companies showed that some aspects of the green transition are persevering despite geopolitical tensions.” What does this mean for the consensus process and reform?  In the aftermath of COP31, many commentators have called for a reform of the COP process. The European Commission is “drawing up plans to overhaul the UN climate summit process, warning that the current negotiating system risks becoming ineffective because a single country can block an agreement among nearly 200 parties”, according to Euronews .  Many other commentators shared the view that the COP process must be reformed. Marco Lambertini, convenor of the Nature Positive Initiative, said in Reuters : “We must be clear: reform remains essential. COPs are cumbersome, expensive, bureaucratic, environmentally unfriendly and frustratingly slow. The consensus rule – adopted in the climate and nature conferences – allows a handful of countries to dilute ambition in the main plenary deliberations. Too often, fossil fuel and agrochemical lobbies interfere with negotiations and obstruct progress. This must change.” Similarly, York University’s Kapoor said in Al Jazeera that the current system results in “an international forum in which the most reluctant participants can limit what everyone else is allowed to say, let alone do”.  The Associated Press ’ Prengaman wrote that “reforms floated over the years include shortening the conference from its current two weeks, limiting it just to delegates and reducing its overall size”. The Independent ’s climate correspondent, Nick Ferris, said the “collapse” of the talks “represents a shocking nadir in the history of COPs”, adding that “the process requires urgent reform”.  Similarly, Pilita Clark, the Financial Times associate editor and business columnist, said “the disaster that was the climate gathering in Antalya should prompt overdue reform”.  Justin Worland, a senior correspondent at Time , likened this year’s summit to the 2009 COP in Copenhagen. He added: “Following the defeat, negotiators went back to the drawing board and created the architecture that led to the Paris Agreement. Today, there’s another opportunity for reinvention.” (For more on COP reform, see Carbon Brief ’s interviews with 16 experts on the topic.) Could COP31 send a ‘positive signal’?  While many editorials lamented the failure of COP31 to agree on the Antalya pact, there were various articles that highlighted a more positive view.  In the Guardian , Dr Bill Hare , chief executive of Climate Analytics , wrote that COP31 was “a line in the sand moment, a victory for multilateralism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no”. He continued:  “The [cover decision that parties] rejected barely recognised the catastrophic climate emergency we’re facing, let alone signalled a definitive move away from fossil fuels.” Others shared the view that numerous countries rejecting the cover decision due to its failure to mention fossil fuels could be seen as a significant moment of pushback. In an interview in Le Monde , Prof Johan Rockström , director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany, said that it is “better to have this kind of crisis and to do something good with it, rather than having a watered-down agreement”. He added:  “It will have a very positive signal: It means that the world is taking risks seriously. The world is taking science seriously.” An editorial in Bloomberg stated that COP31 should “serve as a call for action”, pushing like-minded governments to continue working together to make progress. It added:  “The outcome at COP31, discouraging as it was, strongly suggests that much of the world remains committed to fighting climate change. More than 100 governments, led by the EU, opposed a final declaration that – amid pressure from Russia, Saudi Arabia and other fossil-fuel producers – omitted any reference to the transition away from fossil fuels.”  In Reuters , columnist Antony Currie wrote that the failure to adopt the cover decision could in fact be “healthy”. Elsewhere, in Inside Story , the University of Sheffield’s r Jacobs argued that “this COP’s failure might have been what the world needed”.  Related CB Live: Carbon Brief journalists discuss key COP31 outcomes 24.11.2026 COP31 Antalya COP31: Key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at the UN climate talks in Antalya 24.11.2026 COP31 Antalya COP31: Key outcomes agreed at the UN climate talks in Antalya 23.11.2026 COP31 Antalya Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time 17.11.2026 Emissions The post Media reaction: Who is to blame for COP31 ‘failure’? appeared first on Carbon Brief .

title: Hong Kong government rules out official Tai Po fire memorial, announces HK$630 million in new victim grants
zh_title: 香港政府排除设立官方大埔火灾纪念馆，宣布新增6.3亿港元遇难者补助金
summary: 香港政府在大埔火灾一周年之前宣布，不会举办任何官方纪念活动，同时公布了针对悲剧受害者的新补贴计划。 2025年12月10日，一束鲜花被留在大埔宏福苑附近的路边。2025年11月26日，一场致命大火，吞没了该住宅区八个街区中的七个。照片：何凯莉/HKFP。政务司司长陈家伟周二在商业电台表示，当局不会举办任何活动悼念火灾遇难者，因为
content:
香港政府在大埔火灾一周年之前宣布，不会举办任何官方纪念活动，同时公布了针对悲剧受害者的新补贴计划。 2025年12月10日，一束鲜花被留在大埔宏福苑附近的路边。2025年11月26日，一场致命大火，吞没了该住宅区八个街区中的七个。照片：何凯莉/HKFP。政务司司长陈家伟周二在商业电台表示，当局不会举办任何活动哀悼火灾遇难者，因为社区已经开展了各种活动，包括宗教团体组织的活动。陈补充说，政府不会阻碍合法的纪念活动，并且在某些情况下会提供安排交通等协助。不过，陈敦促公众“谨慎”选择纪念活动，并指出网上有些人试图利用纪念活动“制造麻烦”。陈的这番言论是在 11 月 26 日大埔火灾一周年纪念日之前发表的。一些纪念活动的组织者似乎面临着当局的压力，一些教堂收到了警方的询问，活动突然被取消。与此同时，政府宣布为火灾受害者提供两项新的补助金，总额约为6.3亿港元，帮助他们“尽快开始新的生活”。民政及青年事务局局长麦惠文会见传媒。
民政及青年事务局局长麦家丽周二向传媒表示，在“新起点支援津贴”计划下，每间单位的业主将获发30万港元的补助金，而每名死者家属将获发20万港元的补助金。这些补助金将从宏福苑支援基金中拨出，该基金是一项政府主导的基金，已向企业和公众筹集了 45 亿港元。麦说，火灾发生一年后，支持基金“已基本用完”。该基金约28亿港元已指定用于支持政府买断受火灾影响的宏福苑住宅小区的所有物业。 “化悲痛为动力” 去年11月26日，大埔宏福苑住宅小区发生火灾。当该庄园正在进行大规模翻修工程时，它始于一栋建筑，并迅速蔓延到其他六个街区。这是该市几十年来最严重的火灾，夺去了 168 人的生命，其中包括 10 名家庭佣工，并导致数千人无家可归。调查这起致命火灾的独立委员会一个月前向政府提交了一份关于火灾原因和建议的报告。行政长官李家超在10月下旬的新闻发布会上带领高层官员宣布时任房屋署署长何温妮因火灾辞职，并根据委员会的建议采取了一系列改革措施。
布政司陈家祥。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。陈表示，政府将全面落实火灾后成立的独立委员会提出的全部 120 项建议。他补充说，其中近 30 项建议已经推出，其余近 90% 的建议要么已准备好实施，要么已经在实施中，其中绝大多数将于明年完成。 “我也是香港人。这件事太严重了，令人心碎和悲伤……现在已经一年多了。”

【原文 English Original】
The Hong Kong government has announced ahead of the first anniversary of the fatal Tai Po fire that it will not host any official memorial activities, while unveiling new subsidy schemes for victims of the tragedy. A bouquet of flowers is left on a roadside near Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po, on December 10, 2025. A deadly blaze broke out on November 26, 2025, and engulfed seven of the eight blocks of the housing estate. Photo: Kelly Ho/HKFP. Chief Secretary for Administration Eric Chan said on Commercial Radio on Tuesday that authorities would not host any events to mourn the fire victims, as various activities, including those organised by religious groups, were already underway in the community. Chan added that the government would not obstruct legal memorial activities and would, in some cases, offer assistance such as arranging transportation. However, Chan urged the public to choose memorial activities “carefully,” noting that some people online were attempting to use memorial events to “make trouble.” Chan’s remarks came ahead of the first anniversary of the Tai Po fire on November 26. Organisers of some memorial activities have appeared to face pressure from authorities, with some churches receiving police enquiries and an event abruptly cancelled . Meanwhile, the government announced two new grants for the fire victims, totalling around HK$630 million, to help them “start a new life as soon as possible.” Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak meets the press. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak told the press on Tuesday that under the “New Beginning Support Grants” scheme, the owner of each flat would be offered HK$300,000, while another grant of HK$200,000 would be provided to the family of each deceased victim. The grants will be disbursed from the Support Fund for Wang Fuk Court, a government-led fund that has raised HK$4.5 billion from corporations and members of the public. Mak said that one year after the fire, the support fund “has been largely used up.” About HK$2.8 billion from the fund has been earmarked to support the government’s buyout of all property titles at the fire-hit Wang Fuk Court residential estate. ‘Channel sorrow into motivation’ On November 26 last year, a blaze broke out at the Wang Fuk Court residential estate in Tai Po. It started in one building and quickly spread to six other blocks while the estate was undergoing a large-scale renovation project. It was the deadliest blaze the city had seen in decades, claiming 168 lives, including 10 domestic workers, and leaving thousands homeless. An independent committee probing the deadly fire submitted a report on its causes and recommendations to the government a month ago. Chief Executive John Lee led top officials at a press conference in late October to announce that then-housing chief Winnie Ho had resigned over the blaze , alongside a series of reform measures based on the committee’s recommendations. Chief Secretary Eric Chan. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Chan said the government would fully implement all 120 recommendations put forward by the independent committee established following the fire. Nearly 30 of the recommendations have already been rolled out, while nearly 90 per cent of the remainder are either ready for implementation or already underway, with the vast majority set to be completed next year, he added. “I am also a Hongkonger. This incident was so severe, heartbreaking and sad… It has now been a year and our hearts are heavy. But from the perspective of the government, we should channel our sorrow into motivation for transformation, and make sure there will not be another such incident in the future,” Chan said in Cantonese.

title: Truths, Lies, and Prospects for the New Cross-Strait Security Complex in the Taiwan and Luzon Straits
zh_title: 台湾吕宋海峡新的两岸安全复合体的真相、谎言与前景
source: 华盛顿全球台湾研究中心
summary: 下载整期 PDF 简介 当前霍尔木兹海峡的危机表明了战略性地缘政治瓶颈如何影响全球供应链。吕宋岛和台湾海峡也不例外。曾经被学者和政治家想象为孤立和分裂的这些西太平洋阻塞点，一旦太平洋地区爆发重大冲突，就有可能损害世界经济动脉。在去年的另一篇《全球台湾简报》文章中，作者创造了“新的海峡两岸安全复合体”（NCSSC）一词来表示菲律宾的巩固地位。
content:
下载整期 PDF 简介 当前霍尔木兹海峡的危机表明了战略性地缘政治瓶颈如何影响全球供应链。吕宋岛和台湾海峡也不例外。曾经被学者和政治家想象为孤立和分裂的这些西太平洋阻塞点，一旦太平洋地区爆发重大冲突，就有可能损害世界经济动脉。在去年的另一篇《全球台湾简报》文章中，笔者创造了“新的海峡两岸安全复合体”（NCSSC）一词，以表示菲律宾巩固其群岛和海上防御：将西菲律宾海（WPS）和吕宋海峡作为共同关注点，并将吕宋海峡的未来安全与台湾海峡的安全联系起来。简而言之，NCSSC指的是两岸政治体之间发生和交叉的物质、制度和认知模式。笔者认为，国家社会保障委员会并不是一个空词。它代表了多个参与者遵守的有机行动框架：包括中华人民共和国（PRC）、台湾、菲律宾、美国和日本。该框架的一个值得注意的方面是认知方面如何影响互动的物质和制度模式。
简而言之，虽然一些行为者最近正在恢复过去的真相，即菲律宾伊瓦坦人民和台湾道族人民之间的过去联系，以塑造未来的关系，但还有一些行为者也在利用过去散布谎言。这包括中华人民共和国淡化这种联系，以及对巴丹群岛的主权声索。最终，国家安全安全委员会敦促各国和其他行为者为更广泛的印太地区的未来安全议程制定更明确的政策和灵活的机制。交互框架？众所周知，菲律宾在推行其外交和安全政策方面总是得过且过。文献争论它是否有一个深思熟虑的大战略，但有一件事是肯定的：台湾的未来现在在马尼拉的视野中，因为它看到中华人民共和国不受限制的地区野心。正如菲律宾领导人的言论和官方文件所指出的那样，“被拖入潜在的冲突”是一回事。然而，认识到其在更广泛的印度太平洋地区的地缘政治重要性是另一回事。 NCSSC 是一个合理的框架，可以了解区域参与者在近期和遥远的未来如何互动。最近发生的事件显示了这种互动的规律性。从积极的角度来看，我们可以看到台湾人和菲律宾人在历史和文化上如何通过海洋联系在一起。 2026年6月，来自台湾最南端岛屿兰屿的20名涛人驶入菲律宾最北端岛屿巴丹群岛玛哈涛的一个港口。
这是一段约 111 英里的旅程，乘坐的是名为 Tatala（陶族人所称）或 Tataya（巴丹群岛伊瓦坦人所称）的传统木船。陶人与伊瓦坦人之间如此深厚的联系——尽管由于殖民主义而休眠了 300 年——展示了该地区的当代人民如何通过复制这种 4000 年的移民和航海实践来讲述这些闻所未闻的故事。事实上，这种重燃提醒人们注意它们与南岛语系的联系。尽管缺乏高级政府官员对陶伊-伊瓦坦交流的明确支持声明，菲律宾运输安全办公室战略性地

【原文 English Original】
DOWNLOAD FULL ISSUE PDF Introduction The current crisis in the Strait of Hormuz demonstrates how strategic geopolitical chokepoints can affect the global supply chain. The Luzon and Taiwan Straits are no different. Once imagined by academics and politicians to be isolated and separated, these Western Pacific chokepoints have the potential to harm the world’s economic arteries should a major conflict erupt in the Pacific Region. In a separate Global Taiwan Brief article from last year, this author coined the term, “New Cross-Strait Security Complex” (NCSSC) to denote the Philippines’ consolidation of its archipelagic and maritime defense: interlocking the West Philippine Sea (WPS) and Luzon Strait as a common concern, and linking the Luzon Strait’s future security with that of the Taiwan Strait. Put simply, NCSSC refers to the material, institutional, and cognitive patterns occurring and intersecting between the polities of the two straits. This author argues that the NCSSC is not an empty term. It represents an organic framework of action observed by multiple actors: including the People’s Republic of China (PRC), Taiwan, the Philippines, the United States, and Japan. One notable dimension of this framework comes with how the cognitive aspect affects the material and institutional patterns of interactions. Simply put, while some actors are recently recovering truths of the past—namely, the past connection between the Philippines’ Ivatan people, and Taiwan’s Tao people—to shape the future relations, still others are also using the past to spread lies. This includes the PRC’s downplay of that connection, and claims over the Batanes Islands. Ultimately, the NCSSC impels states and other actors to produce clearer policies with flexible mechanisms for the future security agenda in the broader Indo-Pacific region. A Framework of Interaction? The Philippines is known to muddle through in pursuing its foreign and security policies. The literature debates whether or not it has a deliberate grand strategy , yet one thing is certain: the future of Taiwan is now in Manila’s sights as it sees the PRC’s regional ambitions unrestrained. “To be dragged into a potential conflict”—as noted by Philippine leaders’ rhetoric and official documents —is one thing. However, to appreciate its geopolitical importance in the broader Indo-Pacific is another. The NCSSC serves as a sensible framework to see how regional actors might interact in the immediate and distant future. Recent events show the regularity of such interaction. On a positive note, we can see how Taiwanese and Filipinos are historically and culturally linked by the seas. In June 2026, 20 Tao people from Orchid Island (Lanyu, 蘭嶼 ), Taiwan’s southernmost island, sailed into a port in Mahatao, Batanes, the Philippines’ northernmost island. This was a journey of about 111 miles using a traditional wooden boat known as Tatala (as known by the Tao people) or Tataya (as known by the Ivatans of Batanes). Such deep connections between the Taos and Ivatans—although dormant for 300 years due to colonialism—demonstrates how contemporary peoples of this region are making these unheard stories heard by replicating this 4000-year practice of migration and seafaring. Indeed, such rekindling serves as a reminder of their Austronesian linkage. Though lacking an explicit supportive statement of the Tao-Ivatan exchange by higher government officials, the Philippines’ Office for Transportation Security strategically framed its press release about Manila’s resolve to “ensure that the country’s northern maritime gateways remain protected and efficient” in the case of “welcoming communities.” Image: The Batanes Strait, between Taiwan and the northern Philippines. In 2026, PRC government institutions began to advance the claim that the Batanes Islands (part of the Philippines) were Chinese territory, based on the extension of the continental shelf from Taiwan. (Image source: Google Maps ) Interestingly, two Chinese officials— Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan, and Consul and Head of Post Li Xiaoyan of the Chinese Consulate in Laoag, Ilocos Norte— arrived in Batanes on the same day as the Tao people’s arrival for an “official visit” to the province’s officials. On the one hand, this visit serves to remind Philippine officials of Manila’s “One-China Policy.” On the other hand, it also means that Beijing is now playing into the logic of the NCSSC, which serves as a prognosis for broader regional tensions. Some academics from the PRC contest the “ Out of Taiwan” theory of Austronesian linkage between the Tao and Ivatan peoples. Rather, they prefer to propagate Beijing’s narrative of historic rights over Taiwan, contending that these indigenous peoples came instead from mainland southern China. In July 2026, a Global Times article reported that several PRC-based academics at an academic symposium in Jinan University ( 暨南大學 ) asserted that the Batanes Islands “are legally China’s sovereign territory and form a natural geographic extension of China’s Taiwan island,” on the basis of the 1898 Treaty of Paris and the so-called “Japan-Philippines maritime delimitation talks.” In other words, by virtue of PRC’s historic claims on Taiwan and the Tao’s linkage to the Ivatans, Batanes is allegedly an integral part of the PRC. Philippine government officials have rebuked such PRC academic’s claims on Batanes. For instance, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. noted at the sidelines of the West Philippine Sea summit that such talking points by PRC academics validated his agency’s assessment that Beijing wants to control the Western Pacific. Moreover, given that there is no serious legal basis for such claims, Teodoro noted that “it’s a joke.” Separately, Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro noted that the government would not listen to unofficial channels, while her agency’s spokesperson Analyn Ratonel said that “flights of fancy should not be dignified with a response” since “the Philippines’ sovereignty over Batanes is settled and not up for debate.” Batanes’ lone District House Representative, Ciriaco Gato Jr., similarly rebuked such claims, noting that “any challenge to our status is not merely a geopolitical provocation; it is an affront to our identity that we will not tolerate.” The Philippine’s National Historical Commission (NHC) debunked the Chinese scholarly claims, noting that there is a continuous shelf extending from Northern Luzon through the Babuyan and Batanes Islands and into parts of the Taiwan archipelago based on “current satellite and oceanographic data.” There were also reported circulations among Chinese social media apps last year suggesting that the Philippine province of Palawan—which puts the Municipality of Kalayaan in the WPS under its jurisdiction—is allegedly part of China, by virtue of Ming-era Admiral Zheng He’s explorations. At the macro-level, the Philippine government recognizes that such Chinese talking points are reinforced by foreign influence and malign interference (FIMI) operations —various kinetic activities that aim to alter Filipino solidarity in favor of PRC’s narratives. All Set for the Future? These latest events demonstrate that the framework of interaction demonstrated by the NCSSC does not only involve material and institutional aspects, but also the most basic of human cognitive elements—identity, historical memory, and people-to-people linkage—which are all essential to make the case for brokering the regional commons. They also point to a common denominator: the PRC’s irredentist and unrestrained expansion. However, the NCSSC also opens novel methods for various stakeholders to explore opportunities to assert their agency. The first opportunity refers to cognitive patterns. Whether by constraints or deliberate choice, the Taiwanese government has yet to make any comments on the claim by PRC-based academics regarding Batanes. While ignoring Chinese talking points against the Philippines may sound risk-averse, there is an equal harm inherent in isolating these comments outside the PRC’s broader FIMI operations. Taiwan’s political and security apparatuses would be well advised to invest their attention in curating counter-responses. Moreover, both Manila and Taipei must also leverage linkages between Filipino and Taiwanese cultural communities, academics, think tanks, and civil society organizations, to counter the PRC’s FIMI operational logic. The second opportunity refers to institutional patterns. Since Taiwan is de facto limited in its diplomatic options, the Philippines—with its rapidly expanding strategic partnerships—could serve as a node of a broader security network by framing the Luzon and Taiwan Straits as strategic nerves that cannot be unilaterally occupied by one regional hegemon. Rather, the Straits represent a politically plural area in which to enforce a rules-based international order. This would mean enhancing logistical points of entry and exchange through increased port security, diversifying areas of cooperation between their respective coast guards, fisheries agreements, and anti-piracy and anti-smuggling frameworks, among others. Moreover, while Filipino and American officials argue that Balikatan exercises are solely for Philippine defense, and not intended as a stage for a Taiwan contingency, Filipino and other regional scholars and analysts otherwise note that they are not mutually exclusive. Here, wargaming centers by academics and think tanks can intensify stress-testing assumptions into wider grand strategic considerations, which ripple into Track 1.5/2 dialogues and influence public opinion. The third opportunity refers to material patterns. So far, it is microchip discourse which catches the main attention of the PRC, the US, and other global players on this NCSSC. Minilateral forums serve as cost-efficient avenues in addressing shortcomings of multilateral forums that have been hijacked by PRC’s “Global South Champion” narrative. Moreover, informal talks—like the “Smart Harbor” forum in December 2025 between Taipei and Philippine officials—demonstrate the balance between strategic autonomy and risk-aversion. The Luzon Economic Corridor, which feeds into the US’s Pax Silica initiative to counter the PRC’s World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), are both welcome developments. Taiwan has stated on separate occasions that it is willing to expand economic corridors with the Philippines, either through its proposed “ Silicon Prosperity Initiative ” or as an external node with Pax Silica . So far, Pax Silica has not been well received by most Filipinos, largely due to the lack of an accurate and transparent blueprint, which in turn caused fear among local communities. So far, the Philippines rejection of a diplomatic immunity bargain by the United States in the proposed Pax Silica compound in North Luzon are very well noted points to rebuke PRC narratives of the Philippines “as an American Puppet.” However, the broader goal must be the ability of the Philippines to become a formidable node of the global supply chain through state-led development—not “independent” for its own sake—while addressing local woes. In sum, there is a need for more assertive Philippine counterproposals to serve the country’s industrial interests if it is to become Taiwan’s capable partner. Strategic uncertainty will continue to pervade the 21 st century, and the new geopolitical reality of the NCSSC has now emerged around which all stakeholders must carefully design their approach. They must set clear policy interests while maintaining flexible mechanisms. As for the Philippines and Taiwan, they have an opportunity to set their shared path by modeling such interactions. The main point: The Philippines is becoming more relevant to the future of Taiwan’s security, as the two island states find their security concerns ever-more connected. It is time for all stakeholders to integrate the New Cross-Strait Security Complex as part of the broader regional security architecture. They should and can achieve this through clearer policies, with flexible and responsive mechanisms for future interaction. The post Truths, Lies, and Prospects for the New Cross-Strait Security Complex in the Taiwan and Luzon Straits appeared first on Global Taiwan Institute .

title: Double Dragon: How Taiwan and South Korea Can Collaborate through Chips

下载整期 PDF 台湾和韩国是亚洲四小龙中人口和经济总量最大的两个国家，两国是激烈的竞争对手，尤其是在半导体制造业。但它们对中国市场的共同依赖已成为双方都无法单独解决的弱点。每个人都控制着全球半导体制造的关键节点，它们共同可能构成全球硬件生态系统的瓶颈。台北和首尔应该合作开拓新市场并与大国进行谈判。他们在一起所拥有的影响力是任何一个人都无法单独有效地运用的。台湾和韩国是竞争对手，也是伙伴，长期以来一直是死对头。 1992年首尔从台北转而承认北京这一相对较新的记忆，给许多台湾人留下了挥之不去的背叛感，因为韩国是亚洲最后一个与台湾断绝外交关系的国家。据称，在2000年代和2010年代，韩国三星电子推行“杀台”计划，旨在削弱台湾的芯片制造能力。此外，2010年亚运会跆拳道比赛的有争议的裁判，也被称为“索克门”，严重侵蚀了双边的公众善意。 2012年，富士康创始人郭台铭在讨论与三星的竞争时，使用具有种族主义贬义的“高丽棒子”来指代韩国人，引发强烈批评，进一步助长韩国的反台情绪。
鉴于这段痛苦的历史和所涉及的非常现实的财务利益，韩国和台湾芯片公司的竞争常常被相互对抗的感觉所掩盖。过去，外部试图协调台北和首尔的芯片政策——例如总统乔·拜登的“芯片4联盟”概念——失败了，因为他们没有充分考虑台湾和韩国领先芯片制造商之间激烈竞争的逻辑。然而，不健康的竞争和民族主义不应该让任何一方蒙蔽双眼。如今，两个邻近的东亚民主国家及其制造业冠军之间的协同关系比许多人想象的要强得多。台裔英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋近期分别于5月底和6月初连续访问台湾和韩国，受到两地热烈欢迎。这样的反应说明了两国经济在当今半导体行业中的相互联系和互补程度有多深。黄先生还因其对促进美韩关系的贡献而被授予今年的詹姆斯·范弗利特奖。在经济上，亚洲邻国建立了持久的关系。 2025年，韩国是台湾第三大贸易伙伴，台湾是韩国第四大贸易伙伴。此外，两个经济体之间已经存在部分劳动分工。
台湾公司，尤其是台湾积体电路制造股份有限公司（台积电、台湾积体电路制造股份有限公司）制造先进的逻辑芯片，而韩国的三星和 SK 海力士则在存储器领域占据主导地位。这些公司（以及两国）是当今人工智能革命不可或缺的一部分，无论是在训练人工智能模型还是为数据中心提供服务方面。到2025年，两国经济体的双边芯片贸易额将超过600亿美元，其中台湾的先进逻辑芯片支持韩国人工智能计算基础设施的快速发展，而台湾则封装了许多韩国制造的高带宽内存（HBM）芯片。 2025年台湾进口额约493亿美元

【原文 English Original】
DOWNLOAD FULL ISSUE PDF Taiwan and South Korea, the two largest of the Four Asian Dragons by population and economic output, are fierce rivals, especially in the semiconductor manufacturing industry. But their common reliance on China’s market has become a vulnerability that neither can address alone. Each controls crucial nodes of global semiconductor manufacturing, and together they could constitute a chokepoint in the global hardware ecosystem. Taipei and Seoul should collaborate to open new markets and negotiate with major powers. Together, they have leverage that neither one can wield so effectively alone. Rivals, but Also Partners Taiwan and South Korea have long been bitter rivals. The relatively recent memory of Seoul switching recognition from Taipei to Beijing in 1992 has left a lingering sense of betrayal among many Taiwanese, as South Korea was the last country in Asia to end diplomatic relations with Taiwan. In the 2000s and 2010s, South Korea’s Samsung Electronics allegedly pursued a “kill Taiwan” plan aimed at undermining Taiwan’s chipmaking capabilities. Furthermore, the contested judgment in the taekwondo competition at the 2010 Asian Games, also called “ Sockgate ,” sharply eroded bilateral public goodwill. In 2012, Foxconn founder Terry Gou (郭台銘), while discussing competition with Samsung, used the derogatory racist slur, gaoli bangzi (高麗棒子), to refer to Koreans, prompting strong criticism and further fueling anti-Taiwanese sentiment in South Korea. Given this bitter history and the very real financial stakes involved, the South Korean and Taiwanese chip firm rivalry is often shaded by feelings of mutual antagonism. In the past, outside attempts to align Taipei and Seoul’s chip policies—such as President Joe Biden’s “Chip 4 Alliance” concept —fell short because they did not adequately reckon with the logic of heated competition between leading Taiwanese and South Korean chipmakers. However, unhealthy rivalry and nationalism should not blind either side. The two neighboring East Asian democracies, together with their manufacturing champions, have a far more synergistic relationship today than many assume. Taiwanese American Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s (黃仁勳) recent consecutive visits to Taiwan and South Korea in late May and early June, respectively, garnered warm welcomes in both places. Such a reaction speaks to how deeply interconnected and complementary the two economies have become in today’s semiconductor industry. Huang was also awarded this year’s James A. Van Fleet Award for his contributions to the promotion of US-South Korea relations. Economically, the Asian neighbors have built enduring ties. In 2025, South Korea was Taiwan’s third-largest trading partner, while Taiwan was South Korea’s fourth-largest . Furthermore, a partial division of labor already exists between the two economies. Taiwanese firms, notably Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC, 台灣積體電路製造股份有限公司), manufacture advanced logic chips , while South Korea’s Samsung and SK Hynix dominate memory. These companies (and both countries) are integral to today’s AI revolution, both for training AI models and supplying data centers. The two economies conducted over USD 60 billion in bilateral chip trade in 2025, with Taiwan’s advanced logic chips supporting rapid AI compute infrastructure development in South Korea, while Taiwan packages many South Korean-made high bandwidth memory (HBM) chips. In 2025, Taiwan imported around USD 49.3 billion worth of integrated circuits from South Korea, representing 37.7 percent of Taiwan’s chip imports, far more than from any other country. South Korea accounted for a smaller but still significant share of Taiwan’s integrated circuit exports , around USD 18.4 billion, or 8.8 percent. Shared Challenges Yet despite this growing industrial interdependence, Taiwan and South Korea remain exposed to the same strategic vulnerability: both of them depend heavily on China as a major downstream market for their chips. China’s booming electronics industry consumes vast quantities of semiconductor chips for everything from iPhones to appliances to AI data centers. In 2025, 51.2 percent of Taiwan’s chip exports went to mainland China or Hong Kong, while 41.7 percent of South Korean chip exports headed to the PRC. Such overwhelming reliance on one market—especially one that is actively subsidizing its own domestic chip manufacturers to gradually reduce foreign dependence—carries substantial economic security risk. SK Hynix, Samsung, and TSMC may eventually lose much of China’s demand to state-backed Chinese firms. Moreover, Beijing’s increasingly aggressive security posture and willingness to coerce smaller economies make China a fundamentally unreliable customer. Taiwan and South Korea have long recognized this problem, and each has pursued its own trade reorientation over the past decade. Taipei launched the “New Southbound Policy” under former president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) in 2016. Seoul followed in 2017 by initiating its “New Southern Policy” under then-president Moon Jae-in. These policies succeeded in deepening economic relations with other markets—especially those in Southeast Asia—but have failed to fundamentally reorient chip exports away from China. At the time, the political impetus and market opportunities were simply insufficient. Image: A semiconductor chip manufactured by SK Hynix, one of South Korea’s major chip manufacturers. Taiwan and South Korea manufacturers have faced intense competition qin the market for advanced chips. (Image source: Wikimedia Commons ) How to Team Up Through Chips Today, Seoul and Taipei cannot afford to go it alone. Reducing the relative weight of the Chinese market for their chip exports is not only a security imperative; it is an economic necessity as China’s indigenous chip ecosystem gains ground . Building on the complementary strengths of their semiconductor industries, South Korea and Taiwan could establish an industry-led bilateral working group led by their chip giants—TSMC, Samsung, and SK Hynix—to coordinate semiconductor trade and investment policy. Given the absence of formal diplomatic relations, a direct government-to-government framework with ministerial leadership would not be realistic. However, the sheer economic and monetary weight of these private firms and their close ties to their respective governments would give a cooperative framework substantial influence and credibility. For instance, Taiwan’s National Development Fund is a major shareholder in TSMC, while TSMC founder and former CEO Morris Chang led Taiwan’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) delegation seven times between 2006 and 2023. Similarly, given its strong relationships with Korean chip firms, the Lee Jae Myung administration has a record of leveraging its commercial involvement to pursue decisive political objectives . For instance, ahead of the August 2026 election in South Korea for Democratic Party leadership, Lee promoted a major semiconductor cluster in Jeolla Province backed by planned investment from Samsung and SK Hynix. The initiative benefited one of Lee’s cabinet officials, Kim Min-seok, helping him win the election for party leader to replace Lee’s prominent rival within the party, Jung Chung-rae. Critics accused the administration of using corporate investment to tilt politics in Lee’s favor. Yet, this example demonstrates that Seoul maintains substantial influence over its domestic semiconductor industry—and could work effectively with those firms to facilitate de facto economic collaboration with their Taiwanese counterparts that prioritizes national rather than private interests. Similarly, TSMC — which was established with Taipei’s financial and political backing in 1987 — retains close ties to Taiwan’s political leadership. Taiwanese and South Korean industry associations and companies would provide the institutional backbone of the working group and serve as the primary channel for bilateral engagement, with which the governments could easily and regularly engage. Trade and economic government officials could participate discreetly at the working level or through the two sides’ representative offices. More senior officials would have the opportunity to speak directly in private meetings alongside multilateral institutions in which both are represented, such as the APEC, to coordinate the working group. Some level of unofficial government contact is prudent to ensure that the nominally private sector working group advances the interests of South Korea and Taiwan as a whole, as well as those of their chip firms. This working group would have two primary aims: (1) to develop a common strategy to cultivate new markets; and (2) to coordinate negotiations on new trade and investment agreements with major economies from a position of greater strength. One Strategy, One Face Taiwanese and South Korean chips flow primarily to three sectors: cloud computing infrastructure; consumer goods such as electronics , appliances and automobiles ; and telecommunications equipment. Yet China’s massive output in all three categories has created a gravitational pull that has been hard for Taiwanese and Korean chip firms to escape. As a result, any joint Taiwan-South Korea strategy for cultivating overseas markets and negotiating trade agreements must go beyond setting up chip packaging facilities or even fabs. They must push for a broader set of economic reforms in those markets that will facilitate the rapid development of consumer electronics manufacturing and cloud computing infrastructure. India holds the most potential. Unlike in Southeast Asia , Chinese investment and 5G telecommunications penetration are fairly low , and the country has massive room for growth. Individual Taiwanese and South Korean firms such as Foxconn, Samsung, and Hyundai have had success with particular projects that received special Indian government attention and support. Indeed, the Indian government has repeatedly identified electronics, automobiles, and semiconductors as key sectors to bolster India’s manufacturing output. But India’s complex regulatory environment, bureaucratic proceduralism, infrastructure development bottlenecks, and sometimes counterproductive labor laws mean that India’s operating environment remains very difficult for foreign investors. [1] As a result, India has failed to generate an electronics manufacturing ecosystem—and chip demand—that can rival China’s. By speaking with one voice to New Delhi as the only two economies capable of helping fulfill India’s ambitions in electronics and semiconductor manufacturing, Seoul and Taipei might make greater progress in pressing for reforms in India than either could alone. They might also open greater access for Taiwanese and South Korean firms to a more populated market than China—one which has yet to expend its demographic dividend. The same logic applies to Taiwan’s and South Korea’s policies vis-à-vis the United States. In recent years, successive US administrations have pressed Taiwanese and South Korean chipmakers to expand manufacturing on American soil, from the Biden Administration’s CHIPS and Science Act to the Trump Administration’s greater demands for investments in the United States. Washington’s desire to reshore enough chip production to sustain its defense capabilities and economic system in a supply shock is a rational pursuit. However, as long as key inputs, downstream packaging, and testing still occur outside of the United States, domestic chip fabrication alone is inadequate to ensure US economic resilience. Moreover, a substantial share of the world’s chips still end up in electronics made in Asia. Even if the United States can ensure a bare minimum supply at home for military use and cloud services providers, it will have to look beyond its borders for sufficient demand to make US chip production economical in the long run. Image: Then-President Joseph Biden and then-President Yoon Suk-yeol visiting a Samsung semiconductor plant in South Korea (May 2022), (Image source: Wikimedia Commons ) More recent US administrations have focused on boosting foreign investment in the United States. A Washington willing to subordinate political and geostrategic partnerships in favor of a maximum reshoring effort might seek to play Taipei and Seoul against each other by inducing them to pledge ever greater semiconductor investments. This tactic could gradually hollow out the manufacturing capacity underpinning their respective “silicon shields,” leaving both more vulnerable to security threats from China in the long run — even if the most advanced logic chips are still produced in Taiwan. Instead of competing to offer ever-larger investments and concessions, Taipei and Seoul should coordinate the scale, terms, and technological scope of their US investments. Rather than sending an ultimatum to Washington, Taipei and Seoul could provide a roadmap for a sustained Taiwan-South Korea-US trilateral partnership on semiconductor innovation and fabrication to support US-led AI stack dominance (which covers the whole production chain from critical minerals and energy to semiconductors and telecommunications equipment, upon which the development and rollout of AI software relies). This triangle would be based on mutual trust and common economic and security interests. This would be far more beneficial to all involved—including the United States—than haphazard investment pledges. Targeted investments would complement ongoing economic security projects (such as the Hanwha Philly Shipyard in Philadelphia ) and help anchor chip fab suppliers in the United States. They would also allow Taiwanese and South Korean chip firms to better serve their US customers; indeed, this was part of the rationale that made the initial TSMC plant in Arizona feasible. More direct cooperation between Taipei, Seoul, and Washington may also allow all three parties to identify and capitalize on new production synergies of which US policymakers may not be aware. The main point : Ongoing commercial rivalry and nationalist sentiments show that the Taiwan-South Korea partnership will not be easy. But in continuing to work alone—and sometimes at odds—Taipei and Seoul are leaving leverage on the table that could secure their symbiotic prosperity for years to come. [1] Devesh Kapur and Arvind Subramanian, A Sixth of Humanity: Independent India’s Development Odyssey (Gurugram: HarperCollins Publishers India, 2025). title: Battle for the Capital: Inside the 2026 Taipei Mayoral Race, Part 2
