summary: 下载整期 PDF 封面图片：台北市长电视辩论主办方提供照片（来源：记者） 编者注：这是两部分系列中的第二篇文章。第一篇文章《首都之战：2026年台北市长竞选内幕（上）》于10月30日发表。作为现任台北市长的中国国民党蒋万安面临着与民进党提名候选人沈伯洋连任的巨大压力。尽管他们的背景有相似之处
content:
下载整期 PDF 封面图片：台北市长电视辩论主办方提供照片（来源：记者） 编者注：这是两部分系列中的第二篇文章。第一篇文章《首都之战：2026年台北市长竞选内幕（上）》于10月30日发表。作为现任台北市长的中国国民党蒋万安面临着与民进党提名候选人沈伯洋连任的巨大压力。尽管他们的背景和公众形象相似，但他们的政治声誉、政策问题立场和竞选风格却截然不同。随着11月28日大选（台湾规模较大的“九合一”地方选举的一部分）临近，全岛都在关注“洋流”或“洋流”（见下文）是否会导致未来四年不同的政治格局。竞争候选人的背景 作为目前国内外关注焦点的台北市长竞选的两位领先候选人，蒋和沉在经历和公众形象方面有一些惊人的相似之处。蒋和沈都与台北有着深厚的渊源，因为他们都在这座城市长大，并就读于著名的建国中学，该中学被誉为台湾最好的男子高中。
他们杰出的高等教育背景也强化了他们的精英形象：蒋获得了宾夕法尼亚大学法学硕士学位（LL.M.）和法学博士学位（J.D.），而沉获得了宾夕法尼亚大学法学硕士学位和法学博士学位。加州大学欧文分校犯罪学、法律和社会学位。在台湾政治中，学历和教育资历起着“极其重要”的作用。台湾的竞选广告牌、传单和其他宣传材料往往侧重于突出候选人的教育资历而不是其他特征，因为许多台湾选民将候选人的教育水平和母校的声望视为其执政能力的指标。台湾知名政界人士大多至少拥有硕士学位，而拥有博士学位的人竞选立法或市长级别的公职也很常见。因此，毫不奇怪，在2026年竞选台北市长的六名候选人中，其中五人拥有博士学位。学位或法学博士（第六名候选人拥有硕士学位）。此外，蒋、沈均是各自政党的中年一代，年龄相近，政治履历也较新。
国民党和民进党的重要人物均年龄偏大，据观察，当地政客的平均年龄正在增加。相比之下，两位台北市长候选人被认为是各自政党的“新鲜血液”。 2015年当选立委，2020年赢得台北市长选举；沉在2023年首次进入立法院。无论2026年的选举结果如何，他们都将成为未来十年各自政治阵营中的后起之秀。尽管有上述共同点，两人的政治声誉和道路却截然不同。例如，蒋氏的家族关系

DOWNLOAD FULL ISSUE PDF Cover i mage: Photo provided by the Taipei Mayoral Television Debate organizers (Source: The Reporter ) Editor’s Note: This is the second article in a two-part series. The first article, “ Battle for the Capital: Inside the 2026 Taipei Mayoral Race, Part 1 ,” was published by GTI on October 30. As the incumbent Taipei mayor, Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Kuomintang (KMT, 中國國民黨) faces immense pressure to succeed in his re-election bid against Puma Shen ( 沈伯洋 ), the candidate nominated by the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP, 民主進步黨). Despite the similarities in their backgrounds and public image, their political reputations, stances on policy issues, and campaign styles set them apart. As the election (part of Taiwan’s larger “Nine-in-One” local elections) approaches on November 28, the whole island is watching whether the “Ocean Current,” or “Yang Liu” (洋流) (see further below) , will lead to a different political landscape over the next four years. The Background of the Competing Candidates As the two leading candidates in the Taipei mayoral race—a race now at the center of national and international attention—Chiang and Shen share a few striking similarities in terms of their experience and public image. Both Chiang and Shen have deep ties to Taipei, as they both grew up in the city and attended the famous Chien Kuo High School (建國中學) that is revered as the premier high school for boys in Taiwan. Their prominent higher educational backgrounds also reinforce their elite images: Chiang obtained a Master of Laws (LL.M.) degree and a Juris Doctor (J.D.) from the University of Pennsylvania, while Shen earned a LL.M. degree from the University of Pennsylvania and a Ph.D. degree in Criminology, Law, and Society from the University of California, Irvine. In Taiwan politics, academic qualifications and educational credentials play a role of “ outsized significance . ” It is often the case that Taiwanese campaign billboards, flyers, and other promotional materials focus on highlighting the candidates’ educational credentials over other characteristics, since many Taiwanese voters view candidates’ level of education and the prestige of their alma maters as an indicator of their ability to govern. The majority of well-known Taiwan politicians hold a master’s degree a t a minimum , and it is quite common to see those with doctorate degrees running for public office at the legislative or mayoral level . Therefore, it is no surprise that, out of the six candidates running for Taipei mayor in 2026, five of them hold either a Ph.D. degree or J.D. (the sixth candidate has a master’s degree). In addition, both Chiang and Shen represent the middle-age generation of their respective political parties, sharing similar ages and relatively new political resumes. The more prominent figures of both the KMT and DPP tend to be older, and it has been observed that the average age of local politicians is increasing. In contrast, the two Taipei mayoral candidates are considered the “new blood” of their respective parties. Chiang was elected as a legislator in 2015 and won the Taipei mayor election in 2020; Shen first entered the Legislative Yuan (LY) in 2023. Regardless of the 2026 election results, both of them are set to be rising stars within their respective political camps for the next decade. In spite of the commonalities mentioned above, the two men have quite different political reputations and paths. For example, Chiang’s familial connection has been in the center of public debate for years before the current election cycle. His father, Chiang Hsiao-yen (蔣孝嚴)—who claimed to be the descendant of Chiang Kai-shek (蔣中正) and Chiang Ching-kuo (蔣經國)—was a former minister of foreign affairs and former KMT secretary general. On one hand, the Chiang family name makes the KMT candidate an insider in Taiwanese politics, and the prestige of being the fourth generation of the Chiang family has allowed Chiang Wan-an to enjoy a public reputation following his return from the United States to Taiwan. On the other hand, Chiang’s bloodline credibility has been challenged, as some doubt Chiang’s actual familial connection with Chiang Ching-kuo. Additionally, the incumbent has only apologized to victims of the White Terror (白色恐怖) in his role as Taipei mayor, while some have argued that he should bear the burden as a descendant of the former authoritarian president. Compared to Chiang’s insider status as part of a prominent political dynasty, Shen has been seen as more of a political outsider, with a previous academic career and extensive experience in the nonprofit sector. He is an associate professor in criminology at National Taipei University, with research interests in the field of white-collar crimes. In 2019, he founded the Doublethink Lab (台灣民主實驗室), an NGO analyzing informational and cognitive warfare; and Kuma Academy (黑熊學院) in 2023, a civic group advocating for civil defense. Some are concerned about Shen’s late entry to Taiwan’s politics and his relative lack of administrative experience. Others are worried that Shen’s expertise in foreign interference and brash political style could make him overly provocative for local governance. Image: Taipei mayoral candidates Chiang Wan-an of the KMT (left) and Puma Shen of the DPP (right) shake hands before their televised debate on October 31. (Image source: Central News Agency ) Salient Policy Discussions Throughout the Taipei mayoral campaign, both sides have had heated debates on various policy issues, including drug treatment , school lunch quality , tree trimming , and traffic safety . In terms of the race between Chiang and Shen, the debates surrounding child welfare and the potential relocation of Songshan Airport (松山機場) have drawn the most public attention. Songshan Airport Relocation One of Chiang’s main policy proposals is a plan to relocate Songshan Airport and replace it with a Taipei AI park. In the relocation plan , Chiang pledged to build an AI industry zone, public green space, and a sustainable community with residential areas, historical preservation sites , and transportation networks. Chiang envisioned that the new AI park would create a comprehensive industrial network by connecting with multiple neighboring technological parks: Beitou-Shilin Technology Park (北投士林科技園區), Neihu Technology Park (內湖科技園區), National Biotechnology Research Park (國家生技 研 究園區) and Nangang Software Park (南港軟體園區). The proposal estimates that, over time, the AI park would create an estimated 65 thousand job opportunities, and generate NTD 12 trillion in output value. However, there is pushback against the plan from both the central government and local governments. The Ministry of Transportation and Communication (MOTC, 交通部) has expressed concern about the feasibility of the plan, as well as air transportation capacity. If the relocation project is carried out, Taoyuan International Airport will have to take on significant additional air traffic; yet, as its original design was intended for international rather than domestic flights, it will take around 10 years to increase Taoyuan Airport’s capacity to a level necessary for the loss of Songshan. The Ministry of Interior (MOI, 內政部) has also pointed out that Songshan Airport is critical for search-and-rescue in northern Taiwan, since it also serves as the Songshan Base for the National Air Service Corps (空中勤務總隊). In addition, Penghu County and Taitung County have opposed the policy proposal, on grounds that Songshan Airport has played an important role in medical transportation for the outlying islands and eastern Taiwan. While Shen also agreed that the Songshan relocation plan is worth discussing, he emphasized the necessity to prioritize issues of national defense, medical transportation from rural areas, and disaster relief. Child Welfare Major child abuse cases during Chiang’s current mayorship have sparked public attention on both candidates’ child welfare policy. Since 2022, Taipei has seen eight serious child abuse cases and 115 minor victims. The severity of minor abuse incidents has put the Taipei City government under the spotlight. The Audit Office (審計部) of the Control Yuan (監察院) revealed that Taipei City has not incorporated the assessment system introduced by the central government into its own case screening mechanism, and up to 303 minor welfare reports have been delayed since last August. The Control Yuan has also censured the Taipei City government for negligence on many child abuse cases—including multiple sexual abuse cases at the Piramide pre-school (培諾米達幼兒園) first reported in 2022, the Kaikai Case (剴剴案) in 2023, and a sexual abuse case against a minor employee of McDonald’s restaurant in 2024. Shen has criticized the minor protection mechanisms of Chiang’s government and pledged to make child welfare a policy priority. He and other DPP legislators held a press conference in July accusing the Taipei City government of failing to contact relevant agencies and carrying out procedures only out of formality, revealing the necessity for systemic adjustment. Along with other social welfare policies, Shen proposed to establish a Children and Teenager Safety Governing Center (兒少安全治理中心) under the Taipei Research Institute (台北 研 究院) to integrate data from multiple agencies in analyzing major incidents and reviewing policy responses. He has also stated that he will strive to improve the system and well-being of social workers. In response to Shen and other critics, Chiang affirmed that the Taipei City government has strengthened cross-agency networks regarding childcare management. He also proposed a “7+1 Improvement Plan,” which covers measures such as increasing visitation frequency, strengthening childcare professionals’ training, and providing mental health services. Shen’s Surprising Performance and the “Ocean Current” (“Yang Liu”) Image: A large flag reading “Ocean Current” ( 洋流 , “Yang Liu”) waves above supporters at the opening of Puma Shen’s Taipei campaign headquarters. The term has been adopted as a slogan by Puma Shen supporters. (Image source: qhfan ) Given Shen’s image as a political outsider, many have been surprised by the level of support he has received. The “Ocean Current,” or “Yang Liu” (洋流) , which is derived from Shen’s name, illustrates the island-wide popularity of his campaign. One major attribute to the phenomenon could be the shift of policy focus. This refers not only to particular policy proposals, but also Shen’s entire re-branding in the campaign. During multiple campaigning events and media appearances, he has focused extensively on local issues—such as urban planning, social welfare, and education—while downplaying his usual emphasis on defense and foreign interference. Another tactic that has successfully built up Shen’s active support base is his interactions with voters of different generations. His campaign has attracted the younger generation with non-traditional measures. The interactive features of his campaign website illustrate policy proposals to the younger population, who are comfortable with and reliant on digital interface. His campaign team also extended the normal scope of public policy discussions by collaborating with writers, poets, and artists to create magazines . Shen also endeavors to reach independent voters who are concerned about economic issues and skeptical of the two major parties. He invites voters to in-person “soapbox” (肥皂箱) events to directly express their concerns and needs in daily life. He has also attended multiple interviews , including those held by “Pan-Blue” hosts, to expand target audiences and break out of partisan echo chambers. The impressive civic engagement of Shen’s supporters is also a critical factor in the widespread “Ocean Current” phenomenon. It is worth noting that the “Ocean Current” theme started as a grassroot movement initiated by Shen’s supporters. They turned political enthusiasm into community building through designing and distributing campaign merch, coordinating neighborhood gatherings, and participating in policy discussions. The bottom-up mobilization has effectively complemented Shen’s strategy to re-brand and interact outside of the echo chamber, creating an unprecedented political phenomenon. Can DPP Break the “Blue North and Green South”? Image: Chiang Wan-an of the KMT (top) and Puma Shen of the DPP (bottom) . (Source: jamesonwu1972 and qhfan ) The emergence of the “Ocean Current” movement has surprised the capital city, which has historically been a KMT stronghold. Yet, it remains unknown whether Shen can break the pattern of “Blue North and Green South.” In addition to local governance, the upcoming elections could also alter the national political dynamic in Taiwan. While the DPP holds executive power, it has been facing constant political deadlock in the Legislative Yuan (LY), in which a coalition of the KMT and the Taiwan People’s Party (台灣民眾黨) holds the majority. Tension between the Executive Yuan (EY), the LY, and local government has also reached its height after the LY’s budget cuts earlier this year, as some counties and municipalities receive proportionally less funding than others. The upcoming elections will be an opportunity for the DPP to challenge the KMT’s strong hold on local politics—and a fight for the KMT to defend its base by preventing the spillover effect of Shen’s “Ocean Wave” into other mayoral races. The main point: In Taiwan’s current round of “Nine-in-One” local elections scheduled for November 28, the highest profile race is the Taipei mayoral election. The current campaign pits incumbent mayor Chiang Wan-an of the KMT (a reputed descendant of Chiang Kai-shek) against challenger Puma Shen (Shen Bo-yang) of the DPP. Although Taipei is traditionally a “blue” KMT stronghold, Shen has mounted a stronger-than-expected campaign for the capital city’s top job. As the Taipei mayorship is arguably the most prominent elected position in Taiwan aside from the presidency, the outcome of the election could have implications for future island-wide politics. The post Battle for the Capital: Inside the 2026 Taipei Mayoral Race, Part 2 appeared first on Global Taiwan Institute .

title: Taiwan as a Partner and Leader in Disaster Prevention and Management
zh_title: 台湾作为灾害预防和管理的合作伙伴和领导者
source: 华盛顿全球台湾研究中心
summary: 下载整期 PDF 2026 年，台湾展示了如何优先考虑国内外的防灾、管理和备灾工作。内政部公布的“2026年救灾及汛期整备”计划鼓励跨部门协作，设立偏远地区应急物资和远程通信项目，进一步发展搜救能力。此外，8 月举行的 2026 年汉光演习显示台湾越来越重视对灾害的两级响应：
content:
下载整期 PDF 2026 年，台湾展示了如何优先考虑国内外的防灾、管理和备灾工作。内政部公布的“2026年救灾及汛期整备”计划鼓励跨部门协作，设立偏远地区应急物资和远程通信项目，进一步发展搜救能力。此外，8月份的2026汉光演习表明台湾对两级灾难响应的日益重视：它展示了军队应对危机的能力，以及地方政府和民间通过建立紧急行动中心来应对危机的能力，同时应对互联网速度的大幅下降。最值得注意的是，政府在 7.7 级集集地震（集集大地震或 921 大地震）周年纪念日举办了一年一度的“国家防灾日”，这场 1999 年的灾难导致 2400 人死亡、1 万人受伤、10 万人无家可归。今年的活动重点测试了紧急广播系统（包括手机、电视和广播）和技术，并动员了近 20 万名民间救灾人员和 5000 名急救志愿者进行当地培训。同日，赖清德总统会见台湾外交伙伴，为“世界灾害管理联盟”（WADM）揭牌。
他表示，WADM是“55年来第一个由台湾牵头成立的政府间组织”。这些里程碑使台湾能够加强与美国和欧盟的关系，并与其外交盟友，特别是太平洋地区的盟友建立伙伴关系。因此，台湾可以加强民主友好国家网络，共享灾害管理信息和策略，并确保在灾害发生时保护平民。赖清德总统（中）与世界灾害管理联盟（WADM）成员国代表及其他政府观察员合影。 （来源：Wikimedia Commons） 台湾在防灾方面的国际合作 美国 特朗普政府避免在灾害管理方面扮演世界领导者的角色。这样做留下了一个由中华人民共和国（PRC）等国家填补的权力真空。 2025 年缅甸地震就是一个例子，中国首先提供了货币援助和实地人员援助 — — 相比之下，美国其他组织则较晚做出临时响应。这在很大程度上归因于美国国际开发署（USAID）的虚拟灭绝，否则该机构将接管西方国家的救援。然而，这种趋势与美国在印太地区的长期领导地位背道而驰。
以美国在2004年节礼日海啸后的援助为例：美国军方利用美国国际开发署、农业部和国防部提供的超过8.41亿美元的政府资金提供了人道主义援助。在拜登政府末期，美国行动者在2024年花莲地震后随叫随到提供援助。在基层，捐款是通过台美民间社会组织的筹款活动引导的。台湾公共机构与美国联邦机构的合作

【原文 English Original】
DOWNLOAD FULL ISSUE PDF In 2026, Taiwan has demonstrated how it prioritized disaster prevention, management, and preparedness at home and abroad. The “ 2026 Disaster Response and Flood-Season Preparedness ( 115年救災及汛期整備 )” plan, announced by the Ministry of the Interior (內政部, MOI), encouraged cross-agency collaboration, set up projects for emergency supplies and remote communication for isolated areas, and further developed search and rescue capabilities. Additionally, the 2026 Han Kuang exercises in August showcased Taiwan’s increased attention toward a two-level response to disasters: it demonstrated the military’s ability to respond to crises— as well as the capacity of local governments and civilians to adapt—by establishing emergency operations centers, while dealing with a massive slowdown in internet speed . Most notably, the government hosted its annual “ Disaster Prevention Day ” (國家防災日) on the anniversary of the 7.7-scale Jiji Earthquake ( 集集大地震 or 921大地震 ), a 1999 tragedy that left 2400 deceased, 10,000 injured, and 100,000 homeless. This year, the event featured testing of emergency broadcast systems (including cell phones, television, and radio) and technology, as well as the mobilization of almost 200,000 civilian disaster responders, plus 5000 volunteer first responders, for local training. On that same day, President Lai Ching-Te ( 賴清德) met with Taiwan’s diplomatic partners, inaugurating the “ World Alliance for Disaster Management ” ( 世界災害管理聯盟, WADM). He stated that the WADM is the “first intergovernmental organization spearheaded and established by Taiwan in 55 years.” These milestones allow Taiwan to strengthen its relations with the US and European Union (EU), and partner with its diplomatic allies, especially those in the Pacific. Thus, Taiwan can strengthen a network of democratic friendly nations, share information and strategies for disaster management, and ensure civilians’ protection in disaster scenarios. President Lai Ching-Te (center) with representatives from member states of the World Alliance for Disaster Management (WADM) and other governmental observers. (Source: Wikimedia Commons ) Taiwan’s International Cooperation in Disaster Prevention The United States The Trump Administration has avoided acting as a world leader in disaster management. In doing so, it has left a vacuum of authority that has been filled by countries such as the People’s Republic of China (PRC). The 2025 Myanmar earthquake is an example, where the PRC was first in providing monetary aid, and on-the-ground personnel assistance –compared to the late, ad-hoc response of remaining US organizations. This was largely attributed to the United States Agency for International Development’s (USAID) virtual extinction , which otherwise would have taken the reins in providing relief from the West. This trend, however, is contrary to the US’ long history of leadership in the Indo-Pacific. Take, for example, the US’ assistance in the wake of the Boxing Day Tsunami in 2004: the US military provided humanitarian aid, utilizing more than USD 841 million in government funding from USAID, the Department of Agriculture, and the Department of Defense. At the tail end of the Biden Administration, US actors were on call to provide assistance following the 2024 Hualien earthquake. At the grassroots level, donations were directed through fundraising efforts by Taiwanese American civil society organizations . Public Taiwanese collaboration with the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) has been limited to superficial signaling, with the sole instance of in-person activity being the invitation of the National Science and Technology Center for Disaster Reduction (國家災害防救科技中心, NCDR) to the 2018 National Level Exercise International Observer Program. While some of Taiwan’s disaster-focused institutions, such as the Taiwan Community Emergency Response Team (臺灣民間自主緊急應變隊, T-CERT), are based on FEMA initiatives, these counterparts are facing opposite fortunes when it comes to government relevancy in their home countries. The American organization is facing top-down pressure as executive calls continue for states to take up the mantle of local emergency response. Recently, though, the US and Taiwan’s disaster management partnerships have found a new level, operating with the help of various US state entities. The Taipei Economic and Cultural Office (TECO) in Miami met in March with the Florida Division of Emergency Management to discuss “collaboration on disaster management and resilience initiatives.” Even in the first year of the Trump Administration, Taiwan itself highlighted its outward viewpoint as the US was turning inward: TECO in Houston donated 350,000 USD to relief efforts in the aftermath of the debilitating 2025 Texas floods. Civil society on both sides are also facilitating funding or garnering support for local and global disaster management initiatives. American NGOs such Spirit of America are helping fund a “ mesh network of communications ” across the island, and a drone training program to boot. Across the Pacific, The Taiwan-Asia Exchange Foundation (台灣亞洲交流基金會, TAEF) is helping facilitate inter-civil society organization (CSO) dialogue and stronger cross-sector partnerships. The non-governmental aspect should especially be emphasized, noting that the actions of some other countries’ NGOs remain firmly influenced by state desires. It goes without saying that Washington understands Taipei’s importance to the US from an economic and geopolitical point of view. Nevertheless, a natural disaster might create the same consequences as a foreign attack , thereby putting critical industries and supply chain nodes at risk. The European Union Taiwan’s relations with the Europe and the EU in particular rest on the the ideals of common democratic values , and is marked in economic terms by the ties between Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC, 台灣積體電路製造公司 ) and the European Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (ESMC). In terms of disaster prevention and civil defense, the European Parliament has recognized Taiwan’s “whole-of-society resilience” initiative in the face of PRC coercion. Additionally, a group of organizations concerned with resilience initiatives—the European Economic and Trade Office in Taiwan (EETO), Forward Alliance (a Taiwanese think tank for civil defense), and Samaritan International (a European-based NGO network)— met in September this year to workshop civilian solutions to disasters in both areas. Lutz Gullner, head of the EETO, called Taiwan “one of the reference points for anything related to natural disasters”, citing their expertise. Diplomatic Allies in the Pacific Taiwan’s allies in the Pacific are already suffering from some of the worst effects of climate change. In response, Taiwan has organized international action pathways: along with the US, Taiwan hosted a Global Cooperation and Training Framework (GCTF) workshop “Disaster Management in the Pacific” in New Zealand, bringing about public-private partnerships from a host of Pacific-facing countries. It also highlighted Taiwan’s technical and logistical capabilities in combatting earthquakes, hurricanes, and floods, and its practices and resources that can be shared across the Indo-Pacific. In Tuvalu, Taiwan worked with the US under the Biden Administration to fund climate response projects . While these initiatives have faded in Trump’s second term , Taiwan can still assume a leading role in organizing similar plurilateral funding projects for its island partners across the Pacific, using its own history and experience of natural disaster recovery as a diplomatic strategy. Challenges to Taiwan’s Growing Role in Disaster Management The PRC pressures Taiwan, limiting its international partnerships in all sectors. In the field of disaster management, this manifests in Beijing having long blocked Taiwan’s full membership in the World Health Organization (WHO). It has also used its network of state-funded, controlled, and affiliated media to advocate for its global leadership role, showing off Chinese progress in “global disaster governance” during International Day for Disaster Reduction on October 13. Furthermore, the PRC’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI, 一帶一路) features the “ Belt and Road International Cooperation Mechanism for Disaster Risk Reduction and Emergency Management ” ( 一帶一路自然災害防治與緊急管理國際合作機制 ,), which aims to increase investment and good governance measures with regards to combating the risk of disasters in affiliated nations. However, the PRC’s history of humanitarian work has not been consistent, as shown by examples across Asia, and is often tied to its own resource security . China’s disaster help in Southeast Asia has been tinged by conditional questions of South China Sea sovereignty in the case of the Philippines, and for Indonesia , claims of restrained help. China has also failed to fully address domestic disaster relief, such as the cases of flash floods on the Tibet-Nepal border earlier this year. While China did provide emergency supplies and cash assistance to the Nepali government, much more could have been done proactively to mitigate the effects of the disaster, or at least work with authorities to evacuate locals beforehand. Moreover, Beijing concealed the extent of the damage on the Tibetan side. In this regard, inviting the PRC’s assistance in disaster relief is akin to inviting Beijing to pursue initiatives that prioritize the flow of at-risk goods into Chinese hands. Thus, Taiwan can promote its less conditional and more equitable framework for disaster assistance. Policy Recommendations Based on the aforementioned, Taiwan should: 1. Expand the World Alliance for Disaster Management The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (外交部, MOFA) should seek to expand the number of observers and partners of the WADM beyond the likes of the United States, Japan, Poland, and the Philippines. This momentum should be harnessed to gather support from the free world, and counter the pressure of China’s similar organizations, incentivizing non-interventionist support for countries’ disaster preparation. 2. Strengthen Initiatives of Disaster Prevention and Management with the United States Taiwan should invite US federal and local representatives to future iterations of Disaster Prevention Day , to exchange insights and lessons learned in this field. Furthermore, while the 2026 Han Kuang exercises officially featured American observers , these were featured mainly in military components. Taiwanese disaster management personnel should play a role in directly inviting American guests and other willing participants to take part in civilian components, too. Having friendly observers thinking about, and even participating in a whole-of-society Taiwanese response—to include managing severed communication lines, rescuing those in isolated areas, or even an evacuation of the president—by experiencing it firsthand is critical experience that can help the US and others respond most effectively in a time of need. The MOI should seek to work further with FEMA to drum up support, exchange techniques and capabilities, and partner on research initiatives for disaster prevention and management. Organizing collaboration with the National Disaster and Emergency Management University ( NDEMU ) would help both sides strengthen communication and the ability to move populations before disasters strike. Encouraging a reversal of the Trump Administration’s push to minimize national response funding is key for getting their assistance in case of any Taiwan contingency. In this same vein, funding can be delegated to cooperation through civil society organizations, and to joint training of T-CERT with American equivalents and other interested parties. This does not mean, though, that Taiwan should ignore US states’ willingness to cooperate. On a subnational level, Taiwan should locate more places to host private and public events—not just in cities with a TECO Office like San Francisco or Seattle, but also in smaller municipalities across the Pacific, Atlantic, and the Gulf of Mexico. A focus should be placed on liaison activities such as those conducted by the TECO Miami office with the Florida government. Workshops with American locales and further local governments across Asia and the Pacific should highlight Taiwan’s disaster response strengths, and encourage these places to exchange best strategies for preparation and real time response. 3. Seek Further Collaboration with the European Union Given the experience of the EU, Taiwan should seek opportunities for collaboration regarding the use of nuclear power and other energy sources that allow self sufficiency under threatening conditions. It should take advantage of a changing culture around nuclear energy , even if the reasons for this are not expressly from a disaster response point of view. It can also look to co-fund projects within its borders with interested EU partners–expanding the reach of, for example, the National Fire Agency (消防署, NFA), which has sought to expand its assistance into the larger Indo-Pacific region . Additionally, in light of the European Parliament’s language supporting “contingency planning” for Taiwan, MOFA should seek more detailed agreements with the EU (or even willing individual nations such as the Baltic states ). Such agreements could cover a number of functional areas, to include infrastructure reconstruction and food security. 4. Sign MOUs with Pacific Allies Taiwan should sign memoranda of understanding with Pacific research and development-based partners, collaborating with experts who know of specific islands’ vulnerabilities—thereby strengthening Taiwan’s position in the region amid PRC pressure, and further building connections with its diplomatic allies in the region. It can target both academic groups such as the University of Auckland’s Pacific Climate Research Team, as well independent organizations like the Pacific Resilience Partnership . In the same vein, it should look to monitor and get involved in up-to-now bilateral frameworks for tsunami relief, such as in the case of Hawaii and Samoa’s National Disaster Preparedness Baseline Assessment (NDPBA). Conclusion Natural and geopolitical factors compel Taiwan to be ready for disasters. However, Taiwanese people are not isolated from the goodwill of the rest of the world. Given its geography and aforementioned history, Taiwan has the capabilities to become a reliable partner in disaster management around the world. Taiwan should leverage its capabilities and share its expertise, thereby strengthening both its own resilience and its relationships across the democratic world. The main point: Taiwan should further collaborate with the US and the EU with regards to disaster prevention and management, especially utilizing its mastery of subnational and civil society-based diplomacy, while taking a leadership role in disaster preparation and as a research collaborator amongst its diplomatic partners in the Pacific. This outreach will help skirt the challenges it faces in terms of pressure on the global stage. The post Taiwan as a Partner and Leader in Disaster Prevention and Management appeared first on Global Taiwan Institute .

title: The Agents Howard Lutnick Pulled off Their Jobs
zh_title: 特工霍华德·卢特尼克完成了他们的工作
summary: 商务部长霍华德·卢特尼克在上任之初就疏远了他的常规安全人员，其中一些人辞职了。他不必四处寻找替代者。商务部自己的工业和安全局雇用携带武器并有权逮捕人员的执法人员。该部门重新指派其中一些人担任卢特尼克的私人保镖，从而摆脱了原本可以阻止人工智能芯片走私到中国的特工职责。相反，他们现在会乘坐他的私人飞机旅行并守卫他的各个住所，
content:
商务部长霍华德·卢特尼克在上任之初就疏远了他的常规安全人员，其中一些人辞职了。他不必四处寻找替代者。商务部自己的工业和安全局雇用携带武器并有权逮捕人员的执法人员。该部门重新指派其中一些人担任卢特尼克的私人保镖，从而摆脱了原本可以阻止人工智能芯片走私到中国的特工职责。据五位知情人士透露，他们现在将乘坐他的私人飞机出行并看守他的各个住所。一些商务官员对卢特尼克为了保护自己而转移人员感到困惑，因为美国正竞相在先进人工智能领域保持领先于中国。国际清算银行是美国执行出口管制的主要机构，其代理人接受过培训，以防止美国珍贵技术落入坏人之手。从理论上讲，他们应该站在阻止非法人工智能芯片交易的最前线——这是围绕英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋及其与涉嫌中国间谍的关系引发争议的核心问题。 （黄承认了此事，但​​表示他不知道该女子可能是中国间谍。）BIS 特工接受过执法许多方面的培训，包括犯罪现场调查和反恐。
然而，他们没有接受过保护贵宾和政要的培训。商务部有自己的安全办公室，至少从 1986 年起就向秘书提供保护。但这种保护传统上比为更密切参与国家安全的高级官员提供的保护要轻，后者被认为更有可能成为目标。前官员告诉我们，任命 BIS 特工担任保镖似乎是因为卢特尼克希望获得与国防部长和司法部长等其他内阁成员相当的细节。民主党人和一些共和党人质疑为什么卢特尼克没有采取更多措施来阻止英伟达和其他公司非法销售先进芯片，或者扩大以国家安全为由禁止进行此类采购的公司名单。特别是，立法者希望更多地了解 Lutnick 对 Megaspeed 的处理方式，Megaspeed 是一家总部位于新加坡的公司，因潜在的芯片走私而受到美国商务部和司法部的调查。即使大约一年前，美国情报部门认定 Megaspeed 高管 Alice Huang 为中国情报资产，并与黄仁勋有恋爱关系，商务部也没有将 Megaspeed 列入贸易黑名单。
该公司昨天才被列入名单，就在同一天，英伟达董事会在特朗普总统的压力下恢复了黄仁勋担任公司总裁和首席执行官的职务。然而，迟来的列入黑名单似乎更具象征意义，而不是实质性的：一位贸易专家表示，由于将 Megaspeed 添加到名单中的法规的编写方式，该公司仍然可以获得多种类型的人工智能芯片。工业安全局只有不到200名特工；他们中的大多数人在美国各地的 10 个办事处工作，还有大约十几个在海外工作。目前尚不清楚有多少特工受到卢特尼克保护人员轮换的影响。二

【原文 English Original】
E arly in his tenure , Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick so alienated members of his regular security detail that some of them quit. He didn’t have to look far for replacements. The Department of Commerce’s own Bureau of Industry and Security employs law-enforcement agents who carry weapons and have the power to arrest people. The department reassigned some of them to serve as Lutnick’s personal bodyguards, pulling away from their duties agents who might otherwise have prevented the smuggling of AI chips to China. Instead, they would now travel on his private jet and guard his various homes, according to five people with knowledge of the matter. Some commerce officials were baffled that Lutnick had diverted personnel for his own protection as the United States is racing to stay ahead of China on advanced artificial intelligence. BIS is the nation’s leading bureau for the enforcement of export controls, and its agents are trained to keep prized U.S. technology out of the wrong hands. In theory, they should be on the front lines of the effort to prevent illicit AI-chip trading—the issue at the center of the controversy over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. (Huang has admitted to the affair but said that he hadn’t known that the woman might have been a Chinese spy.) BIS agents are trained in many aspects of law enforcement, including crime-scene investigation and counterterrorism. They are not, however, trained in protecting VIPs and dignitaries. The Commerce Department has its own Office of Security, and secretaries have been provided with protection since at least 1986. But that protection has traditionally been lighter than what’s provided to senior officials who are more closely involved in national security, who are considered more likely targets. The assignment of BIS agents as bodyguards, former officials told us, seemed driven by Lutnick’s desire to have a detail comparable to that of other Cabinet members, such as the secretary of defense and the attorney general. Democrats and some Republicans have questioned why Lutnick hasn’t done more to prevent illegal sales of advanced chips from Nvidia and other firms, or expanded the list of companies that are barred on national-security grounds from making such purchases. In particular, lawmakers want to know more about Lutnick’s approach to Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that’s under investigation by Commerce and the Justice Department for potential chip smuggling. Even after U.S. intelligence, about a year ago, identified the Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as a Chinese-intelligence asset who was in a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, the Commerce Department didn’t put Megaspeed on its trade blacklist. The company was added only yesterday, the same day that Nvidia’s board restored Jensen Huang to his roles as the company’s president and chief executive, under pressure from President Trump. The belated addition to the blacklist appears to have been more symbolic than substantive, however: One trade expert suggested that because of the way the regulation adding Megaspeed to the list was written, the company would still have access to many types of AI chips. T he Bureau of Industry and Security has fewer than 200 special agents; most of them work in 10 field offices across the United States, and about a dozen or so work overseas. It wasn’t clear how many agents were affected by the rotations onto and off Lutnick’s protection staff. Two former officials told us that the assignment usually involved three to four agents at a time. A Commerce Department official said in a statement that “at a time when the Secretary was facing the highest level of credible threats in the Department’s history some agents were temporarily detailed to augment executive protection.” The official added that the number of agents at BIS has increased, though she didn’t provide numbers. As artificial intelligence has boomed, the bureau has struggled to keep pace with the global trade in U.S. chips, suggesting that it could ill-afford the secondment of agents elsewhere. The Commerce Department’s Office of the Inspector General, in a June report, found that BIS has not taken adequate action to enforce export controls on goods destined for China and Hong Kong. In a report a month earlier, it found similar enforcement failures regarding Russia and Belarus. [ Read: The limits of positive thinking ] Overall, the number of public penalties and enforcement actions for violating U.S.-export rules has fallen since Lutnick took office in February 2025. Across 2023 and 2024, the annual case rate was close to 100; in the 17 months from March 2025 to the start of August, the annualized rate dropped to about half that, according to The Export Practitioner , a trade publication. Amid the furor over Nvidia, the inspector general last week began an evaluation of the bureau’s oversight of advanced-computing chips. Current and former commerce officials we spoke with put the blame for the bureau’s lackluster performance on Lutnick and his team. They contend that Lutnick and senior officials have repeatedly stressed Trump’s interest in a détente with China and have placed commercial interests above national security. Trump has made clear his desire for a new China trade deal and last week sought to further improve relations with President Xi Jinping at a summit in Shenzhen . Trump’s approach runs counter to the administration’s aggressive posturing about the need to restrict Chinese trade. The diversion of agents to serve in Lutnick’s protective detail has sapped expert resources and prevented agents from doing the high-stakes work they are hired and trained to perform, current and former officials told us. “They’re not trained for protective detail,” one current official told us. “These are professional investigators.” A former official called it “completely inappropriate” to pull agents to protect Lutnick. The Commerce Department, meanwhile, is seeking an increase in staffing. In April, Lutnick told the House Appropriations Subcommittee that BIS needed additional resources and enforcement personnel, including 290 new enforcement officers, to prevent the diversion of semiconductors to China and to protect American innovation. He didn’t mention the redeployment of some of the officers whom BIS already employed. L utnick , a friend of Trump’s and a former Wall Street executive, is one of the Cabinet’s wealthiest members. His most recent financial-disclosure form lists his holdings, which include a $25 million mansion that he purchased in 2024 in the Berkley neighborhood of Washington, D.C. The house, modeled after France’s Château du Grand-Lucé, was until recently the most expensive home ever sold in the capital. Lutnick also owns properties in New York City, the Hamptons, and South Florida. He made much of his money as the CEO of Cantor Fitzgerald, a New York financial firm, where his two sons, Brandon and Kyle, hold senior leadership positions. Cantor also held approximately 1.8 million Nvidia shares as of the end of June, which were valued at the time at $362 million, according to the company’s financial disclosures. (The firm has said that it has no material proprietary position in Nvidia, and its holdings mainly arise from its services for clients.) [ Read: The president’s most annoying buddy ] Lutnick no longer has a financial interest in Cantor Fitzgerald, but some in Congress have argued that his close family ties to the firm represent a conflict of interest. Some White House officials have privately expressed similar worries, according to several current and former administration officials. Despite these concerns, and Lutnick’s well-documented feuds with others at the top of the administration, Trump has consistently rebuffed pushes to drop his friend from the Cabinet. Jack Rodriquez-Vars contributed to this report.

title: Recon Marines Join Finnish Naval Exercise, Baltic NATO Naval Drills

summary: 2026 年 11 月 7 日，美国海军陆战队部队侦察连、第 2 侦察营、第 2 海军陆战师在芬兰南部海岸的北约增强警戒活动波罗的海哨兵期间进行船只行动。美国海军陆战队照片 作为芬兰海军演习和北约增强警戒活动 (eVA) 波罗的海哨兵的一部分，四打海军陆战队侦察兵本周将在芬兰执行任务。芬兰海军的窄水域 26-2 演习将于周三在芬兰南部沿海地区和芬兰湾开始。此次演习将持续到12月。 4. 练习是
content:
2026 年 11 月 7 日，美国海军陆战队部队侦察连、第 2 侦察营、第 2 海军陆战师在芬兰南部海岸的北约增强警戒活动波罗的海哨兵期间进行船只行动。美国海军陆战队照片 作为芬兰海军演习和北约增强警戒活动 (eVA) 波罗的海哨兵的一部分，四打海军陆战队侦察兵本周将在芬兰执行任务。芬兰海军的窄水域 26-2 演习将于周三在芬兰南部沿海地区和芬兰湾开始。此次演习将持续到12月。 4. 此次演习是芬兰海军秋季的主要演习，芬兰海军舰艇和部队与北约盟国在波罗的海北部及其沿岸进行联合海军作战训练。据芬兰海军新闻稿称，除了芬兰人员、船只和飞机外，爱沙尼亚海军指挥和支援舰EML Wambola (A433)以及约50名美国海军陆战队人员也将参加此次演习。这支海军陆战队共有四​​打成员，来自海军陆战队第二师第二侦察营和驻扎在北卡罗来纳州勒琼海军陆战队基地的第二海军陆战队远征军信息大队。该大队于 10 月初在欧洲海军陆战队轮调部队 (MRF-E) 的指挥下进行前沿部署，当时他们的任务是向芬兰提供先进的远征监视和战术侦察能力，同时与波罗的海哨兵指挥下的终点海岸旅一起作战。
该部队部署的能力包括 Stalker VXE-30 无人机系统 (UAS)。芬兰国防军和边防部队的约 3,500 名人员，包括应征入伍者和预备役军人，正在参加“狭窄水域 26-2”行动。新闻稿中写道：“这次演习是测试 12 月份应征入伍的部队组成技能的机会，也是训练预备役人员执行战时任务的机会。”芬兰陆军和芬兰空军将在南海岸和波罗的海北部利用直升机、战斗机和无人系统进行与演习相关的飞行活动。美国海军陆战队参谋中士。巴尼·南 (Barney South) 是海军陆战队第二师第二侦察营第二部队侦察连的一名海军陆战队队员，在 2026 年 5 月 22 日于芬兰穆斯塔马举行的狭窄水域 26 演习中，在两栖插入期间占据安全位置。 美国海军陆战队照片 芬兰海军还将利用这次演习让芬兰公司测试新技术，包括各种无人系统以及监视和保护设备。海军操作环境。该军种将收集演习的反馈，用它来评估测试系统对海军防御的贡献。演习结束后，美国海军陆战队将恢复参加自10月以来一直在进行的波罗的海哨兵活动。
北约于 2025 年 1 月启动了波罗的海哨兵，以阻止进一步破坏波罗的海关键水下基础设施的企图。根据美国海军陆战队在北约演习中发布的信息，在 10 月份的波罗的海哨兵期间，美国海军陆战队与芬兰部队合作提供远征监视和战术侦察能力，加强海域意识并支持保护重要海底基础设施的努力。 “这一努力展示了海军陆战队远征能力如何补充盟军海上力量、提高信息能力

【原文 English Original】
U.S. Marines with Force Reconnaissance Company, 2d Reconnaissance Battalion, 2d Marine Division, conduct boat operations during NATO Enhanced Vigilance Activity Baltic Sentry off the coast of southern Finland, Nov. 7, 2026. US Marine Corps photo Four dozen Reconnaissance Marines will operate in Finland this week as part of a Finnish naval exercise and NATO’s enhanced Vigilant Activity (eVA) Baltic Sentry. The Finnish Navy’s Narrow Waters 26-2 drill will begin Wednesday in the coastal areas of Southern Finland and in the Gulf of Finland. The exercise will run throughDec. 4. The exercise is the Finnish Navy’s main exercise in autumn and involves Finnish Navy ships and troops and NATO allies training in combined naval operations in the northern Baltic Sea and its coast. In addition to Finnish personnel, ships and aircraft, Estonian Navy command and support ship EML Wambola (A433) and about 50 U.S. Marine Corps personnel will participate in the exercise, according to a Finnish Navy news release . The Marine force –four dozen members – are from 2nd Reconnaissance Battalion, 2nd Marine Division and II Marine Expeditionary Force Information Group based out of Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune, N.C. The group were forward deployed in early October under Marine Rotational Force-Europe (MRF-E) when they were tasked to Finland to provide advanced expeditionary surveillance and tactical reconnaissance capabilities while operating alongside the Finish Coastal Brigade under Baltic Sentry. The capabilities fielded by the unit include the Stalker VXE-30 Unmanned Aerial System (UAS). Approximately 3,500 personnel, including conscripts and reservists, of the Finnish Defense Forces and Border Guard are participating in Narrow Waters 26-2. “The exercise is an opportunity to test the skills of conscripts mustering out in December in their unit compositions, and train reservists for their wartime tasks,” reads the release. The Finnish Army and Finnish Air Force will conduct exercise-related flight activity with helicopters, fighters and unmanned systems on the south coast and northern Baltic Sea. U.S. Marine Corps Staff Sgt. Barney South, a force reconnaissance Marine with 2nd Force Reconnaissance Company, 2nd Reconnaissance Battalion, 2nd Marine Division, holds a security position during an amphibious insertion as part of exercise Narrow Waters 26 in Mustamaa, Finland, May 22, 2026. US Marine Corps photo The Finnish Navy will also use the exercise to have Finnish companies test new technology, including various unmanned systems and surveillance and protection equipment, in a naval operating environment. The service will collect feedback from the exercise, using it to assess the contribution of the tested systems to naval defense. Following completion of the exercise, the U.S. Marines will resume their participation in Baltic Sentry activities, which has been ongoing since October. NATO launched Baltic Sentry in January of 2025 to deter further attempts to damage critical underwater infrastructure in the Baltic Sea. During Baltic Sentry in October, U.S. Marines worked alongside Finnish forces to provide expeditionary surveillance and tactical reconnaissance capabilities, strengthening maritime domain awareness and supporting efforts to protect critical undersea infrastructure, according to a U.S. Marine Corps release on the NATO exercise. “The effort demonstrated how Marine Corps expeditionary capabilities can complement Allied maritime forces, improve information sharing, and contribute to security across the Baltic maritime environment,” reads the release. U.S. Marine Corps Major General Daniel Shipley, Commander, U.S. Marine Corps Forces Europe and Africa, met with Rear Admiral Tuomas Tiilikainen, Commander of the Finnish Navy on Nov. 6 in Finland to discuss NATO interoperability, the U.S.-Finnish defense relationship and the role of combined forces in defending the Alliance’s northern and eastern flanks, according to the release. The engagement highlighted the ongoing partnership between the U.S. Marine Corps and Finnish Navy and the importance of integrating capabilities within a broader Nordic force prepared to defend NATO territory, reads the release. U.S. Marines with 2nd Force Reconnaissance Company, 2nd Reconnaissance Battalion, 2nd Marine Division, board a U-600 Jurmo LCP Watercat M12 during Finnish weapons and boat familiarization training as part of exercise Narrow Waters 26 in Upinniemi, Finland, May 15, 2026. US Marine Corps photo In Narrow Waters 26.2, Finnish, Estonian and U.S. forces will train together to refine maritime command and control, reconnaissance, fire coordination and Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) defense. The exercise is meant to strengthen participants’ ability to share information, synchronize operations and integrate complementary capabilities in a complex maritime environment, reads the release. “When Allies train together in demanding environments, we build the trust, capability, and combat credibility required to operate as one combined force,” said Shipley in the release. “Our Finnish allies are highly capable. The [U.S] Marines are here to sharpen interoperability with Finnish and Estonian allies, strengthen maritime readiness, and ensure our Alliance remains prepared to meet any challenge.” Finnish, Estonian and U.S. personnel will train at the task group, task unit and unit levels to strengthen coordination and improve their ability to operate together. The Recon Marines will contribute reconnaissance, fires liaison and coordination, command and control, and CBRN defense capabilities. “These contributions will help participating forces strengthen maritime domain awareness, integrate air and missile defense, coordinate strike capabilities, and rehearse responses to CBRN threats,” reads the release. As part of its transition to Force Design 2030, the Marine Corps has not only been carrying out training in distributed and dispersed operations in the Indo-Pacific but also in Northern Europe. Along with participation in Baltic Sentry, the service deployed expeditionary long-range missile systems to Norway in August and September under Operation Atlantic City 26 . The Marine Corps also continues to carry out conventional warfare training in Norway with 3,000 Marines deploying to Norway in March for exercise Cold Response .

互动：跟踪 COP31 气候峰会上的谈判文本 互动：在 COP31 气候变化峰会上谁想要什么 由于严重分歧阻碍了就主席主导的协议达成一致，《联合国气候变化框架公约》主席西蒙·斯蒂尔表示“深感失望”，他谈到了联合国气候进程的“改进、现代化和改革的空间”。闭幕全体会议。其中包括为全球“公正转型”建立新“机制”的相当有限的或程序性的成果，以及对遭受气候灾难的国家的支持。不过，谈判之外还取得了一些进展，越来越多的国家联盟倡导“摆脱”化石燃料的“路线图”。随着主席国推动“电气化”成为关键主题，约 80 个国家还签署了到 2035 年确保 35% 的最终能源消耗来自电力的全球目标。在此，Carbon Brief 深入分析了安塔利亚会议在 COP31 谈判内外的所有关键成果。

Print article Share Article Contents Expand menu Close Formal negotiations Turkish and Australian leadership Cover decision COP reform Adaptation Finance Just transition work programme Loss and damage Gender Article 6 Agriculture and food security Mitigation work programme Response measures Action for climate empowerment Trade Second global stocktake Long-term goal review Around the COP Fossil fuels Action agenda Global leaders Electrification China at COP31 Ocean Deforestation Methane New climate science Food and water NDCs Protests and access Road to COP32 and beyond The COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, have failed to reach agreement on a “pact” that lacked clear references to curbing fossil fuels or scaling up climate finance . The “Antalya pact”, proposed by the joint Turkish-Australian presidency, was rejected in the final hours by the EU, the UK and several climate-vulnerable nations. Meanwhile, many developing countries criticised the lack of progress on climate finance and indecision on a proposed $120bn target for funding climate adaptation. COP31 coverage COP31: How Ed Miliband answered Carbon Brief readers’ questions Analysis: Climate-finance pledges fall 70% as countries meet at COP31 Analysis: Which countries have sent the most delegates to COP31? Q&A: What is the Belém-Antalya mechanism for a ‘just transition’? Interactive: Tracking negotiating texts at the COP31 climate summit Interactive: Who wants what at the COP31 climate change summit With stark divisions preventing agreement on the presidency-led pact, UNFCCC chief Simon Stiell expressed “deep disappointment”, speaking of “scope to improve, modernise and reform” the UN climate process. Despite a chaotic endgame that saw the overrunning COP become the longest in history, it did not end in complete failure, with many items adopted in the closing plenary. These included fairly limited or procedural outcomes on a new “ mechanism ” for global “ just transitions ”, plus support for countries struck by climate disasters. There was some progress beyond the negotiations, though, with growing coalitions of nations championing “ roadmaps ” for “transitioning away” from fossil fuels. With the presidency promoting “ electrification ” as a key theme, around 80 nations also signed up to a global target of securing 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035. Here, Carbon Brief provides in-depth analysis of all the key outcomes from Antalya, both inside and outside the COP31 negotiations. (See Carbon Brief’s coverage of COP30 , COP29 , COP28 , COP27 , COP26 , COP25 , COP24 , COP23 , COP22 , COP21 and COP20 .) Formal negotiations Turkish and Australian leadership Cover decision COP reform Adaptation Finance Just transition work programme Loss and damage Gender Article 6 Agriculture and food security Mitigation work programme Response measures Action for climate empowerment Trade Second global stocktake Long-term goal review Guidance on NDCs Rio synergies Around the COP Fossil fuels Action agenda Global leaders Electrification China at COP31 Ocean Deforestation Methane New climate science Food and water NDCs Protests and access Road to COP32 and beyond Formal negotiations Turkish and Australian leadership Turkey and Australia presided over the longest COP in history – and failed to find consensus on their proposed “cover decision”, exposing deep fractures between countries on key issues such as fossil fuels and the need for developed nations to meet climate-finance pledges. Experts told Carbon Brief that, strictly, the talks did not “collapse” as several negotiated items were still adopted. Rather, the rejection of the cover decision represented, for the first time, “those who want a higher level of ambition actively reject[ing] the lowest common denominator on offer”, said one veteran observer. Dispute over who would host COP31 – representing the “western Europe and other states” region – had gone on for three years . In the end, the two main rivals, Turkey and Australia, agreed to a deal last year at COP30 that the summit would take place in Antalya, Turkey, with Australia acting as “president of negotiations”. COP31 president and Turkish minister Murat Kurum and COP31 “president of negotiations” and Australian minister Chris Bowen. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis Critics questioned whether either country was well-placed to host, given their ongoing fossil-fuel expansion. Turkey faced criticism for announcing the discovery of two new oil fields on the eve of the summit, while recent Carbon Brief analysis found that Australia is the third-largest CO2 exporter in history because of its fossil-fuel production. Ahead of the summit, the presidency released four official letters outlining a vision for COP31. The first letter , written by COP31 president Murat Kurum in April 2026, confirmed the appointment of Australian climate minister Chris Bowen as “president of the negotiations” and announced that a pre-COP would be held in Fiji in October. The second letter , authored by both Kurum and Bowen from the Copenhagen climate ministerial in May, said that “COP31 presents a vital opportunity to further accelerate…in the areas of clean energy, electrification and resilient infrastructure”. The third letter , published in August 2026, gave more details on the presidency’s plans for the “ action agenda ” – the part of the UN process that mobilises coalitions of nations and non-state actors to push climate action further. This letter also introduced a key aim from the presidency to get countries to agree to increase electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035 (often referred to as “35 by 35”). (See: Electrification .) The final letter , published in October ahead of the pre-COP in Fiji, said that the presidency would centre on “delivering a COP focused on accelerating implementation, electrification and resilience in an uncertain world”. It added that “many parties have emphasised the importance of reviewing and continuously improving UNFCCC processes, to ensure it remains fit for purpose, sustainable and focused as negotiations evolve over time”, adding: “At COP31, we will hold presidency consultations to hear parties’ views on how to strengthen UNFCCC processes, to ensure growing demands are met and to effectively deploy resources.” The pre-COP in Fiji was held from 5-8 October and was attended by 3,000 people. In this somewhat intimate setting, Bowen announced that Turkey and Australia had agreed to negotiate a “presidency-led” cover decision at COP31. He added that revealing this before COP was part of the presidency’s “upfront, transparent and consultative approach”. Later that month, the presidency named the five ministerial pairs from developed and developing countries that would take key negotiation issues forward at COP31. These issues were mitigation, adaptation, finance, just transition and oceans. COP31 kicked off on 9 November, with climate negotiations scholar (and Carbon Brief contributing editor ) Dr Joanna Depledge noting that it was clear from the summit’s opening ceremony that “Australia [was] the junior partner” in the presidency. COP’s opening day ran late into the night as the presidency worked to avert a fight over proposed changes to the summit’s negotiations agenda. Simon Evans 9 November 2026, 10:40 GMT COP31: Agenda adopted! Agenda adopted! Moments ago in Antalya, Turkey, COP31 president Murat Kurum outlined how an “agenda fight” has been averted, despite various proposals for additions to proceedings. This came after a short delay, while a series of huddles took place on… Read more on CB Connect → The next day, in plenary, Kurum announced that a resolution had been found. He said that calls for new agenda items on adaptation finance and trade were rejected, whereas an item on a new climate finance “work programme” had been added. (The EU expressed “deep concern” about the addition.) Kurum added that two extra proposed items on mountains and climate change – made more poignant by recent catastrophic floods in Nepal – were also not added to the agenda. However, he said that the presidency would instead hold consultations on the topic. Though an early scrap over the agenda was avoided, the summit’s opening days were plagued with logistical problems. Attendees were forced to spend hours navigating traffic and queues just to get into the venue – sparking serious access concerns . A crowded roadbridge near the COP31 entrance in Antalya, Turkey. Credit: ZUMA Press, Inc. / Alamy Stock Photo The problems persisted into the first day of the world leaders’ summit on 11 November, when delegates were informed that they should travel between the hours of 5-7am to secure access to the venue. Ire only grew when security staff still let people in after this time. On Friday morning, the presidency released a “reflections” text from its consultations with countries on what they would like to see in a cover decision. This was an “informal note” with a bullet-pointed list of topics that might be included. On Saturday evening, Kurum told a press conference that “around 30 countries” had indicated support for the 35 by 35 pledge. However, he had little to share on progress in the negotiations and eluded questions on how he planned to include “fossil fuels” in the cover decision. In the small hours of Sunday morning, half-way through the summit, Kurum announced presidency and ministerial consultations on “outstanding political issues”. He also invited ministers to a “divan” – a group meeting, not a daybed – to discuss cross-cutting issues. On Monday afternoon, the presidency dropped an 18-page first draft of its proposed cover decision – along with a short “ presidency note ” explaining that all elements were still in play, including whether or not they should appear in a final text. (See: Cover decision .) At a press conference, Bowen told journalists that the presidency decided to release the text “early” to allow parties to debate on it for as long as possible and acknowledged that it would need to be “refined” down. On Wednesday evening, the presidency held its divan, where delegation heads sat in a circle and were asked to share their priorities for finding consensus in the negotiations. Countries take part in a “divan” at COP31. Credit: UNFCCC / Flickr Speaking at the divan, Kurum told parties that the second draft cover decision would be published that evening. In the end, the second draft cover decision was published on Thursday. Later that day, Kurum and Bowen spoke at a press conference, talking up their latest draft with lofty claims that it could “achieve [the] covenant of 1.5C and nothing more”. However, the second draft was rejected by countries and civil society alike. (See: Cover decision .) On Friday – the summit’s last scheduled day – the mood at COP soured. With few official updates, delegates relied on ever-changing rumours about when a new text might emerge. Negotiations on other key issues also remained stuck, as civil society dubbed it the “worst COP in history” at a press conference attended by Carbon Brief.  In the evening, the presidency opened the closing plenary to gavel through non-contentious items – and announced that a new text would not be released until Saturday morning.  They were interrupted by a protester wearing a shirt that said “you are killing the future” and with a red noose around their neck. As talks ran into overtime on Saturday, any kind of official update failed to arrive.  An open letter signed by 100 civil society organisations told the presidency it was “on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs the UNFCCC has ever had”. As Turkish support staff started packing down the party pavilions, behind-the-scenes disputes between country ministers intensified. Carbon Brief understands that 126 countries – made up of the EU, UK, the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), the Independent Association of Latin America and the Caribbean (AILAC), the Umbrella Group (UG) and least-developed countries (LDCs) – approached the presidency as a united front to demand changes to the cover decision. These changes included on how it referenced transitioning away from fossil fuels, adaptation finance and carbon capture and storage. width: 64px; align-self: start; } } Membership Connect with our community Join CB+ A new draft cover decision did not arrive until the early hours of Sunday morning.  With official updates still few and far between, rumours swirled that many countries were still not happy with this iteration of the text and planned to reject it. Later that day, another version of the text arrived – but it contained only minor changes. In a fiery final plenary session on Sunday afternoon, several countries rejected the cover decision – citing reasons including its failure to respond to humanity’s overshoot of 1.5C of global warming, its failure to clearly mention fossil fuels and its lack of clear figures for adaptation finance. (See: Cover decision .) While countries rejected the cover decision, they did find consensus on other texts, including for the just transition work programme , the global goal on adaptation , the climate finance work programme , carbon markets , long-term finance and “Article 2.1c”. The final gavel came down at 7:33pm local time – nearly 50 hours after the summit’s scheduled end. This makes COP31 the longest in history.  Cover decision The final draft of a COP31 “cover decision” was rejected by at least 32 countries during a chaotic – and, at times, acrimonious –  closing plenary in Antalya. Towards the end of the summit, Kurum had told a press conference attended by Carbon Brief that he wanted the cover decision to be known as the “Antalya accord”. (This was later amended in the last formal draft to be the “Antalya pact”.) But, in the closing plenary, the EU told the assembled delegates: “We will not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” According to Carbon Brief’s tally during the closing plenary, the agreement was also explicitly rejected by Panama, the Marshall Islands, Belize, Norway and Vanuatu. After it was clear that the pact would not be adopted, the 44-member LDCs, the UK, South Korea and Japan all said that consensus had not been reached, a softer form of indicating dissent. The six-member environmental integrity group (EIG) also registered its “concerns” with the text. For months ahead of the summit, the Turkish and Australian presidencies had been talking up the idea of a COP31 cover decision – an overarching political statement. Indeed, Bowen had publicly raised the idea of a COP31 cover decision at last year’s COP30 in Brazil, even before the agreement to act as joint president with Turkey had been finalised. In his opening speech in Antalya, Bowen said that he had agreed with Kurum to take forward a “presidency-initiated, party-driven [cover] decision for COP31”. He had said at a pre-COP in Fiji: “There is a clear expectation that COP31 must respond to the global moment – to send a clear message to accelerate implementation…And to demonstrate our continued commitment to multilateralism, to international cooperation and to the Paris Agreement.” Bowen stressed that this should not lead to a “lengthy political statement”, but that he wanted it to respond to the imminent “ overshoot ” of 1.5C, the “catastrophic impacts” of warming and the “tangible progress” being made in the energy transition. For Turkey, the cover decision became a vehicle to promote what had started out as its voluntary target for electricity to make up 35% of global final energy by 2035. (See: Electrification .)  While early on, Russia publicly challenged the legal basis for a cover decision, given it was not on the official agenda, these procedural objections fell away as the summit continued. Many other recent COPs have issued cover decisions, setting a firm precedent . Carbon Brief understands that legal advice from the UNFCCC secretariat confirmed the broad authority of the presidency to initiate a cover decision in Antalya. Nevertheless, many parties remained unhappy about the existence of the cover decision, the process by which it was put together and the impact it had on time for other negotiations. For the LMDCs, India told the closing plenary: “We are also acutely aware that [the cover decision] has taken away our attention from the mandated items of the agenda, which we had to deliver.” It had quickly become clear that Bowen’s ambitions for a brief cover decision would be in vain, when a lengthy 144-paragraph “ reflections ” text was released on 16 November. Simon Evans 13 November 2026, 05:55 GMT NEW: COP31 cover decision ‘reflections’ text Today, Friday 13 November, the COP31 presidency published a “reflections” text on consultations it has been holding with heads of national delegations on a potential “cover decision”. This is not a fully formed draft text, but instead contains an organised… Read more on CB Connect → This document was a compilation of all the issues that parties had put forward for inclusion, ranging from quantified climate-finance goals through to firm timelines for the next assessment report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). Other ideas included that developed countries should reach net-zero emissions by 2030, that certain trade policies should be “phase[d] out” next year and that the largely defunct Kyoto Protocol should be resurrected, with binding carbon targets for developed nations. The text also included the presidencies’ favoured “35 by 35” electrification target , as well as language on the transition away from fossil fuels. (See: Fossil fuels .) A second iteration – in reality, the first fully formed draft cover decision – was published on 19 November, consisting of just 80 paragraphs. This version was immediately criticised for having excised any mention of fossil fuels, as well as deleting the $120bn adaptation-finance target wanted by developing countries. (See: Adaptation .) It retained the “35 by 35” target, but only as one of a menu of options, listed as areas for “global cooperation” to “keep 1.5C within reach”. Paragraph 36 of the second draft cover text. Source: UNFCCC . Controversially, this menu of options – indicated by the wording “inter alia”, meaning “among other things” – also included numerical targets for carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS), apparently as “ quid pro quo ” for the quantified electrification target. The same day, in a highly unusual move, Panama issued an open letter stating that it would “formally object” to any decision not meeting demands including a “cap on oil production”. Panama environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro. A third and supposedly “final” version of the cover decision was published at around 3am local time on Sunday 22 November, already deep into overtime at the summit. This still did not make any direct reference to fossil fuels or the $120bn adaptation finance target. It also removed language that had called for the next IPCC reports to be published ahead of the second “global stocktake”. Carbon Brief has seen proposed revisions presented to the presidency by a 126-nation coalition of countries, including the EU, LDCs, AOSIS, AILAC, EIG and Umbrella groups. They asked for the paragraph above – numbered 36 in the second draft and 40 in the third – to be replaced with a direct link to the first global stocktake, which included the transition away from fossil fuels. (They did not suggest an explicit use of the words “fossil fuels”.) The group also wanted the sub-paragraph with numerical targets for CCUS to be deleted. However, a fourth and final version of the “Antalya pact”, published a few hours later, made only minor changes, softening language on CCUS to “increasing” rather than “accelerating”, while also weakening the language around the timeline for the next IPCC reports. On the last scheduled day of negotiations, Bowen had told journalists: “The world is wondering whether multilateralism can deliver. I think it can.” But the presidencies’ efforts to secure a cover decision were, ultimately, unsuccessful. The UK told the closing plenary: “What is before us is not commensurate with the urgency of overshoot, the scale of the climate crisis or the impacts already being felt…It is the lowest common denominator…[rather than presenting] bold collective ambition on climate action.” Not all parties were opposed to the Antalya pact. Ghana, for the African group, said it could support the decision, despite the lack of specificity on topics including adaptation finance and trade measures.
