Saudi Arabia, for the Arab group, said that they had continued to “engage constructively” on the cover decision, “despite all of the issues that were taken off the table”, including on finance and historical emissions . It also said: “We cannot reconcile a position that stated so publicly that we need to keep 1.5C within reach and, yet, calling CCUS technologies greenwashing.” Russia explained its steadfast opposition to “any wording on fossil fuels” – despite the wording agreed by consensus at COP28. It criticised “slogans” around the use of fossil fuels, arguing that even in 1.5C pathways, there was an ongoing role for oil and gas. While the failure to adopt a cover decision has been widely compared to the collapsed Copenhagen climate talks in 2015, experts told Carbon Brief this comparison was flawed. Nevertheless, they said it could end the recent trend of COPs attempting to secure a cover decision, as well as sparking renewed reflections on how to reform the process. Paul Watkinson , the French chief negotiator at Paris COP21, told Carbon Brief: “This time it is the political bet of the presidency on a cover decision that has not worked…I think this needs a deeper reflection on what we are trying to achieve – there are limits to political signals in a decision – and we ought to think [about] what we can achieve through the COP and how to make it work better.” The failure of the Antalya pact meant that initiatives on oceans, methane, mountains – and on COP reform itself – were all lost from the formal outcome of the summit. While some may be revisited at future COPs, not all have a clear place on the agenda. COP reform As COP31 ended without agreement on the proposed “Antalya pact”, much of the immediate response focused on perceived shortcomings in the UN climate process. In his closing remarks , UNFCCC executive secretary Simon Stiell said there were “lessons that must be learned” for the consensus-driven process: “Clearly, there is also scope to improve, modernise and reform. But not only because of what happened here. But also because we must evolve in this era of implementation.” In fact, one of the COP31 presidency’s stated priorities had been reforming COPs – or what they described as “strengthen[ing] UNFCCC processes”.  COP reform was discussed during the summit, including at a press conference where Panama environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro told journalists: “The COP has become an exercise in futility…192 countries will not agree on every single comma and every single period…especially those countries that produce carbon-based fuels.” In practice, such bombastic statements were far removed from the on-going discussions and country submissions on COP reform , which had already begun in Brazil last year.  These discussions were integrated into the formal negotiations under the heading of “ arrangements for intergovernmental meetings ” (AIM).  At the Bonn climate talks in June, Australia, along with Turkey, offered to conduct informal consultations on increasing UNFCCC “efficiency” at COP31.  The African group asked for legal clarity and cautioned that “efficiency should not be equated with reducing budgets or removing agenda items” necessary to tackle climate change, according to the Earth Negotiations Bulletin .  Early in the talks, the COP31 presidency published a concept note calling for “forward-looking and exploratory” discussions on what a “strong and effective UNFCCC process” could look like. It also initiated “presidency consultations” on the matter, despite the lack of a clear mandate for doing so. In the presidency consultations, responses included multi-year planning, retiring old agenda items and “avoiding unnecessary cover decisions”.  Several countries – including Russia, the African group, AILAC and the LMDCs – questioned the need for separate discussions and whether these were solely for the cover decision, given they were already underway in the AIM negotiations.  Russia said it “did not consent to elevating this discussion to high political level” and that it was unclear “why such a significant amount of negotiating time [was] being devoted” to these roundtables without a clear objective.  Drafts of the presidency’s failed cover decision included “high-level consultations” under COP presidencies on “strengthening the UNFCCC process”. During the final plenary, Peru, for AILAC, called for a “clear rule on votes” and an independent review of the COP process’s efficiency. Peru’s environment director Andrés Martín Garrido Sánchez said: “To negotiate in good faith is not a courtesy; it’s an obligation. It means not using delays as a strategy. It means negotiating text in the room in the view of everyone, with every party being heard before a decision is gavelled. It means not taking issues hostage…We are not proposing matters against the consensus. This way of negotiating is not leading us to where the world needs us to be.”  With the Antalya pact rejected, these discussions will still continue under AIM in Bonn in 2027. .cb-tweet img{ border: solid 1.25px #333333; border-radius: 5px; } @media (max-width:650px){ .cb-tweet{ width:100%; } } Adaptation While efforts to specify that tripling adaptation finance meant $120bn by 2035 failed to make it into any final texts, COP31 did see a breakthrough on channelling carbon-market revenues into the UN adaptation fund . Disagreements over finance dominated negotiations within the “ global goal on adaptation ” (GGA).  This followed a “call for efforts” to triple adaptation finance by 2035, which was agreed last year at COP30. That target was originally proposed by the LDCs as a “tripling of grant-based adaptation finance by 2030 to at least $120bn”.  Last year’s final agreement was considerably weaker and lacked key details – including the baseline for tripling and what kinds of funding would be counted towards it. Ahead of the start of COP31, the African group requested that the tripling goal be added to the agenda, providing a potential space to discuss these outstanding issues. African group request for agenda item on tripling adaptation finance. Source: UNFCCC . This request was rejected . As a result, the question of where the goal should be discussed quickly arose as a fault line. It was debated within the GGA, the climate finance “work programme”, as well as the proposed “cover decision”.  As negotiations got underway, the G77 and China coalition of developing countries argued that adaptation finance should be discussed in the GGA rooms.  The EU, UK, environmental integrity group (EIG), Norway and Canada all wanted adaptation finance discussed under the climate finance work programme. This would place the tripling goal within the broader $300bn target for 2035 – meaning adaptation finance could come from a wide variety of sources, not just developed-country grants. Over the first week of negotiations, two GGA draft texts were released, both of which included specific references to tripling adaptation finance to $120bn per year by 2035.  This would use a baseline of 2025, when the previous target to double adaptation finance to $40bn per year came to an end.  Draft GGA text on 13 November. Source: UNFCCC . Over the second week of COP31, parties continued to disagree over the home and baseline for the tripling target.  The first draft text on the cover decision – reflecting ideas put forward by parties – included relatively ambitious language that tripling finance for adaptation “should reach at least $120bn”. However, the “$120bn” was absent from the next draft and an accompanying GGA text . NGO network Climate Action Network (CAN) reported that France – as co-chair of the ministerial climate-finance negotiations – had proposed a 2019 baseline, which would reduce the tripling target to just $60bn a year by 2035.  For context, the latest UNEP report on adaptation suggests that developing countries will need a total of $305bn every year by 2035 to meet their adaptation needs. Ultimately, neither the GGA, the climate finance work programme nor the failed cover decision specifically contained a baseline or target figure for tripling adaptation finance. Bethan Laughlin , senior policy specialist at ZSL (Zoological Society of London), told Carbon Brief that the failure to agree a baseline does a “colossal amount of damage, because it is a continued betrayal of promises for finance of all types”.  Beyond finance, parties worked to establish an expert taskforce that could refine the set of 59 “indicators” for the global goal on adaptation, which had been agreed at COP30, as part of the two-year “Belém-Addis vision”. These are the metrics that countries will use to assess their progress in adapting to climate change. Speaking to Carbon Brief, Emilie Beauchamp , senior adaptation expert at International Institute for Sustainable Development ( IISD ), highlighted that the indicators had been pushed through in Brazil without full engagement from parties. She added:   “It ties into the bigger picture, which is that [the] Brazilian presidency’s cover decision didn’t leave any space for countries not to adopt these 59 indicators. These are complex and incomplete, which means most countries aren’t happy with them.” Parties agreed on the need for a “two-tier” approach to resolving this, with a taskforce undertaking technical work on the indicators and then a policy alignment process for testing them. However, the composition of the taskforce quickly became a sticking point, just as it had in Bonn earlier in the year, according to ENB .  The 19 November draft GGA text still contained three options on the taskforce’s composition, including a mix of experts nominated either by regions, the chairs of the UNFCCC subsidiary bodies or by UN organisations and other non-party stakeholders.  Parties also disagreed on references in the GGA text to the Paris Agreement and “common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities” ( CBDR-RC ), plus on recognition of the importance of the 1.5C goal in limiting the need for adaptation.  While the final decision agreed at COP31 does not mention overshoot or 1.5C, it does provide clarity on the taskforce. It “agrees” that six experts will be nominated per UN regional group, in addition to three experts nominated by the LDCs and three by small island developing states.  With so much time and focus given to the finance question, smaller technical aspects of the GGA negotiations struggled to find consensus across the two weeks of COP31.  Laughlin said:  “I think we are seeing these big-number finance issues as absolutely fundamental, but we’re also seeing the technical elements of the process, where the real work of implementation is done, be significantly challenged and, in my view, denigrated into obsolescence.” Observers told Carbon Brief that there had not been sufficient time given to the GGA, as well as items such as national adaptation plans (NAPs). One said that more than double the negotiating time had been devoted to the cover decision than to mandated items, such as the GGA, MWP and JTWP, over the first week.  Beauchamp told Carbon Brief she hoped that COP32 president Ethiopia would “break this pattern”.  Beyond the GGA, other adaptation items also proved challenging at COP31.  G77 and China huddle during informal consultations on national adaptation plans. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis. The adaptation fund is the oldest dedicated UN climate fund and was set up as part under the Kyoto Protocol. Now, it is in the process of transitioning to exclusively serve the 2015 Paris Agreement. This will allow it to access 5% of the revenues generated by the agreement’s Article 6.4 carbon market.  This process has previously been delayed by disagreements over the makeup of the fund’s board.  The expectation has been that under the Paris Agreement, the board would have set quotas for “developed” and “developing” nations – the terms used in the treaty – instead of  “Annex I” and “non-Annex I” nations, as it has done in the past.  Some parties see this distinction as important, because the UNFCCC annexes clearly separate a small group of predominantly European and industrialised states from other nations, whereas the “developed-developing” division is less clearly defined. Joe Thwaites , international climate finance director at Natural Resources Defense Council , told Carbon Brief that parties “can’t access” the Article 6.4 “share of proceeds” until this is resolved. A draft text released on 18 November continued to include references to both “developed countries” and parties “included in Annex I to the convention” within square brackets.  Ultimately, the final decision confirmed that there will be regional quotas instead of “developed” and “developing”, but it also confirmed that developing countries will continue to have a majority of seats on the board.  Thwaites described the resolution of the adaptation fund negotiations as “one bright spot” from the climate summit, noting: “The decisions at COP31 enable the fund to receive a share of carbon-trading proceeds under the Paris Agreement crediting mechanism, which will not be subject to the politics of national budget processes.”  Negotiations on NAPs , adaptation communications and adaptation committee discussions all ended with procedural conclusions, meaning no substantive agreement was reached.  One adaptation area with more progress was “matters relating to the LDCs”, an agenda item where parties discuss support and adaptation planning for the 44 LDCs .   Despite “difficult negotiations”, on the second Wednesday of COP31, parties agreed to a decision that establishes a “LDCs national adaptation plan implementation platform” under the LDCs expert group.  ENB quoted a delegate saying: “This decision may not make the headlines, but it means a lot for the more than one billion most vulnerable people who benefit from the work under this agenda item.” Finance As COP31 ended in disputes and finger-pointing, a major complaint by many parties was the failure to agree progress on climate finance. In their closing speeches, several developing-country figures expressed “profound concern”, accusing developed countries of “refusing to engage” on this “essential” issue.  Finance talks ended with little – beyond decisions to hold more meetings. There was no progress on “tripling adaptation finance”, despite efforts to flesh out this goal. (See: Adaptation .)  Finance negotiations took place amid major aid cuts by developed countries and, as revealed by Carbon Brief, a corresponding 70% drop in the amount of public climate funding being pledged. COP31 co-president Australia drew heavy criticism from NGOs for failing to commit new funds, along with other major donors, such as Germany, France and Japan.  Meanwhile, pledges to UN climate funds fell to their lowest levels in years, with few new commitments in Antalya.  Protesters at COP31 calling for climate finance. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis . Two years ago, nations agreed on a “ new collective quantified goal ” (NCQG), which involves developed countries “taking the lead” in raising $300bn in climate finance a year by 2035. A variety of sources are expected to feed into this goal, including multilateral development banks , UN climate funds and private finance “mobilised” by public investments.  In recent years, roughly a third of total climate finance has been public finance from developed countries. The provision of funds by these nations now looks less certain , amid economic struggles and pressure to raise military spending. Developing countries, therefore, came to COP31 looking for assurances. Finance was discussed across most rooms in Antalya, but negotiations around a climate finance “ work programme ” – set up at COP30 last year – were the main venue for this push. Developing countries had wanted to create this space to discuss finance “provision” under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement, which says developed countries “shall provide” finance. This is taken to mean public funding – such as aid spending – from developed countries. (The NCQG, on the other hand, is a “mobilisation” goal, meaning it covers various funding sources, including private finance “mobilised” by public investments.) This came amid concerns that developed countries were trying to transfer responsibility onto others. Abdulkani Barrow , Somalia’s lead negotiator, told Carbon Brief: “Africa does not want developed countries’ historical financial responsibilities to become diluted by a general expectation that private investors, developing countries and other financial actors should provide the money.” However, due to pressure from developed countries, the work programme was set up with a broader remit, including Article 9.1 “in the context of Article 9…as a whole”.  Following initial talks in June, the programme was only added to the COP31 agenda due to a continued push by developing countries. The EU remained “deeply concerned” about its inclusion.   Coming into COP31, developing countries continued to insist that the work programme should focus exclusively on Article 9.1.  Some developing-country groups, notably the Like-Minded Developing Countries (LMDCs) and the Arab group , said it should consider ways to secure more from developed countries, including “burden-sharing arrangements”. They also argued for an extensive new set of talks and other activities. Extract from “work programme on climate finance” text from 15 November, showing an option for “burden-sharing arrangements”. Source: UNFCCC . Such ideas were unacceptable for developed countries, who generally wanted a far more limited set of actions that were “non-prescriptive” and “non-punitive”.  They argued that the talks should be based on the existing $300bn mobilisation goal, stressing that they were already contributing tens of billions a year. Prior to COP31, Wopke Hoekstra, European commissioner for climate, told Bloomberg that “any conversation on new fresh money is dead in the water”. Article 6 Negotiations at COP31 on carbon trading under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement reopened many familiar arguments over how tightly such activities should be regulated. Beatriz Granziera , senior policy adviser at The Nature Conservancy (TNC), told Carbon Brief: “Discussions repeatedly came back to familiar trade-offs: practicality versus conservativeness; flexibility versus oversight; and how to scale much-needed participation and investment while maintaining environmental integrity.” Agreement was, ultimately, reached on both bilateral trading under Article 6.2 and the international carbon market under Article 6.4. Carbon trading between countries under Article 6.2 is only subject to light-touch rules, such as reporting on the use of the process and a “technical expert review” of national reports. Across 16 national reports checked so far, these reviews found 543 “inconsistencies”, 115 of which were “significant”. None of the reports were found to be without issue. An initial draft text at Antalya “note[d these issues] with concern”, adding that “many…are significant” and relate to “environmental integrity” – in other words, whether or not emissions are actually being cut. It asked parties to address issues “at the earliest opportunity”. However, this entire paragraph disappeared in the final, agreed text . Instead, the decision “takes note” of the information in the technical reports, without asking for any response. Given its confidentiality provisions, campaign groups have long described Article 6.2 as a “ wild west ” for carbon trading and the COP31 outcome does nothing to tighten the rules. They are particularly relevant for nations where controls on emissions or deforestation pose a risk to communities and the economy.  In recent years, the forum has been where trade and climate issues have been discussed.  In 2024, COP29 in Baku established a four-year work plan on response measures, including the “cross-border impacts” of climate-change measures. This created a formal space to discuss and assess trade-related climate measures in UN climate talks.  COP30 in Belém established a two-day “global dialogue” on response measures each year from 2026-29. The first was in Bangkok from 21-22 September 2026, focusing on economic diversification and on how to manage impacts on vulnerable populations. COP31 also conducted its first annual ministerial high-level round table on response measures on 17 November. Credit: Kubilay Ciftci / UNFCCC In Antalya, three key disputes emerged. The first was on what activities the forum would undertake in 2027 and, second, how it would consider recommendations from its Katowice Committee (KCI) of experts. The third was on whether – and how – response measures would inform the second “ global stocktake ”. At the start of negotiations, countries – including the African group, AOSIS, South Korea and China – called for a wide range of activities next year. One of these included a new “cross-border” impact assessment of response measures. On 16 November, the EU suggested removing an activity that refers to Article 3.5 of the 1992 UN climate convention, covering trade and an “open international economic system”.  Eventually, countries settled on four different activities. These include a workshop next June for the most affected countries to learn how to report these impacts, plus another workshop at COP32 on “technological solutions” to reduce climate impacts. As work on the second global stocktake (GST2) gets underway, countries disagreed on how response measures would feed into it. As of 19 November , the same four options remained on the table, including one with “no text”.  One option, supported by G77 and China, “decide[d]” that all of the outputs of the forum – dialogues, workshops, technical reports and case studies – would serve as substantive inputs to GST2.  This option “urged” that the cross-border impact assessment be conducted “before and during” GST2, including metrics such as inflation, trade flows, household income, employment and debt. Canada and the EU warned that this would change the global stocktake’s “well-established function”, reported Earth Negotiations Bulletin .  However, Switzerland, Norway, EU and the UK supported a compromise option – where countries could submit their views on the “social and economic impacts of response measures” as input to GST2.  Eventually, the option explicitly containing a cross-border impact assessment as an input to  GST2 was deleted from the final draft .   Instead, the text “recognises” that inputs to GST2 are “non-exhaustive” and “affirms” that all the forum’s outputs will feed into the stocktake’s technical assessment. This includes work on cross-border impacts – including trade measures – and how to report and analyse them. At the same time, it “invites” countries to submit their views on the “social and economic consequences” of response measures by 28 February 2027, which would also inform the stocktake. During the final plenary, the EU told delegates it objected to the adoption of the decision on response measures, on the grounds that it “contains provisions that are highly problematic”, as well as “the lack of recognition of the best available science”.  This was supported by Canada and the UK, with the latter adding: “We cannot accept any outcome that seeks to undermine and unduly influence the next global stocktake.” Brazil and Saudi Arabia both expressed their disappointment with the rejection of the text. Brazil said that the draft “excludes the voices of developing countries, the very countries that struggle to address the social and economic impacts of mitigation measures”. It asked for a formal note that the role and mandate of the forum were being “undermined”. This area of the negotiations aims to encourage people to engage in climate action in different ways – through education, training, public awareness and access to information. COP27 had agreed to a four-year “action plan” on ACE that ends this year. COP31 was due to have agreed a new plan for 2027-2031, with some parties wanting it to address “misinformation and disinformation” related to climate change. During the Antalya talks, Russia, along with Saudi Arabia and Paraguay, objected to including a reference to countering climate-related “misinformation and disinformation”, reported ENB . It added that Russia described this as amounting to the censorship of other scientific views. Russia also made repeated efforts to replace previously agreed language on “gender-responsive” action with the phrase “gender-sensitive”. A draft decision , proposed by the presidency on 21 November, “note[d] the need to enhance efforts to promote and support the integrity of information on climate change”. The proposal also “recognise[d] the centrality of equity and the best available science for effective climate action and policymaking, as provided by the IPCC”. It then set out an action plan for continued work from 2027-2031. Notably, while references to “misinformation” had been removed, it still talked of “ensuring that the public has access to reliable, accurate climate information and is equipped with adequate climate literacy skills”. Draft text for the ACE “action plan”, published 21 November. Source: UNFCCC . During the closing plenary, however, Russia said it “reject[ed]” the “censorship of science” and that it “objected” to the draft text on action for climate empowerment. It said discussions had been “held hostage by considerations which are not part of the climate process”. The EU and the UK for the Umbrella group expressed their “surprise” at Russia’s objection. The UK said this topic was “very important for our group” and that “respect for gender equality and all identities is core to an effective, inclusive and meaningful process”. The COP president told the plenary that, “in light of the objection from the Russian Federation”, the issue of action for climate for empowerment would be deferred until the Bonn talks in June 2027. In a statement, campaign group Climate Action Against Disinformation said: “The ACE action plan should have been a milestone for truth at COP31. Instead, the Russian federation – the epicentre of climate disinformation – blocked its adoption, standing alone against 193 other[s].” Trade After the creation of three annual “dialogues” on trade within the COP30 Belém “global mutirão” decision, the topic was not expected to feature on the official agenda, even if it was likely to come up in other negotiating tracks. But, in the end, the rejection of not only the cover decision, but also agreements on “response measures” and agriculture, meant that trade was entirely missing from the COP31 outcome. (See: Response measures and Agriculture .) (A request from the African group to add trade to the COP31 agenda was also rejected .) Trade and climate featured strongly in the first “ reflections ” text on a cover decision, which was a compilation of suggestions from parties. Paragraph 119 of the first draft “call[ed] on” developed countries to “phase out unilateral…trade-restrictive measures” by the end of 2027. Commonly cited examples of what this might refer to include the EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism and deforestation law. (See: Agriculture and food security .) First draft of the COP31 cover decision. Source: UNFCCC The phase-out call was, expectedly, cut from the second iteration of the cover text.    Speaking to Carbon Brief, global policy advisor at Greenpeace East Asia Yao Zhe said: “No one thought it would survive, probably even the ones [who] proposed it. But I see it as an indication that [countries] are persistent in pushing the trade angle.” Yao added that she expected China, with the African group, to “aim for higher” on trade at next year’s COP32 summit. In the end, with the “Antalya pact” failing, none of the references to trade survived the conference. In the closing plenary, Russia, Venezuela, Brazil, Iran, Kenya – with the Arab and African groups – lamented how the issue of trade was treated in the talks, with Saudi Arabia saying developing countries were told “this is a matter that is completely off the table”. Russia’s representative remarked that “climate policy should not turn into trade policy by other means”, calling customs tariffs on “green” supply chains “old colonial distribution of labour under a new green banner.” Ghana, for the African group, pointed out “no firm treatment” of trade measures at COP31. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis Ghana and Kenya both flagged the lack of “firm treatment” of trade measures and hinted that it would be a priority for them at COP32. Kenya’s delegate said: “Unilateral trade measures are only noted. African economies bear their costs, while the decision merely notes their views.”  Second global stocktake Against a backdrop of fraught negotiations, the second “ global stocktake ” (GST) was launched at a high-level event in the middle of the second week of COP31. The GST is the Paris Agreement’s five-yearly “ reality check ”, measuring whether the world’s collective efforts are enough to sufficiently cut emissions and prepare for climate impacts. The first stocktake culminated in Dubai at COP28 in 2023, resulting in the first-ever global commitment to “transition away from fossil fuels ”, among various other pledges. GST2 will run until 2028, meaning COP33 will have to address the likely shortfall between the Paris Agreement’s goals and reality. An important question hanging over this process is whether parties will have access to the latest IPCC science in time for the second GST, as a small group of countries push for the next IPCC report to be published after the stocktake. (See: Cover text. ) COP31 also featured a “dialogue” on how the lessons of the first GST could inform countries’ future NDCs.  Parties such as the EU and climate-vulnerable nations argued for a more substantial outcome that included guidance for the second GST and references to the 1.5C target. This was opposed by many developing countries. In the end, parties decided on a procedural outcome without any of the more ambitious language that had appeared in previous drafts . Long-term goal review COP31 was unable to agree on whether to start a third “periodic review” of the UN climate convention ’s long-term goal and progress towards meeting it. The goal of the 1992 convention is to avoid “dangerous” climate change, a target that was defined at COP16 in 2010 as a warming limit of 2C. COP16 also said that this goal – and progress towards meeting it – should be subject to “periodic review”. The first review , in 2013-2015, helped secure the Paris 1.5C limit. At the start of the second review at COP25 , some parties disputed the need for the process, given the existence of five-yearly “ global stocktakes ” of progress under the Paris Agreement. Underlying this disagreement is the fact that the convention has distinct country requirements for developed and developing parties, whereas the Paris regime does not. Discussions on a third review stalled at COP29 and continued at COP30. Some developed countries said it was “ redundant ”, while developing countries wanted it to continue. In Antalya, countries were split over whether to begin a third periodic review, whether to delay it until publication of the next IPCC report, or whether to discontinue the process. The final COP31 text “notes the consideration” of the matter and decides to continue talking at COP32 next year. At the first closing plenary , China, along with India for the LMDCs and Saudi Arabia for the Arab group, expressed their “concern” over the lack of agreement. China said: “We are seriously concerned that some developed country parties…in the name of streamlined process…substantively tried to terminate this mechanism.” For AOSIS, Palau “regret[ted]” the lack of progress on what it said was the “only dedicated space to reflect on the 1.5C limit on the basis of substantive scientific input”. Guidance on NDCs COP31 was unable to agree on further guidance for countries when preparing their climate pledges under the Paris Agreement, known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs). This issue has been disputed in the past, with talks also failing at COP29 in Baku two years ago. In Antalya, parties were once again split over whether to issue further guidance Developed and vulnerable countries – including the EU and small island states – want more guidance, to prompt stronger implementation and more transparent pledges. The LMDCs, the Arab group and African group, prefer to avoid what they see as prescriptive further guidance that could impinge on the “nationally determined” nature of the documents. The negotiations were subject to “ rule 16 ”, meaning they ended without agreement and will resume at the next session of the talks in Bonn next June. Rio synergies To the dismay of many countries, negotiations on the need for “synergies” between the three Rio conventions of climate change, biodiversity loss and land desertification ended with the adoption of just a one-line text .  The text simply states that, during negotiations under this item – known as “cooperation with other international organisations” – there was an “exchanges of views” and an agreement to “continue consideration at the next session”. The agreed text for the “cooperation with other international organisations” agenda item. Source: UNFCCC . On 10 November – the second day of COP – ENB reported that Russia, supported by the Arab group, “opposed continuing the discussion” on Rio synergies. Speaking on the behalf of 14 small island developing states in plenary on 14 November, Fiji said it was “deeply disappointed” by the outcome. It told delegates: “We came to Antalya ready to advance cooperation across Rio conventions and to foster synergies in national implementation. That is what all parties agreed to do when we left Bonn . We did not do that. Not because the issues were too difficult, but because we were never permitted to discuss them in the way we intended to do so. “At the very first informal consultation, before a single substantive proposal had been heard, the intention to invoke ‘ rule 16 ’ was announced by one group of party. We offered repeatedly to address any and all concerns. That offer was not taken up. Substantive discussion was blocked from the very first hour to the last.” The EIG, Panama for AILAC, the UK for the Umbrella group and the EU all expressed similar disappointment. Around the COP Fossil fuels The issue of “transitioning away from fossil fuels” dominated again at COP31, with countries leaving the talks still deeply divided on how it should be taken forward. Including “transitioning away from fossil fuels” in the cover decision was one of the key asks of a group of 126 countries spanning Europe, the small island states, parts of Latin America and the Caribbean and other major developed countries. In the end, several countries rejected the proposed cover decision over its lack of a clear reference to fossil fuels, with the EU saying: “We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” Fossil fuels also featured prominently on the sidelines at COP, with more than 80 side events and talks dedicated to the topic, Carbon Brief understands. In addition, eight European and small island nations announced intentions to release national roadmaps away from fossil fuels – bringing the total number with such plans up to 27. The first major event on fossil fuels took place on the summit’s second day, when the Brazilian COP30 presidency formally presented its global fossil-fuel roadmap to a packed-out plenary room. However, COP31 presidents Kurum and Bowen were conspicuously absent. The next day, during his speech at the world leaders’ summit, Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva called on Turkey and Australia to “ensure that the recommendations contained in [the roadmaps] are disseminated and incorporated into the next global stocktake ”. On Friday morning, the presidency released a “reflections” text from its consultations with countries on what they would like to see in a cover decision. This included a bullet point saying some parties would like to see “transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems” included in the text. (This language was first agreed by countries as part of the first global stocktake at COP28 in Dubai in 2023.) On the same day, Irene Vélez Torres, Colombia’s former environment minister, told journalists that a mere repetition of language agreed in Dubai would not represent progress for many parties. Vélez Torres co-led a first-of-its-kind conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels in Santa Marta in April this year, which was attended by 57 countries. She told the huddle that, regardless of what is agreed by consensus on fossil fuels at COP31, countries committed to transitioning away would continue to take action, saying: “Consensus as a method is not going to stop us anymore…we know it has limited ambition. It is limiting implementation, but this is not going to stop us.” On Monday 16 November, the presidency dropped an 18-page first draft of its proposed cover decision – along with a short “ presidency note ” explaining that all elements were still in play, including whether or not they should appear in a final text.  One part of this draft “call[ed] for accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels, including through the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems”. Another part of the text also “welcome[d]” the Brazil-led global roadmaps on the transition away from fossil fuels and on ending deforestation. The next day, a group of European and small island state ministers held a press conference on the need to transition away from fossil fuels. Denmark, Spain, Portugal and Luxembourg announced that they intend to release new national roadmaps away from fossil fuels.  (Earlier that day, Vanuatu had announced its own national roadmap and the development of a Pacific regional roadmap away from fossil fuels.)  Speaking as a united front, the group of ministers called for the language on fossil fuels contained within the first draft to be strengthened and given more prominence. However, Carbon Brief understands that, behind-the-scenes, hopes that any kind of fossil-fuel language would survive into the second draft cover decision were fast evaporating. On 18 November, a group of global-south ministers held a press conference, attended by Carbon Brief, to show their support for transitioning away from fossil fuels. At the event, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and Guatemala announced that they were joining the fossil fuel treaty , an initiative to develop a legal instrument to control fossil fuels. This brought the total number of countries supporting the treaty up to 30. During the press conference, Panama environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro made headlines with an explosive speech, telling journalists that the world is “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia”. The next day, the co-hosts of the second transitioning away from fossil fuels conference – Tuvalu and Ireland – held a press conference. They confirmed that a pre-conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels would be held in Dublin in May, with the actual conference taking place in Tuvalu in July. Speaking at the press conference, Tuvalu climate minister Maina Talia publicly acknowledged he was not expecting to see transitioning away from fossil fuels in the second draft of the cover decision. The co-hosts also confirmed that a third transitioning away from fossil fuels conference will be held in 2028. (Lula told civil society at COP that Brazil was keen to host it. Carbon Brief understands Cambodia and Ghana are also interested.) Later that day, a second draft cover decision was published. It did not mention “fossil fuels” at all, nor “paragraph 28 of decision 1/CMA.5”, the passage of text from the first global stocktake that calls for countries to contribute to “transitioning away from fossil fuels”. In the evening, Kurum and Bowen held a press conference to defend their second draft and tried to bat away questions from journalists about whether the removal of fossil-fuel language represented “backsliding”. Both presidents cited their push to get countries to sign up to electrification as complementary to transitioning away from fossil fuels, with Bowen telling journalists: “The world agreed at COP28 to transition away from fossil fuels. What we’re about is practical ways to do that. There’s no better way than electrification.”  However, it was widely understood that many countries were not happy with the omission of fossil fuels. As talks ran into overtime on Saturday, any kind of official update on the state of the text failed to materialise.  Tuvalu’s Talia told a cramped press huddle that Pacific island nations had been waiting for the text since last night and were still willing to fight to get transitioning away from fossil fuels back in. Maina Vakafua Talia, Tuvalu’s climate minister, speaks to journalists. Credit: Sandro Basili / Alamy Stock Photo On Saturday evening, the fallout over fossil fuels intensified.  Carbon Brief understands that 126 countries – made up of the EU, UG, AOSIS, AILAC and LDCs – approached the presidency as a united front to demand that transitioning away from fossil fuels featured in the final cover decision. One observer told Carbon Brief that such close cooperation between the EU and AOSIS is “unprecedented” at COP. They added that it might reflect the fact that Ireland, which currently holds the EU presidency, is working closely with Tuvalu on holding the second transitioning away from fossil fuels conference next year. A new draft cover decision did not arrive until the early hours of Sunday morning.  This one also did not directly mention fossil fuels. However, it did “recall” the COP28 UAE consensus “in its entirety”, which itself includes a reference to a “just, orderly and equitable” transition away from fossil fuels. Carbon Brief contributing editor Dr Joanna Depledge wrote on LinkedIn that this oblique reference was “near meaningless”. In a fiery final plenary session on Sunday afternoon, many countries rejected the text – citing its failure to clearly reference transitioning away from fossil fuels as one of the key reasons. (See: Cover decision .) Action agenda Many issues that were intensely negotiated at COP31 – including the electrification goal and fossil-fuel phaseout – also featured in the “ action agenda ”. This is the part of the UN climate process that involves mobilising real-world climate action from non-state actors, including businesses, investors and civil-society groups.  It also covers voluntary actions taken by groups of countries beyond the COP negotiations. When the “Antalya pact” failed to materialise, the presidency’s action agenda package was one of its more substantial outputs.  In this closing remarks at COP31, after the headline negotiated outcome had collapsed, UNFCCC executive secretary Simon Stiell reminded delegates: “This COP process has two tracks. And across the action agenda, COP31 has delivered real progress and concrete results.” With Australia overseeing negotiations, the action agenda was instead a priority for the Turkish presidency, which used COP31 to launch a variety of new projects and “ compacts ”. In a phrase familiar to attendees of previous COPs , Turkish COP31 president Murat Kurum said he wanted an “implementation COP” that would leave people saying: “Something changed in Antalya.” Delegates resting by a wall with the COP31 slogan “dialogue, consensus, action”. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis . Amid global conflict, struggling multilateralism and the imminent breaching of the 1.5C Paris Agreement goal, UN climate talks have repeatedly failed to reach consensus on vital issues. Some have, therefore , welcomed what the Brazilian COP30 presidency called “two-tier multilateralism”, in which parties try to find consensus where they can and, where they cannot, coalitions of willing nations and groups push more ambitious action forward. Kaveh Guilanpour , vice president for international strategies at the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions (C2ES), told Carbon Brief: “There’s a lot of inertia in the formal way of negotiating and we’re trying to find our way to whatever that new thing is, given the foundational era of negotiations is over.” Last year, the Brazilian presidency consolidated hundreds of existing climate initiatives – including many launched at previous COPs – into a streamlined set that could be supported and tracked under the action agenda. This included setting out more than 120 “ plans to accelerate solutions ”, to advance everything from phasing out coal to ending food waste. Tracking by UN Climate Change found that 104 of these plans had seen progress over the past year. By the end of COP31, the total number of plans had increased to 136, with new ones filling “ important gaps ”, such as early warning systems . Crucially, the plans were structured to align with the global stocktake outcomes from COP28 – such as curbing fossil fuels and tripling renewables – which all nations agreed on.  In this way, the revised action agenda is intended to explicitly support negotiated outcomes. Turkey announced 10 “ priority themes ” for the COP31 action agenda, fitting them into the existing framework. By far the most high profile was the “electrification” focus. (See: Electrification .) A book distributed at the summit by the Turkish presidency stated that a “large number of events, declarations and partnerships does not by itself constitute implementation success”. Nevertheless, the presidency did launch many new initiatives, including six voluntary 2035 targets that countries and non-state actors could sign up for.  These included “compacts” to curb the “ energy intensity ” of buildings by 25% and increase the use of “circular materials” in manufacturing to at least 15% by 2035. These initiatives attracted dozens of backers, but gained far less support than the electrification goal. Other notable initiatives pushed by the Turkish presidency include a domestic pledge for “ zero waste districts ” and an “ Antalya artificial intelligence (AI) pledge ”, which focused on curbing data-centre emissions while advancing “AI solutions for climate action”. COP31 also saw progress on two initiatives launched by COP30’s “ global mutirão ” decision that are relevant for the growth of the action agenda. The first was the “ Belém mission to 1.5 ”, which identified key priority areas for countries to meet their climate goals.  The second was the “ global implementation accelerator ”, which was formally established at COP31. This involves presidencies and experts choosing two action-agenda plans each year that are best placed to drive “ positive tipping points ” for climate action.  Cosima Cassel , E3G climate diplomacy lead, told Carbon Brief that this focus, “based on science, not just on the presidency’s priorities…is an extra step in the evolution of the action agenda”. Global climate action high-level event. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis . During a COP31 session on the “accelerator”, COP30 strategy director Túlio Andrade said the Brazilian team wanted it to advance the transition “from a negotiation-focused regime to one very much focused on implementation”. The Turkish presidency also announced a new project called the “ climate implementation bridge ”, while pledging an initial $3m to support its operations. In partnership with the UN Development Programme, the bridge’s goal is to turn nations’ climate plans into “ bankable projects ” and connect them with finance.  Together, the “mission”, “accelerator” and “bridge” form part of a wider “ ecosystem ” that supporters hope will identify and support priority areas of climate action. However, the growing profile of the action agenda has resulted in pushback, with India and the Arab group arguing against any mention of it in formal negotiations. In contrast, Brazil accused the presidency of failing to significantly acknowledge these “concrete instruments and initiatives” in the proposed “Antalya pact”.  Some parties and observers are concerned that the action agenda is a diversion from parties’ obligations under UN climate treaties, such as providing climate finance. Arguing that the focus should instead be on reforming the COP process, Vanuatu climate minister Ralph Regenvanu told Carbon Brief: “Unfortunately, the action agenda has not necessarily led to action. It is indicative, again, that the COP process is broken. While people innovating and coming together to take action is good, it cannot take the place of negotiations.” Developing countries, which often have far fewer delegates , also struggle to follow all the additional activities. In a closing session , Stiell invited parties to nominate focal points so that the UN could help to “connect them with action agenda opportunities all year round”. Guilanpour noted that while “everybody says they want to focus on implementation”, within the traditional COP process this can only apply to “a very rarefied subset of obligations”, such as submitting revised NDCs. He added: “When the rest of the world hears implementation, they want to see pollution in their city going down, their energy bills going down…and that sort of implementation is in the action agenda.” Global leaders COP31’s world leaders’ summit took place during the conference’s first week from 11-12 November. Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva – whose recent re-election was widely interpreted as a timely boost for climate action and multilateralism by delegates – gave a blistering speech in the summit’s opening ceremony. He told other world leaders: “We have started talking more about weapons and tariffs than about the survival of future generations…But the planet cannot be left at the mercy of hegemonic disputes.” He told leaders that he wanted COP30 , which took place last year in the Brazilian city of Belém, to be remembered as the “COP of truth” – but that “science and multilateralism remain under attack”, adding: “It is not by chance that the incorporation of IPCC contributions into the COP negotiation process is in question. Nor is it a coincidence that climate agreements are the favourite targets of reactionary forces at COPs.” He also touted Brazil’s newly released global roadmaps on fossil fuels and deforestation , urging COP31 co-hosts Turkey and Australia to “ensure that the recommendations contained in these documents are disseminated and incorporated into the next global stocktake ”. In one of his final addresses in the role, UN secretary general António Guterres said that the “brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us”, adding: “Leaders – and, in particular, those from developed countries – cannot keep expanding fossil-fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5C.” Turkish leader Recep Tayyip Erdoğan used his address to call on developed countries to “take greater responsibility for emission reductions and financing” and to call out “ecocide” in Gaza. (Erdoğan faced criticism for announcing the discovery of two new oil fields in Turkey on the eve of the summit.) Barbados prime minister Mia Mottley cited Carbon Brief analysis to reprimand developed countries in her address to the world leaders’ summit, telling the room: ”My friends, let us be clear: pledges are not payments. But even the promised pledges are now 70% below previous levels.” UK prime minister Andy Burnham, the only G7 leader to attend the summit, said that electrification is “how we make clean power cheap power”. He also announced the appointment of the country’s first special representative on climate security.  In total, around 70 world leaders spoke at the summit – with many major polluters missing. For the second year, the US did not send any delegates to COP. (Donald Trump took the US out of the Paris Agreement and the UN climate treaty after returning to office.) However, success for Democrats in the US midterm elections, shortly before COP31, lifted hopes that the world’s second-largest emitter could one day return to the talks. “America is all in” – a coalition of mostly Democratic governors, Congress members and local mayors – had a pavilion at COP31 and brought around 120 delegates (a figure larger than many official country delegations ). Speaking on 16 November at a pavilion event attended by Carbon Brief, Jared Huffman , a Democratic Congressional representative from California, said that the midterm results were a “clear rejection” of Trump’s “climate denial” and “wrecking ball to climate and energy policy”. He added: “The next time that we are here at a COP, it will be different…We will be an official Congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives. And soon after that, this yellow part of our lanyard that says ‘observer’ will change and the US will truly be officially back in as part of the negotiati[ons].” Other countries without delegations at the talks included Myanmar and Israel, according to Carbon Brief analysis. More than 92,000 registered for COP, making it potentially the largest in history, found Carbon Brief analysis.
