Electrification Amid a global energy crisis driven by disruption in the trade of fossil fuels, one of the biggest themes of COP31 was electrification.  Much attention was focused on which nations had signed up to a voluntary pledge to “increase the share of electricity in final energy consumption to 35% by 2035”.  For much of COP31, this was expected to be one of the main outcomes in the “Antalya pact” cover text, which ultimately failed to find agreement among parties. (See: Cover decision .) Nevertheless, some countries made public pledges of support for the target during the COP, including in a joint China-Australia statement .  COP31 president Murat Kurum told the closing plenary that “around 80” countries were behind the goal, but a full list was never published. The pledge was launched earlier in the year as a “flagship initiative of the COP31 presidency’s action agenda” – part of its wider goal to “ electrify the world ”. (See: Action agenda .) As explained on CB Connect , it drew from analysis by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), which was explicitly designed to align with the 1.5C target and support the Brazilian COP30 presidency’s “roadmap” for transitioning away from fossil fuels.  Ministers and representatives from Papua New Guinea, Antigua and Barbuda, Zambia, Germany, the Philippines and Colombia hold connected extension cables in a demonstration of their support for electrification. Credit: Carbon Brief. Towards the end of COP31, the presidency launched its “ electrification delivery package ”, capturing 14 newly announced international initiatives and other relevant projects. Among them were an industry-backed “maritime electrification goal” to increase electricity’s share of shipping’s final energy demand to 20% by 2035, as well as projects to boost grid investment, renewables in small-island states and transitions away from coal. One notable initiative was the Electrify Now Finance Coalition – launched with the backing of the COP31 and COP32 presidencies – to “mobilise over $1.2bn for clean electrification projects” in developing countries. At a coalition launch event, featuring ministers from Ethiopia, Germany, Pakistan and several other nations, Bruce Douglas , chief executive of the Global Renewables Alliance , told attendees that at least 25 nations had already put in place policies to drive electrification since the start of the “ Hormuz crisis ”. He said: “We now have the formula for success: renewable energy plus electrification equals secure, affordable and clean energy for all consumers.” China at COP31 Closing COP31 with a signal of “solidarity and multilateralism” was “more important than specific problems”, said China at the opening plenary of the summit. Its climate officials said repeatedly that not every COP required a “ new outcome ” and noted the need to “ manage expectations ”.  These comments seemed prescient when negotiations broke down at the end of COP31 over the cover decision . China had outlined its key aims for COP31 in a press conference held by Li Gao, vice-minister of ecology and environment and delegation head, in late October. These were primarily to commit developed countries to do more on mitigation and finance, as well as to address “unilateralism and protectionism” in the trade of clean-energy technologies. But Li also “commend[ed]” the presidency’s call for countries to pledge to achieve a 35% share of electricity in global final energy consumption by 2035. One of the biggest questions hovering over the COP was whether China would officially support the pledge, which was incorporated into the failed cover text .  While observers had told Carbon Brief from early in the negotiations that it would be very likely that China would support the pledge in some form, the strongest signal came from a joint statement published with Australia in the second week. In it, the two countries “welcome[d] growing international ambition and cooperation on electrification…on a voluntary basis”, mentioning the 35 by 35 goal, as well as recognising various climate, social and economic benefits from the transition. (See: Electrification .)  China-Australia joint statement on climate change and the clean energy transition, published 20 November. Source: State Council of the People’s Republic of China . The cover text had similarly sought to “recognise that electrification has significant benefits in terms of emission reductions, energy security, energy efficiency, economic development and energy access”. The joint statement, however, did not explicitly mention fossil fuels, rather it noted “countries have different transition pathways” and the “importance of secure, affordable, reliable and resilient energy systems during the transition”. Li Shuo , director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI), told Carbon Brief that the “carefully curated” language helped “firm up” support for the electrification pledge – and broader language around energy – in the final draft.  China had published a joint climate statement with the EU ahead of COP30 , as well as ones with the US ahead of COPs including COP21 , COP26 and COP28 . But, unlike these agreements, the Australia-China joint statement “mostly confirms existing relatively unambitious negotiation points and does not advance ambitions” on issues including fossil fuels and decarbonising trade, argued Prof Christoph Nedopil Wang at the University of Queensland . He told Carbon Brief: “Symbolically, it would have been more meaningful to sign a more ambitious statement before COP negotiations began.” As talks broke down at the closing plenary, China endorsed the cover text’s final draft, noting that, although it has “some concerns about the content”, it chose to accept the decision to “push forward our process and show a message of unity and collective efforts”. On 23 November, China’s foreign ministry issued a statement saying:  “We express our disappointment regarding this outcome, but believe that confidence in the multilateral process should not be lost as a result.” “China was not the main blocker for the text”, said ASPI’s Li.  He added that, in his view, even if language around transitioning away from fossil fuels had been made stronger, China would have found it acceptable. China also tried to preserve the mitigation work programme (MWP) at the closing plenary. (See: Mitigation work programme .)  In negotiations, China joined other developing countries in supporting the work programme’s extension through to 2030.  Speaking on behalf of the LMDCs, China emphasised the value of the MWP, but said it needed to “focus on how to eliminate barriers of implementation”, according to Third World Network .  These included developed countries’ lack of mitigation action and financial support, as well as unilateral trade measures, it added.  China, on behalf of the LMDCs, tried to build consensus around the MWP at the closing plenary by suggesting deleting references to the first global stocktake. However, the suggestion was rejected by Russia. Meanwhile, China continued to emphasise the need for a gradual transition away from fossil fuels throughout the COP. “‘Phasing out fossil fuels’ [淘汰化石燃料] is merely a proposition of a small number of countries and has never constituted a consensus”, climate envoy Liu Zhenmin told the Paper .  He added that the energy transition required “gradually replacing fossil fuels” with clean energy over the course of “decades” and that phasing out fossil fuels should not “become a focal point of COP31 negotiations”. A few days later and thousands of miles away, the presidents of China, the US and Russia declared at the APEC Summit that the three countries “plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products” in response to global energy shocks . The China delegation office at COP31 did not respond to Carbon Brief’s request for comment on this matter.  An early push to get trade on the agenda came not from China, but from the African group . In the end, the item was not included on the agenda, though it was raised by China in negotiations on the just transition work programme , adaptation fund and standing committee on finance . The China-Australia joint statement notes “measures taken to combat climate change should not constitute a means of arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination or a disguised restriction on international trade”. Prof Nedopil Wang told Carbon Brief that Australia would be more open to compromise on language with China around cleantech trade than the EU or US, as its economy has few “domestic substitutes for China’s manufactured products”. Text on trade measures were included in the cover decision drafts, though not adopted by parties. China did also focus significant attention on the just transition work programme, which was successfully passed. (See: Just transition work programme .) Speaking at a ministerial roundtable, environment vice-minister Li said that the “just transition is one of the most important agenda items of COP31” and must be operationalised.  In negotiations, China called for the mechanism to recognise the “north-south development gap” and a dedicated body to manage the programme – opposed by the EU. More broadly, the LMDCs urged that the work programme “avoid policy prescriptions” and not be linked to the global stocktake , which they argued would risk creating new obligations. Huang Runqiu, China’s minister for ecology and environment, speaking at a high-level event on the global implementation accelerator. Credit: UNFCCC . Meanwhile, at a high-level dialogue on climate finance, watched by Carbon Brief, environment minister Huang Runqiu said that developed countries’ “climate finance commitments must be honoured and the financing gap narrowed”. Huang called for the new collective quantified goal (NCQG) to be “effectively implemented”, as well as for “establishing a common definition” for climate finance and improving accounting methodologies.  He additionally highlighted the need to improve the “quality of finance”, such as providing more grants and highly concessional loans, support for adaptation and easier access to climate finance. This was echoed by BASIC , who said that “developed countries must set a pathway towards the NCQG goal of $300bn annually” and triple adaptation finance. BASIC also said the climate finance work programme (CFWP) must “operationalise Article 9.1”. The final CFWP text was passed, but only focused on procedural matters, with mentions of tripling adaptation finance and “burden-sharing” in earlier drafts removed . Requests to expand the donor base were also deleted. China maintained its emphasis on Article 9.1 in a number of workstreams, notably through the CFWP and standing committee on finance. Carbon Brief understands that China was also one of two nations driving efforts to ensure that a dialogue on Article 2.1(c) , which ensures finance flows are “consistent” with climate action, remains open and non-binding. On adaptation finance, China underscored on behalf of the LMDCs the need to triple funds, calling for a “clear roadmap and timeline to increase the share of grants, as well as a progress-review mechanism”, said Third World Network . But, in general, ASPI’s Li says, “China’s position was right in the middle of the political spectrum” on most of the issues being negotiated, maintaining a “quiet, but self-assured posture”. An early point of discussion among delegates had been whether China could have signalled greater leadership at COP, such as by announcing a bid to host COP33. News emerged at COP31 that China had, after “ months ” of consideration, decided not to do so.  Prof Hu Bin , associate professor and director of global climate governance research at Tsinghua University ’s Institute of Climate Change and Sustainable Development, told Carbon Brief that “China, politically, is still very hesitant” to claim the role of the leading country on climate. Instead it is focusing on leading in terms of the transition on-the-ground he said, adding: “I still think the reason China doesn’t want to bid for COP33 is internal pressure – the economy is slowing down, local governments are facing lots of pressure for employment and for economic growth.”  Another way in which it was suggested China could display leadership was by helping create consensus around the IPCC’s AR7 report being published in time for the second global stocktake.  At an event at the China pavilion attended by Carbon Brief, Laurence Tubiana, key architect of the Paris Agreement, said she will “count on China to be the torchbearer for the world’s science at the second global stocktake”. But, at the same event, Prof Wang Yi argued that IPCC reports from AR1 to AR6 were “unequivocal that global warming is caused by human activity”. Wang is a professor at the Chinese Academy of Science and a lead advisor to the China delegation. This means the science is clear, “no matter” when AR7 is published, he added. China instead continued to position itself as a champion of the global south, both in negotiations and around the COP. In negotiations, it consistently aligned itself with developing country parties and groups, calling for solutions that would not “widen” the north-south gap. South-south cooperation was the subject of a high-level forum at which China’s vice-president Han Zheng spoke.  Han emphasised that “China will vigorously deepen south-south cooperation” and formally announced a new global south climate leadership training programme, according to a recording of the speech obtained by Carbon Brief. China also signed an agreement with Turkey to invest $15bn in developing 7GW of solar and wind power and 4GW of transmission capacity. This deal “could be seen as part of China’s own contribution to climate finance and accelerating the global energy transition”, even if it’s not “formally accounted”, said Kate Logan , director of the China Climate Hub and climate diplomacy at ASPI .  She added that, at a broader level, it shows that “China will continue exercising its influence through real-economy actions, even while its negotiators press for developed country accountability on finance”. Ocean Ocean advocates had several outcomes to celebrate at COP31 – and also some disappointment. Before the summit started, observers – and many parties – were hopeful of securing a strong outcome for the ocean, especially in light of the pre-COP meeting held in Pacific island states. A letter sent to the COP31 presidencies on 8 October – signed by the African group, the EU (along with its member states) and 24 other countries – called for the COP to “move sustainable ocean-based climate action from recognition to implementation”.  It said that such a move should be “backed by a clear political signal, a coherent plan for integration into the Paris Agreement ambition cycle and its existing means of implementation”. Analysis published by the World Resources Institute (WRI) on 15 November found that 95% of coastal and island countries included “at least one ocean-based action” in their national climate plans. However, it added that “more than 60% of ocean-commitment implementation depends on receiving some form of external support.” Two days later, on the “ocean, seas, nature and land use” thematic day, ministers from France and Brazil announced the launch of the “Blue NDC Challenge implementation task force” at a side event. They also welcomed 10 new countries as members of the Blue NDC Challenge – a group launched at the UN Ocean Conference in Nice, France, in June 2025 to “advance ocean-based climate action”. The same day, the COP31 presidency published the “Antalya Ocean and Seas Compact”, a high-level declaration that it said drew on feedback from parties and discussions at several events, including the UN General Assembly and the Pacific pre-COP.  The document highlights the impacts of climate change on the ocean, recognises the ocean’s importance in climate action and invites parties to strengthen their ocean work. The Antalya Ocean and Seas Compact. Source: COP31 presidency . Dr Tom Pickerell , global ocean programme director at WRI, told Carbon Brief: “It was more of a platform for collective ambition and political alignment, rather than any targets or finance coming through. We wouldn’t say no to it, but if we’d left just with that, it would have been a little bit sad.” Also on the ocean thematic day, the UK government announced a new £20m ($26.2m) funding commitment to marine protection. This comprised £11.8m ($15.5m) to the Global Fund for Coral Reefs and £9m ($11.8m) to the Global Ocean Accounts Partnership , which helps countries measure their progress towards sustainable ocean development. Towards the end of the summit, the “high-level climate-resilient coral reef commitment ” gained six new signatories: Colombia, Haiti, Jamaica, Niue, Samoa and Tuvalu. These governments “commit to protect[ing] reefs identified as having greater potential to persist through climate change”, according to a press release announcing the new countries. In the formal negotiation rooms, ocean groups were closely following discussions around the cover decision, hoping to see the ocean featured prominently there. (See: Cover decision .) Draft versions of the cover text “invite[d]” the development of a multi-year plan for future ocean and climate change dialogues, to be called the “Antalya ocean current”. It also asked for the results of these dialogues to be summarised, along with the “best available science” on the ocean, in a synthesis report that would act as an input to the second global stocktake. However, the cover decision was rejected during the closing plenary. Multiple parties used their interventions during the plenary to express their regret that the work that had been done on the ocean and climate change in the cover text would not move forward. Pickerell told Carbon Brief that while “it wasn’t a ‘blue COP’ after all”, there were still positive takeaways for the ocean. He said: “We’ve left with maybe nothing in writing, but I think we have left with genuine momentum. There does seem to be this shared ambition, to move beyond just the recognition of the ocean…There’s lots of opportunities to take this forward.” Deforestation COP31 was relatively quiet on forests, compared to last year’s summit in Belém.  The presidency held a forest leaders’ summit on 11 November, which was attended by the presidents of Brazil, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of the Congo, along with the prime ministers of the Netherlands and Norway. Much of the summit dwelled on the Brazil-led Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF). Delegates speculated that the summit would yield major new pledges for the fund.  However, only $88m from philanthropies emerged as new contributions at the event. Several countries reiterated past and recent pledges.  Aruna Chandrasekhar 12 November 2026, 14:19 GMT Forest funding pledges fall short Plenary Akdeniz was ringing with applause and chants of “Olé, olé, olé, olé, Lula, Lula!” as Brazil’s president approached the stage for the forest leaders’ summit yesterday evening. Lula – who told the crowd he had lost his voice –… Read more on CB Connect → At the summit, Jonas Gahr Støre, Norway’s prime minister, said:  “I am hopeful we can reach our collective goal of mobilising the initial $10bn dollars and to increase from there through next year and, with this, Norway is ready to contribute up to 20% of that total.” Norway’s “up to $3bn” loan to the fund is conditional upon it hitting the $10bn mark by the end of 2026. At the same time, Støre acknowledged that “it will take some time before payments reach the tropical forest countries and the key people who we want to support”. Speaking at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila on 15 November, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney pledged “an initial contribution of up to” $393m over four years to the TFFF. This means the fund has – so far – mobilised $8.2bn from different international partners, mostly as conditional loans. This leaves it $1.8bn short of a $10bn target for public and philanthropic capital for this year.  Political economist Max Alexander Matthey told Carbon Brief that less capital to invest and fewer risks taken will “lead to a fund that will not be able to deliver on the initially promised $4 per hectare” of protected forest in participating countries, even in a best-case scenario.  Although significant attention was paid to the fossil-fuel roadmap at COP31, far less focus was given to the deforestation one. Chris Dragisic , managing director for global policy at the National Audubon Society , told Carbon Brief that, nonetheless, there were “a couple of countries” that committed to producing national forest roadmaps. She added: “Many others have said, ‘we have a national strategy already’, and they’re looking at this really as an option to accelerate progress…What, for me, is the more interesting thing is that the roadmap recatalysed political will across the board for forests, where these had fallen a little bit off the political radar.” Other forest-related commitments made at COP31 included Bolivia and Indonesia joining the Forest & Climate Leaders’ Partnership and Brazil’s announcement that it is working on an Indigenous peoples’ roadmap. The COP31 presidency also launched the voluntary “Antalya action plan” on global wildfires, which it said would help a “community of countries” to “cooperate on prevention, early warning, landscape resilience and access to resources”. On the penultimate scheduled day of the summit, more than 100 organisations – including Indigenous groups, civil society and research institutions – signed an open letter calling on countries to take the work of the deforestation roadmap forward. It also called for an “international convening” on deforestation to occur in 2027. While an initial draft of the cover text “welcome[d]” the Brazil-led roadmap on deforestation , this was subsequently cut.   The final cover text – which was rejected during the closing plenary – did retain wording on deforestation agreed by countries in the global stocktake at COP28 in Dubai. The text had also included a recognition of nature-based solutions as “essential climate solutions”, although there is significant controversy over their use. Language on deforestation included in the final, rejected draft of the COP31 cover decision. Source: UNFCCC . Methane Cutting emissions of methane , the potent but short-lived greenhouse gas, appeared to have a renewed push at COP31.  This is partly due to the recent confirmation of an “ inevitable ” overshoot of the 1.5C global temperature target . (See: Cover text .)    Inger Andersen , chief of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), referred to this at a COP31 methane event :  “[Methane] leaves the atmosphere quickly, so cutting its emissions is our emergency brake to slow warming.” It is “one of the fastest, cheapest and most effective ways to check global heating in the near-term ”, said UN climate chief Simon Stiell at a 12 November event on non-CO2 greenhouse gases.  At this event, UNEP announced that its methane alert system has flagged five methane leaks across Canada, Iraq, Kazakhstan and Mexico since June 2026, allowing those countries to mitigate 125,000 tonnes of methane.  New private funding of $480m (£366m) was also pledged for action on methane and other “ super pollutants ”. Nine of the 159 countries who backed a 2021 Global Methane Pledge reaffirmed their aim to reduce methane emissions by at least 30% by 2030 at the event, which was co-hosted by Brazil, China and the UK. Belgium, Canada, France, Germany, Indonesia, Micronesia, Norway, the Netherlands and the UK endorsed this “ ministerial declaration ”, committing to accelerate action towards the 2030 goal.  Separately, Australia endorsed a COP30 statement on reducing methane emissions from fossil-fuel production.  At the beginning of the second week of COP31, Mia Mottley , the prime minister of Barbados, launched a petition calling to “reduc[e] methane emissions to near zero”.  On 11 November, the daily COP31 theme centred on “zero waste”. Emine Erdoğan , the Turkish first lady and chair of a UN advisory board on waste, launched a “ global zero waste alliance ”. This aims to “build a strong foundation for cooperation where countries learn from one another” on cutting waste, said Erdoğan at the launch event. Despite this focus, the Guardian reported before COP31 that Turkey has some of the “world’s worst landfill methane leaks”.  .cb-tweet img{ border: solid 1.25px #333333; border-radius: 5px; } @media (max-width:650px){ .cb-tweet{ width:100%; } } New climate science On day one of COP31, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) presented its State of the Climate 2026 update – the latest in its annual series of reports unpacking key climate indicators. The report finds that 2026 will be one of four warmest years on record. The global average surface temperature for January-September 2026 was about 1.47C above the pre-industrial average, says the report.  It adds that El Niño is forecast to continue into early 2027, further boosting global temperatures . At a press conference to launch the report on 9 November, WMO secretary general Prof Celeste Saulo warned that “this 2026-27 El Niño is off the charts ”, adding that “it is different from any El Niño that we have monitored”.  Saulo warned that “we are supercharging our weather” and that “the human and economic cost is unacceptably high”. She continued: “In 2026, millions of people were exposed to unbearable heat, leading to tens of thousands of excess deaths in Europe alone. India and Pakistan and large parts of Asia and North America suffered dangerous heatwaves. And, as we head into the southern hemisphere summer, we will see more. “The catastrophe in China and Nepal showed the dangers of high-mountain disasters for downstream communities.” She concluded with a call to improve early warning systems, stating that “sustained observations from every part of the world are more important than ever”. The following day, the Global Carbon Project released its latest annual assessment on CO2 emissions and carbon sinks. The 21st edition of the report, written by more than 100 experts from around the world, finds that the world is projected to emit 32.8bn tonnes of CO2 this year, marking a 0.4% decrease compared to 2025. According to the report, CO2 emissions from fossil fuels and cement are set to fall by around 0.4% in 2026, largely due to a 1.9% drop in emissions from oil and the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict and the closure of the strait of Hormuz. (This follows separate analysis by Carbon Brief earlier this year suggesting there would be a 0.5% fall due to the Hormuz crisis.) Meanwhile, it finds that emissions from coal are continuing to increase slightly. (For more on the findings, read Carbon Brief’s detailed write-up of the report.) A subset of the report’s authors also published a study in Nature Climate Change on 10 November, stating that “acceleration in clean technology deployment is needed to guarantee emissions peak and subsequent decline”.  Another Nature Climate Change paper , published on the opening day of COP31, finds that regions worldwide may have already experienced around 90-94% of the warming expected when the global average reaches 1.5C above pre-industrial levels.  Food and water A number of initiatives relating to food and water were launched during COP31. “Food security” – including transforming agriculture and focusing on water and drought – was one of the priority themes in the COP31 presidency’s “ action agenda ”. (See: Action agenda .) Despite this, only a few prominent announcements arrived compared to previous years.  On 9 November, when the daily COP theme centred on food, agriculture and health, thinktank Clim-Eat launched a report on the reform of agricultural subsidies. This noted that governments spend approximately $840bn (£638bn) on support and subsidies for agriculture, a sector which majorly contributes to climate change and environmental degradation .  The report outlined ways to move these subsidies towards payments supporting soil health, public infrastructure and increasing farm incomes in a more targeted way.  On 10 November, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) launched a platform aimed at helping countries boost alignment in managing food security, water and climate action, called the “ turquoise nexus initiative “.  Led by Turkey, it will exist within the FAO’s “ food and agriculture for sustainable transformation ” (FAST) partnership, which was launched at COP27 in 2022.  This is designed to boost climate finance for the transformation of food systems, while also supporting efforts on adaptation and other issues.  İbrahim Yumaklı, Turkey’s agriculture minister, said the “turquoise” platform would be used to strengthen existing initiatives, rather than create new ones.  İbrahim Yumaklı, Turkish minister of agriculture, at the launch of the turquoise nexus initiative in Antalya, Turkey on 10 November. Credit: Earth Negotiations Bulletin On 11 November, Ethiopia joined a group of eight other nations in the Alliance of Champions for Food Systems Transformation (ACF), a coalition launched at COP28 in 2023.  This sent a “powerful signal that food systems belong at the heart of climate action”, given that Ethiopia is due to host COP32 next year, said Emma Williams , the head of the ACF secretariat, in a statement . NDCs On 27 October, the UNFCCC released its annual report on nationally determined contributions (NDCs). These documents outline countries’ ambitions, as agreed under the Paris Agreement, to limit greenhouse gas emissions up to 2035. Based on analysis of the latest NDCs, the report says emissions are due to decrease by around 9% by 2035, compared to 2019 levels, if all pledges are implemented – a drop from the 12% reduction estimated in last year’s report . This leaves countries “substantially off track” to limit global temperatures to 1.5C, the report says. A small number of countries announced new NDCs around the time of COP31. Argentina, Botswana, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Egypt, Guatemala, North Macedonia, Palestine and Tajikistan all submitted new pledges in November. Libya also submitted its first-ever NDC, committing to reducing its carbon emissions per unit of its gross domestic product (GDP) by 28% by 2035. Protests and access  Nearly 10,000 people marched through the streets of Antalya on Saturday 14 November, protesting climate change, genocide in Gaza and human-rights abuses in Turkey. “2.8? Unacceptable”Thousands of climate protesters are out on the streets of Antalya right now 🌎 — Daisy Dunne (@daisydunne.carbonbrief.org) 2026-11-14T12:04:26.419Z The middle Saturday of COP is the summit’s traditional “protest day”.  Le Monde reported that Antalya’s protest “stood out for its scale in a country where the space for protest, both environmental and political, is narrow”. Elsewhere at the summit, Swedish campaigner Greta Thunberg made her first appearance at a UN climate summit since COP26 in Glasgow in 2021. Speaking to a huddle of journalists on 12 November, she said: “The climate crisis is already here and now – and it is already a matter of life and death.  “The actions from those in power here are completely detached from reality. As we speak, we are losing priceless lives, ecosystems and species that we will never get back.” Here’s a video of Greta Thunberg speaking alongside global south activists at COP this morning. More from the speakers, including Mohammad Usrof, Sagar Dhakal, Rikki Dank and Celine Isimbi, on CB Connect: connect.carbonbrief.org/t/greta-thun… — Daisy Dunne (@daisydunne.carbonbrief.org) 2026-11-12T09:58:00.064Z She was joined by global-south campaigners, including Mohammed Usrof , a climate activist and researcher from Gaza, who called out countries that continue to supply fossil fuels to Israel, telling journalists: “Corporations continue to fuel not just genocide in Palestine, but the devastation of the world. [There is a] never-ending proliferation of fossil fuels that we are seeing the consequences all over the global majority world. “So, it’s extremely crucial here to recognise what is happening in this COP, the stakes that we are here for [and] the stakes that our lived realities essentially symbolise to these negotiations.” Other speakers alongside Thunberg included Sagar Dhakal , a young Nepalese politician, who said “there are not any words in the dictionary” to describe the catastrophic flash floods in his country earlier this year, in addition to First Nations activist Rikki Dank and Rwanda-DRC activist Celine Isimbi . COP31 was plagued with logistical problems – particularly during the summit’s opening days – forcing delegates to spend hours navigating traffic and queues just to access the venue. The delays sparked serious access concerns, with the ECO newsletter – a daily bulletin put together by campaigners – writing on 11 November: “Participation is not a courtesy the presidency gives out when it’s convenient. It is written into the system. Under Article 4.1(i) of the convention, parties committed to encourage ‘the widest participation’ in this process, including by non-governmental organisations. Article 12 of the Paris Agreement calls for public participation and public access to information. Nobody added a footnote saying ‘subject to traffic conditions’.” During the first part of the final plenary on 20 November, a protester – who was wearing a shirt that said “you are killing the future” – was ejected after standing on a chair with a red noose around their neck. Road to COP32 and beyond At COP30 , it was agreed that COP32 in 2027 will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Under the UN’s regional rotational system for hosting COP, the country will be representing the African region . It will be the first-ever COP hosted by one of the least-developed countries . Ethiopia’s prime minister Abiy Ahmed addressed the world leaders’ summit at COP31, touting his country’s fossil fuel-free electricity grid and pledging to make finance for developing countries a central part of COP32. He told other leaders:  “Dependable finance requires cooperation, even as competition between countries grows. Yet, we discuss climate in one room, development in another, trade and finance in two more. Many of us see it in all four. In each of those rooms we should ask how we will finance the future that we have agreed to build.” (There have been some concerns that conflict in the country might affect its ability to host.) During the first week of COP31, China ruled out hosting COP33 in 2028, which is due to be held in Asia. (In August, Bloomberg reported that the world’s largest emitter was considering hosting the conference.) India had withdrawn a bid to host COP33 in April. Countries that are considering making a bid to host COP33 include Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand, according to the Guardian . In the table below, Carbon Brief has compiled key meetings and milestones leading up to COP32 in Ethiopia. 11-22 January Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction COP1 , New York May Second transitioning away from fossil fuels pre-conference , Dublin, Ireland 7-17 June Bonn climate talks , Germany 19-27 June London climate action week July Second transitioning away from fossil fuels conference , Tuvalu 8-22 September UN general assembly , New York 19-26 September New York climate week 8-19 November COP32 , Addis Ababa, Ethiopia Edited by Dr Simon Evans, Leo Hickman and Molly Lempriere. content:
一年中的大部分时间里，莱特纳平原都没有什么可以为当地人或游客提供的东西。这是布拉格斯巴达足球场对面的一大片毫无特色的土地。表面交替出现灰尘和泥土；有一个巴士停车场，有时还有马戏团。但莱特纳偶尔会举办一些可以让捷克政坛发生倾斜的活动。有时有一点。有时很多。 1989 年 11 月 25 日星期六，大约 75 万人聚集在一起，要求结束捷克斯洛伐克的共产主义政权。第二天，许多人返回，并于 11 月 29 日星期三，议会废除了共产党在社会中的领导地位。这次不会再发生类似的事情，但 11 月 15 日星期日，莱特纳岛上大约有 40 万人参加了自天鹅绒革命以来布拉格最大规模的示威活动。从媒体平台俯瞰旗帜和面孔的海洋时，它看起来很大。数万人聚集在那里抗议政府计划取消每月 10 美元的许可费，该许可费为该国两家公共广播公司捷克电视台和捷克广播电台提供资金。这似乎不是一个令人愤慨的提议，但对许多捷克人来说，这加深了他们对亿万富翁总理安德烈·巴比什及其民粹主义联盟的不信任。这位总理多年来一直在法庭上与欧盟补贴欺诈指控作斗争，他不喜欢公共广播。

For much of the year, Letná Plain has nothing to offer either locals or tourists.  It’s a large, featureless patch of land opposite the Sparta Prague football stadium. The surface alternates between dust and mud; there’s a car park for buses, and sometimes a circus. But every so often, Letná hosts an event that can tilt the world of Czech politics on its axis. Sometimes a little. Sometimes a lot.  On Saturday, November 25, 1989, around 750,000 people gathered to demand the end of Czechoslovakia’s communist regime. The following day, many returned, and on Wednesday, November 29, parliament abolished the Communist Party’s leading role in society. Nothing like that is going to happen this time around, but on Sunday, November 15, there were perhaps 400,000 people on Letná for the largest demonstration in Prague since the Velvet Revolution. It looked huge when viewed from a media platform overlooking an ocean of flags and faces.   The people who had gathered in the tens of thousands were there to protest against government plans to scrap the $10 monthly license fee which funds the nation’s two public broadcasters, Czech TV and Czech Radio. This may not seem an outrageous proposal, but to many Czechs it deepens their distrust of their billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babiš and his populist coalition.   The premier, who has spent years in court fighting EU subsidy fraud allegations , is no fan of public broadcasting.  Get the Latest Sign up to receive regular emails and stay informed about CEPA's work. In 2017, Babiš, who was then finance minister, described Czech TV’s investigative reporters as “a corrupt rabble making reports to order.” In 2024, he said public broadcasters were part of the then governing coalition’s “media division.”  But it is his coalition ally, the far-right SPD party, that has spearheaded the campaign to scrap the license fees and replace them with direct state funding. The fear is that state funds will come with strings pulled by politicians. Tokyo-born businessman Tomio Okamura, the SPD chairman and now parliament’s speaker, has said he would vote for a bill to abolish the broadcasters altogether if someone submitted one.  The third coalition partner is the MAGA-friendly Motorists for Themselves party, which was against scrapping the fees but is now in favor. One Motorist MP said public broadcasting had been turned into a totem by one half of Czech society, which was giving the other half the finger.  What is clear is that the government has not covered itself in glory. After months of vague and occasionally rancorous debate, and just days after all three coalition parties did poorly in Senate and local elections, the first reading of the bill was rushed through parliament in the middle of the night, with a vote scheduled for 4:36 am on Saturday, October 24. The bill envisages a cut in funding of around 15%, reversing an increase introduced by the previous government. Babiš is also floating alternative funding mechanisms, including voluntary contributions, and insists the government will not interfere in editorial decisions.  But there is a glaring contradiction. His government’s own impact assessment identifies the license fee as the funding mechanism that carries the smallest risk to the broadcasters’ independence. Direct state funding, it says, carries the greatest risk.  There has been much talk of “the Nordic model,” without acknowledging that there is no single Nordic model. Finland and Sweden, for example, have dedicated levies collected through the tax system, but Babiš has ruled out a new tax.  Observers are more worried about “the Slovak model.” There, the license fee was abolished in 2023 with a solemn promise to ringfence funding for Slovak Radio and TV and preserve its independence.  The following year, the broadcaster was dissolved by Robert Fico’s populist nationalist government and replaced. Critics say its successor is now toeing the government line. Babiš said he would not be deterred by mass demonstrations, though there was a tiny wobble from Culture Minister Oto Klempíř, who said after talks with Michael McGrath, the European Commissioner for Democracy and Justice, that he wanted to delay further debate on the bill until parliament had begun discussing legislation to implement the European Media Freedom Act.  The 72-year-old prime minister is in a tough spot. He seems tired and barely invested in the issue while his far-right coalition partner insists the fee has to go. Babiš is known to dislike big demonstrations, and the opposition senses an opportunity.  Following Klempíř’s suggestion to kick the issue into the long grass would be a logical course of action for the prime minister, but it may not be one that’s open to him.  Rob Cameron is a Prague-based journalist and broadcaster, and author of https://www.basedinbohemia.com/ where he writes about Central Europe through reporting, analysis and long-form storytelling. title: Choreographing a comeback: What Russia’s Africa policy means for Europe
zh_title: 精心策划东山再起：俄罗斯的非洲政策对欧洲意味着什么
summary: 2026 年 10 月 29 日星期四，领导人在莫斯科举行的俄罗斯-非洲峰会期间合影留念。（Anastasia Barashkova//美联社泳池照片）|图片联盟/Anastasia Barashkova/Pool 路透社来自美联社 |阿纳斯塔西娅·巴拉什科娃 (Anastasia Barashkova) 十月下旬，非洲领导人抵达莫斯科，参加第三次俄罗斯-非洲峰会以及看似无休无止的外交会议。传达的信息很明确：俄罗斯希望恢复与非洲的接触。克里姆林宫试图将俄罗斯描绘成一个重返非洲大陆的全球大国，继承了苏联支持非洲反殖民主义的遗产。
content:
2026 年 10 月 29 日星期四，领导人在莫斯科举行的俄罗斯-非洲峰会期间合影留念。（Anastasia Barashkova//美联社泳池照片）|图片联盟/Anastasia Barashkova/Pool 路透社来自美联社 |阿纳斯塔西娅·巴拉什科娃 (Anastasia Barashkova) 十月下旬，非洲领导人抵达莫斯科，参加第三次俄罗斯-非洲峰会以及看似无休无止的外交会议。传达的信息很明确：俄罗斯希望恢复与非洲的接触。克里姆林宫试图将俄罗斯描绘成一个重返非洲大陆的全球大国，继承了苏联支持非洲反殖民运动的遗产。在 11 月 19 日与习近平和唐纳德·特朗普会面之前，弗拉基米尔·普京还利用这次峰会推进了另一个地缘政治野心：让俄罗斯拥有与苏联曾经享有的相同的全球地位。普京正在寻找一个“新雅尔塔”，在这个新雅尔塔中，他可以以斯大林的角色与另外两个大国就势力范围进行讨价还价。俄罗斯接待非洲领导人，普京在最近的公开露面中看似不经意地提及苏联在国际关系中的作用，以及他的大规模宣传工作，都反映出总统试图将自己描绘成一位有权重新绘制世界政治版图的政治家。然而，尽管莫斯科声称自己具有独特性，但“非洲+1”峰会却是司空见惯的。
欧洲各国政府以及亚洲和中东地区的其他大国经常召开类似的集会来讨好非洲大陆。为了加强其在非洲的地位，欧洲人应该更加直言不讳地表达自己的利益，并为非洲国家提供俄罗斯以外的替代方案。莫斯科扩大其非洲官僚机构 2023 年举行的第二次俄罗斯-非洲峰会因给非洲带来的好处甚少而受到批评。普京的回应是责成众多俄罗斯政府机构和国家支持的行动者与非洲建立更牢固的关系。到 2026 年，这些努力除其他外，已召开了两次部长级会议，旨在加强政府机构之间的联系；在外交部设立新的非洲伙伴关系司；以及统一俄罗斯党的“为了民族自由！”运动和议会倡议将俄罗斯和非洲政党纳入更广泛的反殖民网络。克里姆林宫还举办青年聚会和媒体论坛，以宣传俄罗斯对全球秩序的看法。这些举措与俄罗斯在非洲的军事存在并存，后者仍然是俄罗斯在非洲大陆最重要的影响力来源。然而，乌克兰战争暴露了莫斯科经济和金融资源的局限性。尽管非洲国家正在根据国家发展目标实现伙伴关系多元化，但普京未能实现他在 2019 年设定的五年内与非洲贸易额翻番至 400 亿美元左右的目标。
他现在的目标是到 2030 年达到 500 亿美元。到 2025 年，俄罗斯与非洲的货物贸易总额将达到 270 亿美元，大致相当于其与哈萨克斯坦的贸易额，而欧盟与非洲的货物贸易额则达到 3560 亿欧元。而且，俄罗斯占非洲外国直接投资存量的不到1%，远远落后于中国、美国和欧盟。农业提供了更多有形收益。 2026年上半年，俄罗斯对非洲的农产品出口额达到29亿美元，比2025年同期增长35%。然而，俄罗斯在乌克兰的战争正在扰乱乌克兰的粮食出口。这与寻求可靠供应返回的非洲政府产生了摩擦

Leaders pose for a family photo during the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. (Anastasia Barashkova//Pool Photo via AP) | picture alliance / Anastasia Barashkova/Pool Reuters via AP | Anastasia Barashkova In late October, African leaders arrived in Moscow for the third Russia-Africa summit and a seemingly endless procession of diplomatic meetings. The message was clear: Russia wants to renew its engagement with Africa. The Kremlin seeks to portray Russia as a global power returning to the African continent, carrying the Soviet legacy of support for Africa’s anti-colonial movements. Vladimir Putin also used the summit to advance another geopolitical ambition ahead of the November 19th meeting with Xi Jinping and Donald Trump: for Russia to have the same global standing once enjoyed by the Soviet Union. Putin is searching for a “new Yalta” in which he, in Stalin’s role, can bargain with two other great powers over spheres of influence. Russia’s hosting of African leaders and Putin’s seemingly offhand references to the Soviet Union’s role in international relations during recent public appearances, as well as his massive publicity efforts , reflect the president’s attempt to portray himself as a statesman with the authority to redraw the world’s political map. For all Moscow’s claims of uniqueness , however, “Africa+1” summits are commonplace. European governments and other powers across Asia and the Middle East often convene similar gatherings to court the continent. To strengthen their standing in Africa, Europeans should be more vocal about their interests and offer African countries an alternative to Russia. Moscow expands its Africa bureaucracy The second Russia-Africa summit in 2023 drew criticism for delivering little benefit to Africa. Putin responded by tasking numerous Russian government agencies and state-backed actors to build stronger ties with Africa. By 2026 these efforts had amounted, among other things, to two ministerial conferences that aimed to strengthen ties between government agencies; the establishment of a new Department for Partnership with Africa in the foreign ministry; and United Russia’s “ For the Freedom of Nations!” movement and parliamentary initiatives to bring Russian and African parties into a wider anti-colonial network. The Kremlin also hosted youth gatherings and media forums to promote Russia’s view of the global order . These initiatives sit alongside Russia’s military presence in Africa, which remains its most consequential source of influence on the continent. However, the war in Ukraine has exposed the limits of Moscow’s economic and financial resources. While African countries are diversifying their partnerships based on national development objectives, Putin missed the target he set in 2019 to double trade with Africa to around $40bn in five years. He is now aiming for $50bn by 2030. Russia’s goods trade with Africa totalled $27bn in 2025, roughly matching its trade with Kazakhstan , while EU-Africa goods trade reached €356bn . Moreover, Russia accounts for less than 1% of Africa’s inward foreign direct investment stock, far behind China, the US and the EU . Agriculture offers more tangible gains. Russian agricultural exports to Africa reached $2.9bn in the first half of 2026, up 35% in value on the same period in 2025. However, Russia’s war in Ukraine is disrupting Ukrainian grain exports. This creates friction with African governments seeking the return of reliable supplies via the Black Sea. From trade to sovereignty Moscow has limited prospects of competing economically on the African continent. It is therefore increasingly framing partnerships with African countries ideologically while simultaneously pursuing more pragmatic cooperation in selected sectors, such as technology and agriculture. Putin’s speeches, final declarations and business programmes at the 2019, 2023 and 2026 Russia-Africa summits demonstrate this attempt. Putin’s references to military security and terrorism fell even more sharply in his speeches and almost halved in the final declarations. By 2026, references to sovereignty had gained prominence in both programmes and declarations, highlighting the core of Russia’s Africa strategy and tapping into existing anti- French and European sentiment , especially in West Africa. Putin is also placing greater emphasis on colonialism and multipolarity, grounding Russia’s claim to relevance in its vision of a multipolar world , of which the Kremlin is a champion. Russia is also drawing institutions such as universities and media organisations into its Africa policy, tasking them with facilitating cultural cooperation between Russia and Africa. Such organisations can form part of Russia’s wider disinformation campaigns. Between 2019 and 2026, Putin’s speeches nearly doubled their references to education and the Russian language, while the business programmes used them almost twice as often. The use of information-related terms, such as “media” and “informational agenda”, also more than doubled, largely through new media-forum sessions bringing together Russian and African journalists and media executives as a separate part of the third summit. Russia’s more selective and pragmatic agenda also includes energy, which regained prominence in the programmes and declarations between 2023 and 2026, drawing on Russia’s expertise in nuclear power . And, as part of Russia’s drive for pragmatic cooperation, the country also pursues seemingly uncontroversial themes such as its 2026 declaration on civilian AI . However, this offers African partners little immediate help. Many have more pressing industrial and economic needs. Pendulum partnership African governments choose partners pragmatically, based on their ability to deliver socio-economic growth, industrialisation and job creation Moscow’s bureaucratic expansion and stronger ideological approach are struggling to resonate with its potential partners in Africa. African governments choose partners pragmatically, based on their ability to deliver socio-economic growth, industrialisation and job creation. Even so, most of Moscow’s core partnerships in Africa continue to rest on security cooperation. For example, Russia has deployed forces in Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, and in the Central African Republic (CAR), Libya and Equatorial Guinea. It has also formalised defence cooperation with Togo and continues to pursue a military base in Sudan. The share of African speakers from these eight states at the three Russia-Africa summits rose from 5% in 2019 to 23% in 2026. Speakers from Russia’s BRICS+ partners, Egypt and Ethiopia, brought this up to 30% in 2026. Elsewhere, some African countries’ ties with Moscow fluctuate depending on changes of government and their renewed attempts to diversify partnerships. Ghana’s president John Mahama led his country’s 2026 summit delegation, which saw six Ghanaian speakers in the business programme. Russia and Ghana also reached an agreement on bauxite mining and alumina refining, and Russia has committed to help develop Ghana’s first nuclear power plant. Yet, despite Mahama’s ties to Russia (he studied in the Soviet Union), the speech data show that Ghana retains a pragmatic approach. Mahama’s renewed engagement with Russia perhaps reflects a search for partnerships that best serve Ghana’s national interests. Putin used ideological vocabulary more than twice as often in 2026 as in 2019, while his use of economic terms remained largely static. Among Moscow’s security partners, ideological language held roughly steady between 2023 and 2026, while references to trade, energy and investment doubled. Egypt’s emphasis changed little. President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi used ideological terms as often as Putin in 2019, but by 2026 Putin used them 75% more often than Sisi. African leaders outside the core group of eight security partners plus Egypt and Ethiopia used ideological terms 25% less frequently between 2023 and 2026, while the use of pragmatic vocabulary rose by more than a third. Some countries are scaling back their cooperation with Russia amid limited economic returns and tensions over the war in Ukraine. For example, in 2026, South Africa sent its foreign ministry’s director-general and Nigeria a junior foreign minister , replacing the presidents who attended in 2019. Their business programme speaker counts fell from 14 to five and from seven to three, respectively. An opening for Europe Insights from confidential conversations between ECFR’s Africa programme and African policymakers suggest that the continent’s governments and leaders appreciate a more pragmatic approach from European partners. This involves Europeans acknowledging the legacy of European colonialism in Africa, but also realising that in a fragmented global order Africa has options to choose from. Europe would benefit from identifying where Russian political actors are working at cross-purposes and leveraging this fragmentation in diplomatic negotiations with African partners. For example, the former Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin welcomed the Niger coup in 2023, while Russia’s foreign ministry backed ECOWAS in restoring constitutional order. In the CAR, his son Pavel Prigozhin has held on to Wagner’s operations despite the Russian defence ministry’s efforts to absorb them. As Moscow gives its bureaucratic players a bigger role in Africa, such tensions are likely to grow. The Russia-Africa Action Plan for 2027-2029 contains 236 measures, including joint drone, fertiliser and vaccine production, and cooperation between the African Union and the Russia-led Collective Security Treaty Organisation. But these priorities, and Russia’s bilateral agreements with African countries, can undermine one another: Rosatom requires deep cooperation with Accra to develop the planned nuclear power plant in Ghana, for example, but Russia’s coercive recruitment of Ghanaians for its war against Ukraine risks eroding bilateral trust. Even Mahama, who praised Moscow’s support for Africa’s anti-colonial struggles, has challenged Putin over the practice . Where Moscow’s competing interests undermine its summit promises, Europe can build trust by backing projects that African partners themselves prioritise. An example is the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), for which the EU provided technical and financial support. Despite facing some difficulties, the AfCFTA highlights where European and African strategic interests align—and where Europeans can help Africans reach their objectives, without setting the terms. Europeans also need to understand that, for African partners, pursuing a narrative in which Europe “counters” other actors such as Russia may not land well. Although Africa has considerable growth and market potential, the continent does not want to be approached as an international bargaining field. European governments should instead sharpen their own offer and advance investments in areas such as education and training, technology and engineering. Forums such as the AU-EU Senior Officials Meeting in Addis Ababa are essential for Europe to stay aligned with African priorities, while the participation of high-level European leaders, such as German president Frank-Walter Steinmeier at the upcoming German-African Business Summit in Ghana, signals how seriously they take cooperation. * African partners are not going to wait for European countries to take more responsibility in their approach to economic and trade negotiations. Europeans must ground any partnerships with African countries in reliability—a quality that Russian cooperation has yet to achieve. Both Europe and Africa share a strong belief in multilateralism, political dialogue and collective action. This dialogue, if transformed into a pragmatic, well-coordinated approach , would set Europeans apart from the transactional and extractive approaches of other global players. Source

summary: 三边会谈 + 气候呼吁 + 间谍事件 Linda_Heyer Thu, 11/19/2026 - 14:46 picture league / Win McNamee/Pool Getty Images AsiaPac via AP Download (pdf - 720.16 KB) MERICS Briefs MERICS China Essentials Nov 19, 2026 11 分钟阅读 三边会谈 + 气候呼吁 + 间谍事件 头条新闻 普京习近平按自己的意愿主持峰会，特朗普受到关注，特朗普走上红地毯 美中俄深圳峰会对俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京来说是一次外交胜利，但习近平成为更大的赢家，成功主持了一场可能给峰会蒙上阴影的会议。

三边会谈 + 气候呼吁 + 间谍事件 Linda_Heyer Thu, 11/19/2026 - 14:46 picture league / Win McNamee/Pool Getty Images AsiaPac via AP Download (pdf - 720.16 KB) MERICS Briefs MERICS China Essentials Nov 19, 2026 11 分钟阅读 三边会谈 + 气候呼吁 + 间谍事件 头条新闻 普京习近平按自己的方式主持峰会，特朗普成为众人瞩目的焦点 美中俄深圳峰会对俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京来说是一次外交胜利，但习近平成为了更大的赢家，他成功主持了一场可能让中国在深圳举办的亚太经合组织峰会黯然失色的会议。对于因俄罗斯近五年的侵略乌克兰战争而被西方孤立的普京来说，这次会议提供了一个轻松的机会来展现一位在国际外交最高层仍然受欢迎的领导人的形象。对习近平来说，中国对两位不可预测的客人的精心舞台管理得到了回报，峰会既没有像莫斯科所希望的那样就乌克兰问题达成“雅尔塔式”协议，也没有像美国总统唐纳德·特朗普所建议的那样让北京参与削减核武器谈判。
根据俄罗斯政府会后发布的联合声明，三位领导人确实同意“就减少核风险和防止核扩散进行对话”，但这不应损害北京的既定立场，即美国和俄罗斯必须在中国加入任何谈判之前大幅削减其更庞大的核武库。习近平、普京和特朗普还承诺改革联合国，并同意增加石油产量。也许对维护基于规则的国际秩序的西方国家来说最痛苦的是，该声明还表示，国家官员的豁免权是“根本性的”，国际刑事法院不得滥用其权力，该法院于 2023 年对普京发出了逮捕令。后一点将加剧欧洲的担忧，即美国总统在几个问题上与北京和莫斯科更加一致。但乌克兰的未来并未出现在官方结论中，这一事实使欧洲免于陷入更糟糕的境地。在莫斯科本身提高了对三边会议的期望后，普京似乎急于挽回乌克兰问题上缺乏进展的面子，并强调他已与习近平和特朗普分别讨论了这场战争。深圳的情况也没有暗示新的平等国家“G3”。在他们第 50 次面对面会面时，习近平再次称普京为“老朋友”，但没有像接待特朗普那样到机场接待他。
周四，习近平与特朗普的双边会晤和午餐会持续了很长时间，以至于普京不得不等待三边会议开始。“最重要的事情可能是三边会议最终举行了。习近平让普京得到了他所寻求的关注，同时为特朗普保留了红地毯待遇。通过这样做，他成功地举办了一场可能有风险的会议。”  伊娃·塞沃特 (Eva Seiwert)，MERICS 高级分析师 更多相关主题：为什么习近平可能有自己的理由避免美俄中峰会 – MERICS 伊娃·塞沃特 (Eva Seiwert) 的评论 媒体报道和来源：中国外交部（CN）：习近平会见俄罗斯总统普京 BBC：普京称俄罗斯、美国和中国对全球和平负有“共同责任” 路透社：直播：特朗普、习近平和普京举行了前所未有的三边会谈，重点关注乌克兰和核武器METRIX 1,042,590,000,000 这是中国2026年前10个月的贸易顺差，以美元计算。顺差突破1万亿美元三月

【原文 English Original】
Trilateral talks + Climate call-out + Espionage affair Linda_Heyer Thu, 11/19/2026 - 14:46 picture alliance / Win McNamee/Pool Getty Images AsiaPac via AP Download (pdf - 720.16 KB) MERICS Briefs MERICS China Essentials Nov 19, 2026 11 min read Trilateral talks + Climate call-out + Espionage affair Top story Putin gets the spotlight and Trump the red carpet as Xi runs the summit on his terms The US-China-Russia summit in Shenzhen was a diplomatic win for Russian President Vladimir Putin, but Xi Jinping emerged as the bigger winner, successfully managing a meeting that risked overshadowing the APEC summit China was hosting in the same city. For Putin, isolated by the West over Russia’s near five-year war of aggression against Ukraine, the meeting offered an easy opportunity to project the image of a leader still welcome at the highest level of international diplomacy. For Xi, China’s careful stage management of two unpredictable guests paid off, with the summit neither producing a “Yalta-style” agreement on Ukraine, as Moscow had favored, nor binding Beijing into nuclear-arms reduction talks, as US President Donald Trump had suggested.  The three leaders did agree to “engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing nuclear proliferation,” according to a joint statement released by the Russian government after the meeting, but this should not undermine Beijing’s established position that the US and Russia must make substantial reductions to their much larger arsenals before China joins any talks. Xi, Putin and Trump also committed to reforming the UN and agreed to increase oil production. Perhaps most painfully for Western countries that uphold the rules-based international order, the statement also said immunity for state officials was “fundamental” and that the International Criminal Court, which issued an arrest warrant for Putin in 2023, must not abuse its authority.  This latter point will reinforce European concerns that the US president is more aligned with Beijing and Moscow on several issues. But the fact that the future of Ukraine did not feature in the official conclusions spared Europe from worse. After Moscow itself had raised expectations for the trilateral, Putin appeared keen to save face over this lack of progress on Ukraine, stressing that he had discussed the war separately with Xi and Trump. The optics in Shenzhen also did not suggest a new “G3” of equal countries.  Xi once again called Putin his “old friend” at what was their 50th in-person meeting, but did not receive him at the airport as he did Trump. Xi’s bilateral meeting and lunch with Trump on Thursday ran so long that Putin was left waiting for the trilateral to begin.  "The most significant thing may have been that the trilateral took place at all. Xi gave Putin the spotlight he sought, while reserving the red-carpet treatment for Trump. In doing so, he successfully managed a potentially risky meeting.”  Eva Seiwert , Senior Analyst, MERICS More on the topic: Why Xi may have his own reasons to avert a US-Russia-China summit – MERICS Comment by Eva Seiwert Media coverage and sources: Chinese MFA (CN): 习近平会见俄罗斯总统普京   BBC: Putin says Russia, US, and China share 'joint responsibility' for global peace Reuters: Live: Trump, Xi and Putin hold unprecedented trilateral talks, with Ukraine and nuclear arms in focus METRIX 1,042,590,000,000 This is China’s trade surplus in the first ten months of 2026, in US dollars. The surplus broke the USD 1 trillion mark in October, one month earlier than in 2025, putting it on track to exceed last year’s record annual surplus of USD 1.2 trillion. A surge in foreign demand for electric vehicles, technology and AI-related products has seen exports outpace imports, even though the latter are themselves growing rapidly. Exports of computer parts were up 235 percent, those of semiconductors up 110.8 percent, and those of vehicles up 52.2 percent. (Source: General Administration of Customs )  GRAPHIC OF THE WEEK China exported 41 billion USD more goods to Germany between January and October 2026 than it imported from Europe’s largest economy – almost twice the trade surplus recorded in the same period last year. As the latest issue of the SOAPBOX newsletter on China reported, citing Chinese customs data, this increase accounted for nearly one third of the 69 billion USD increase in China’s trade surplus with the EU as a whole.  China’s surplus with Germany grew almost five times as fast as the 22 percent rise in its surplus with the rest of the EU, which reached USD 270 billion. This highlights Germany’s deep economic ties with China – and its resulting exposure to Chinese competition. As China sells more higher-value products abroad and increasingly sources components domestically, Germany faces a big double squeeze: rising imports and falling exports.  SOAPBOX is a weekly newsletter on EU-China trade relations compiled by Rafael Buendia Jimenez and Ilaria Perla. You can subscribe to the newsletter for free here . TOPICS China uses COP31 to showcase Europe’s dilemma on climate and trade China’s clear position at November’s UN climate change conference in Türkiye stood in stark contrast to Europe’s growing dilemma between its climate ambitions, defensive trade policy toward China and growing reluctance to commit more financing for developing countries dealing with global warming.  Before COP 31, Beijing had emphasized the need to discuss “old issues” of insufficient climate financing and “new challenges” of unilateralism and protectionism, which were harming “collective efforts to address climate change.” But in the end, it was the African Group that proposed putting climate-related trade and climate finance on the agenda. Their contention that Europe’s additional levy on carbon-intensive imports is unfair to Africa reinforced China's argument that European protectionism is undermining global climate cooperation. The EU objected to these proposals, which included the tripling of finance pledges, but did not block the Climate Finance Work Programme – a process to work out how developed countries meet their climate finance obligations to developing nations – as a separate agenda item.  The bloc is under pressure to fill a US-sized financing gap after US President Donald Trump’s withdrawal from the Paris agreement. Domestic opposition to a larger pledge is growing, as the EU is already one of the largest donors worldwide. Europe’s reluctance to step up, together with a lack of high-level European leaders at the conference stands in a stark contrast to China’s dominant cleantech offer to the world.  "The EU faces a dilemma: decarbonization is needed to fight climate change, but Chinese cleantech dominance and exports to the EU are a geoeconomics challenge. As the EU grapples with this, China’s proposed solution – more Chinese cleantech and more climate funding from developed countries – is gaining momentum.” Johanna Krebs , Analyst, MERICS Media coverage and sources : Xinhua (CN): 以“双碳”为牵引加快全面绿色转型——生态环境部介绍我国应对气候变化工作成效 Down to Earth: COP31 Adopts Climate Finance Work Programme Amid Tensions Over Adaptation Funding and Trade Carbon Brief: COP31: Agenda adopted! - Conversations / Policy   Carbon Brief: Interactive: Who wants what at the COP31 climate change summit Euronews: ‘More than just a photo opportunity’: Why are key EU leaders skipping the COP31 Leaders’ Summit? Nvidia’s espionage drama could backfire on Chinese AI ambitions Revelations that the chief executive of US chipmaker Nvidia, Jensen Huang, had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy could deal another blow to China’s AI industry, which is already grappling with an economic slowdown and Beijing’s push for labs to switch to less powerful domestic hardware such as chips designed by Huawei. The US government is openly split between advocates of continued commercial engagement and national-security hawks who want to cut off Chinese access to US AI technology. But pressure from lawmakers in Washington for tighter controls is mounting – and Congress could ultimately override any presidential veto of legislation covering foreign trade. China’s AI stocks, already caught in China’s broader market correction, have slumped again. Huang has not just been Nvidia’s guiding light since co-founding the company in 1993, but he also successfully lobbied US officials, including President Donald Trump, over the last two years to relax chip export controls. US lawmakers now want to crack down on smuggling networks that supply China with the most advanced US-designed AI chips and on schemes that give Chinese companies remote cloud access to powerful chips via data centers located in third countries. The Commerce Department will also soon require companies to obtain licenses for advanced semiconductor exports, re-exports and transfers to data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. Data centers anywhere in the world will need permission to service Chinese companies.  "China's AI future is deeply tied to policy decisions made in Washington, which the networks and choices of a few tech CEOs can shape in fundamental ways. Huang was one of the most influential advocates of maintaining the flow of US AI chips to China. But the espionage allegations will make that position much harder to defend – and leave China’s AI industry with even fewer options.” Rebecca Arcesati , Head of Program (Co-Lead) Science, Technology and Innovation, MERICS Media coverage and sources: The New York Times: The Fall of Jensen Huang Reuters: US to curb China's access to AI chips as Trump heads to Asia Bloomberg: Nvidia Stops Selling AI chips to China Despite US Approval Xi tightens his grip on local party committees – in good time for a fourth term Xi Jinping’s third term as General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) ends in the second half of 2027, but it looks like he is not going anywhere. The CCP’s Central Committee on November 7, 2026, issued revised regulations on the work of local party committees for the first time since 2015. The new rules are meant to improve decision-making by cadres in provinces, cities and counties to make sure central directives are implemented. Maintaining a strong chain of command from the center down to the local level is of paramount importance to the CCP’s ability to meet its goals – and to securing Xi’s position at the apex of the party, making a fourth term increasingly likely. Xi and the other then 22 members of the Politburo had announced the review of the regulation in March. They require officials to shoulder “political responsibility” for ensuring that the Central Committee’s policies are effectively implemented. Contradicting the leadership’s directives, engaging in local protectionism, pursuing prestige projects designed to demonstrate political achievements and improperly increasing local government hidden debt are expressly forbidden. Local party committee members are subject to “lifelong accountability” for rule violations and decision-making errors. Although permanent responsibility already applies to environmental and certain major administrative decisions, this is a significant extension of the mechanism. "The ideologies of Marx, Lenin and Mao have been removed from the regulations, while Xi’s status as ‘core leader’ has been codified. His latest instructions and speeches are now the first item on the agenda at local party meetings. Xi wants to put cadres’ feet to the fire and make sure they get the job done the way he wants it. He looks like a leader who expects to keep a close eye on them for a while yet.”  Alexander Davey , Analyst, MERICS Media coverage and sources: SCMP: Communist Party lays down the internal discipline law for local leader s Xinhua (CN): 《 中国共产党地方委员会工作条例 》 (Regulations on the Work of Local Committees of the Chinese Communist Party) Communist Party Member Network (CN): 《 中国共产党地方委员会工作条例 (2015) 》 (Archived version of the previous 2015 regulations) Lianhe Zaobao Singapore (CN): Revised work regulations of local party committees bans "vanity" projects and "prestige" projects China successfully targets rich to boost income-tax revenue China appears to be having considerable success in taxing its richer residents more. Revenues from personal income tax surged 90 percent in October 2026 from a year earlier, after tax authorities in July introduced rules requiring Chinese residents to pay tax on assets transferred into offshore trusts and on income generated by them. Taxpayers – mostly the country’s ultra-rich – had until late October to comply, effectively closing a loophole used to protect assets from the Chinese state. Tax revenue linked to offshore trusts reached CNY 160 billion in the first ten months of 2026, which suggests personal income-tax revenue from January to October 2026 is likely to have already exceeded the 2025 full-year total of CNY 1.62 trillion (about EUR 221 billion).  China’s overall tax revenue has been rising over the past year, spurred in particular by securities trading. But with China’s AI bubble deflating and share prices falling, the additional personal income tax revenue from offshore trusts is a welcome boost to state finances. Personal income tax accounts for only a portion of total tax revenue. At 9 percent, it carries less weight than value-added tax, which accounts for 39 percent of revenues, or corporate income tax, which accounts for 23 percent. But the increased flow of revenues from taxing offshore trust assets and income will provide additional fiscal room by offsetting declines in land-tax and consumption-tax revenue.  “The surge in personal income tax takings is the latest sign of China’s push to expand its tax base and strengthen public revenues. The recent focus on taxing offshore trusts, most of which are owned by high-net-worth individuals, also opens up other opportunities. It allows authorities to exercise greater oversight over capital outflows and potentially redistribute wealth more evenly.” Sophia Pradels , Analyst, MERICS Media coverage and sources: Xinhua (CN): 离岸信托收益征税平稳有序推进 (Offshore Trust Income Taxation Is Progressing Smoothly and Orderly) Yicai: China’s Personal Income Tax Haul Nearly Doubles in October on Offshore Trust Windfall Financial Times: China warns of ‘severe’ punishment for offshore trust tax evaders MERICS CHINA DIGEST China's economy falters as factory output, retail sales undershoot expectations (Reuters) Chinese retail sales grew just 0.4% year-on-year in October, down from 1.1% in September, while industrial production growth slowed to 4.8%.  (26/11/16) China's Singles Day sales rise 4.8% to USD 1.78 trillion; AI takes larger role (Reuters) China's Singles Day shopping generated CNY 1.78 trillion in revenues, but annual sales growth slowed to 4.8% from 14.2% in 2025 despite weeks of promotions. title: Alice Huang’s Shady Shanghai Ties to Business and Government
zh_title: 艾丽丝·黄与上海商界和政府的不正当关系
summary: 内容摘要：黄仁勋间谍丑闻核心人物、Megaspeed 前高管 Alice Huang 通过上海金融界建立了自己的商业网络。她与因财务不当行为而受到制裁的所谓丈夫康伟和后来涉嫌欺诈和贿赂的谷国平等人物有联系。报道称，美国情报部门认为她是中华人民共和国情报部门的合作伙伴。根据开源研究，目前尚不清楚 Alice Huang 在国家安全部 (MSS) 中的确切角色是什么
content:
内容摘要：黄仁勋间谍丑闻核心人物、Megaspeed 前高管 Alice Huang 通过上海金融界建立了自己的商业网络。她与因财务不当行为而受到制裁的所谓丈夫康伟和后来涉嫌欺诈和贿赂的谷国平等人物有联系。报道称，美国情报部门认为她是中华人民共和国情报部门的合作伙伴。根据开源研究，目前尚不清楚 Alice Huang 在国家安全部 (MSS) 中的确切角色是什么；然而，当她结识黄仁勋时，她的兴趣和事工的兴趣很可能是一致的。黄和康利用他们的游戏业务扩展到半导体和数据中心，并在此过程中成为 Nvidia 的客户。随后，黄仁勋接管了香港游戏公司第七大道在新加坡的国际子公司第七大道国际，并通过马来西亚子公司购买了英伟达芯片。美国当局怀疑这些芯片随后被转运到中国。皇康网络与中国地方政府建立了联系。持有顾国平旗下斐讯公司股份的上海松江区投资机构，在顾国平的犯罪活动导致斐讯公司倒闭后，将股份出售给其网络中的一家公司。
科技巨头英伟达 (Nvidia) 联合创始人兼首席执行官 (CEO) 黄仁勋 (Jensen Huang) 垮台的核心人物是一位名叫黄乐 (Huang Le) 的女性，又名 Alice Huang。媒体报道称，黄女士是英伟达在东南亚最大的客户之一、新加坡计算公司 Megaspeed 的前高管，她与黄仁勋有染。 Megaspeed 涉嫌将受美国出口管制限制的 Nvidia 芯片走私到中华人民共和国（PRC）。报道还称，美国情报部门认为黄女士已被中华人民共和国国家安全部 (MSS) 拉拢（《纽约时报》[NYT]，10 月 29 日；《华盛顿邮报》，11 月 15 日）。 [1] 北京很快否认了这些指控，但一些亲美人士认为中国的知识分子则更加持怀疑态度。他们认为当前的丑闻是特朗普政府内部以及特朗普与“深层政府”之间的内讧的结果（腾讯新闻；X/@Wuuesanren；X/@WoodenHarp，11月10日）。一位上海商人在接受采访时也表达了类似的观点，称黄女士的网络采用了复杂的、多层的公司结构来掩盖最终控制者是谁，并称这种策略是“上海滩从同治皇帝时候就玩的东西了”，指的是19世纪下半叶的早期现代化时期（作者访谈，11月10日）。他相信女士。
黄女士的目的只是将芯片走私到中国。黄出身于上海金融界，她与随后被判犯有金融犯罪的人物的关系表明，她的个人资料应该引起更多的危险信号。她的网络以一家投资公司上海和熙投资管理为中心，该公司是由她所谓的恋人、商人康伟创立的（英国《金融时报》，11 月 10 日）。该网络中的其他主要人物包括黄瑜，英国《金融时报》将其描述为黄女士的妹妹；顾国平

【原文 English Original】
Executive Summary: Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive at the heart of the Jensen Huang spy scandal, built her business network through the world of Shanghai finance. She is linked to figures such as Kang Wei, her alleged husband who has been sanctioned for financial misconduct, and Gu Guoping, who was later implicated in fraud and bribery. Reporting indicates that U.S. intelligence considers her a cooptee of People’s Republic of China (PRC) intelligence services. It remains unclear what Alice Huang’s exact role was for the Ministry of State Security (MSS) based on open-source research; however, it is likely that her interests and that of the ministry converged around the time when she became acquainted with Jensen Huang. Huang and Kang used their gaming business to expand into semiconductors and data centers, becoming an Nvidia customer in the process. Huang then took over Hong Kong-based gaming company 7Road’s international subsidiary based in Singapore, 7Road International, and purchased Nvidia chips through a Malaysian affiliate. U.S. authorities suspect the chips were then transshipped to the PRC. The Huang-Kang network cultivated ties with local governments in the PRC. The investment arm of Shanghai’s Songjiang District, which owned a stake in Gu Guoping’s Phicomm, sold the stake to a company in their network after Phicomm failed in the wake of Gu’s criminal activity. At the center of the downfall of Jensen Huang, the co-founder and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of technology giant Nvidia, is a woman identified as Huang Le (黄乐), also known as Alice Huang. Media reporting alleges that Ms. Huang, a former executive of one of Nvidia’s largest customers in Southeast Asia, the Singapore-based computing company Megaspeed, had an affair with Jensen Huang. Megaspeed has been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips covered by U.S. export control restrictions into the People’s Republic of China (PRC). Reports have also said that U.S. intelligence considered Ms. Huang to have been coopted by the PRC’s Ministry of State Security (MSS) ( New York Times [NYT] , October 29; Washington Post , November 15).  [1] Beijing has been quick to deny these allegations, but some pro-U.S. Chinese intellectuals are more skeptical. They view the current scandal as a consequence of infighting within the Trump administration and between Trump and the “deep state” ( Tencent News ; X/@Wuyuesanren ; X/@WoodenHarp , November 10). In an interview, a Shanghai businessman expressed a similar view, saying that Ms. Huang’s network used an elaborate, multilayered corporate structure to conceal who ultimately controlled it, calling this tactic “the sort of thing Shanghai has been doing since the time of the Tongzhi Emperor” (上海滩从同治皇帝时候就玩的东西了), referring to the period of early modernization in the second half of the 19th century (Author interview, November 10). He believed Ms. Huang’s purpose was simply to smuggle chips into the PRC. Ms. Huang emerged from the world of Shanghai finance, where her connections to figures who have subsequently been found guilty of financial crime suggest that her profile should have raised more red flags. Her network centered on an investment firm, Hexi Investment Management (上海和熙投资管理), which was founded by one her alleged romantic partners, the businessman Kang Wei (康伟) ( Financial Times , November 10). Other major figures in this network include Huang Yu (黄瑜), whom the Financial Times describes as Ms. Huang’s sister; and Gu Guoping (顾国平), the founder of communications company Phicomm (斐讯技术) ( Financial Times , November 10; Caixin , November 10).  [2] Ms. Huang co-founded Shanghai Yunxi (上海韵禧) in 2016, and Huang Yu took over the following year ( The Time Weekly , November 9). (Source: Author’s research) Gaming Served as Gateway to Data Centers For Ms. Huang, as for Nvidia, the gaming industry provided a route into the compute business. PRC game publishers often set up foreign entities to serve overseas markets, providing a legitimate reason to import graphics processors and expand data center capacity. Huang became involved with 7Road Holdings (第七大道), a Hong Kong-listed game developer, after it had acquired a portfolio of gaming businesses held by an entity wholly owned by her and registered in the British Virgin Islands ( Caizhongshe , November 11). A circular announcing the acquisition identified a company owned by Kang Wei, Ningbo Jingxuan (宁波镜瑄), as a “party acting in concert” (一致行动人) with Ms. Huang. It also listed among the portfolio’s operating entities in the PRC a company previously owned by a subsidiary of Century Huatong (世紀華通), another firm with ties to Kang and Huang ( Hong Kong Exchange , September 25, 2019).  [3] With Ms. Huang now behind the scenes, Yunxi expanded her business network into the semiconductor and data center industries through cooperation with 7Road starting in 2022. A 7Road subsidiary committed renminbi (RMB) 330 million ($49 million) to a limited partnership managed by Yunxi whose sole asset was a 5.29 percent stake in a Shanghai-based semiconductor wafer manufacturer ( Hong Kong Exchange , May 24, 2022). 7Road also expanded into the data center and cloud computing businesses in 2019, offering cloud services for gaming and the possibility of third-party data center services in a cooperation framework ( Hong Kong Exchange , December 30, 2019; Hong Kong Exchange , May 9, 2021). A 7Road subsidiary involved in Huang’s gaming portfolio later became a vehicle for 7Road’s cloud computing business, buying graphics processors and servers ( Hong Kong Exchange , September 25, 2019).  [4] In 2022, it raised RMB 150 million ($24 million at the time) through a sale-and-lease-back of equipment that included 9,800 graphics processors ( Hong Kong Exchange , March 15, 2022).
